This surah has 130 verses, though some say it has 127. It has several names. It is called **Surat al-Tawbah** (the Surah of Repentance), because it contains the repentance granted to the believers. It is called **al-Fadihah** (the Exposer), because verses kept coming down about the hypocrites, "among them… and among them," until it nearly left no one unmentioned. It is called **al-Bahuth** (the Investigator), because it searches out the secrets of the hypocrites. It is called **al-Muba'thirah** (the Scatterer), and *al-ba'thirah* means *al-bahth* (searching). It also has other names, such as **al-Muqashqishah** (the Purifier), because it purges one of hypocrisy, that is, it clears a person of it; **al-Mukhziyah** (the Disgracer), because it disgraced the hypocrites; **al-Mutheerah** (the Stirrer), because it stirs up their secrets; **al-Hafirah** (the Digger), because it digs out what they hide; **al-Munakkilah** (the Punisher), because of the punishment it inflicts on them; and **al-Mudamdimah** (the Crusher), because it crushes them.

It is a Madinan surah. Al-Qurtubi said this is agreed upon.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Bara'ah was revealed after the conquest of Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he said: "Surat al-Tawbah was revealed in Madinah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah something similar too.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Durays, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara' that he said: "The last verse to be revealed was ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalalah﴾ (al-Nisa: 176), and the last complete surah was Bara'ah."

The scholars differed over the reason the basmala (the formula "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful") was omitted from its beginning, and they gave several opinions.

The first, narrated from al-Mubarrad and others: it was the custom of the Arabs that when they had a covenant with a people and wished to break it, they would write to them a letter without a basmala at its head. When Bara'ah was revealed to annul the covenant that had existed between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the polytheists, the Prophet (ﷺ) sent it with 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who recited it to them without reciting the basmala, following the Arabs' customary practice.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I asked 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: Why do you not write 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful' at the start of Bara'ah? He said: Because 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful' is a safety assurance, and Bara'ah was revealed with the sword."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Nasa'i, and al-Hakim (who graded it sahih) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I said to 'Uthman ibn 'Affan: What led you to put al-Anfal, which is among the mathani (the surahs of under a hundred verses, recited repeatedly), and Bara'ah, which is among the mi'in (the surahs of about a hundred verses), together, and did not write a line of ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ between them, and placed them among the sab' al-tiwal (the Seven Long Surahs)? What led you to do that? 'Uthman said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would receive, in the course of time, surahs of considerable length, and when something was revealed to him he would call some of those who wrote for him and say: Place these verses in the surah in which such-and-such is mentioned. Al-Anfal was among the first things revealed at Madinah, and Bara'ah was among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed. Its story resembled al-Anfal's, so I thought it was part of it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away without making clear to us that it was part of it. For this reason I joined the two together, did not write a line of ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ between them, and placed them among the Seven Long Surahs."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Raja' that he said: "I asked al-Hasan about al-Anfal and Bara'ah: are they two surahs or one surah? He said: Two surahs."

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Hudhayfah that he said: "They call this surah Surat al-Tawbah, but it is the Surah of Punishment."

These same narrators also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said about this surah: "It is al-Fadihah; it kept on being revealed, 'among them… and among them,' until we thought that none of us would be left without being mentioned in it."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated something similar from 'Umar.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that a man said to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar: "Surat al-Tawbah." Ibn 'Umar said: "Which of its surahs is Surat al-Tawbah?" Then he said: "Did it not do to the people the deeds that it did? We used to call it only al-Muqashqishah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "They call it Surat al-Tawbah, but it is a surah of punishment."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Ishaq that he said: "Bara'ah was called al-Muba'thirah during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) and after him, because it uncovered the hidden secrets of people."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr that he said: "Bara'ah was called al-Munaqqirah, because it probed what was in the hearts of the polytheists."

Abu 'Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu 'Atiyyah al-Hamdani that he said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote: Learn Surat Bara'ah, and teach your women Surat al-Nur."

Among the opinions on the omission of the basmala is that the surah was equal to, or close to, Surat al-Baqarah in length, and that when its beginning dropped out, the basmala dropped out with it. This was narrated from Malik ibn Anas and Ibn 'Ajlan.

Also among the opinions on the omission of the basmala: when they wrote the Mushaf in the caliphate of 'Uthman, the Companions differed. Some of them said: Bara'ah and al-Anfal are one surah. Others said: they are two surahs. So a gap was left between them to satisfy the one who said they were two surahs, and the basmala was left out to satisfy the one who said they were one surah. Both groups were content. This was reported by Kharijah, Abu 'Ismah and others.

The view that makes them one surah is more apparent, because both deal with fighting, and both together are counted as the seventh of the Seven Long Surahs.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 3–4 (part 1 of 2):**

His words: ﴿A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger﴾. *Bara'a* (بَرِئْتُ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ أبْرَأُ بَراءَةً): "I disowned the thing, I disown it with *bara'a*, and I am *bari'* (بَرِيءٌ) of it," when you remove it from yourself and cut the cause between you and it. *Bara'atun* (بَراءَةٌ) is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "this is a disavowal." It may also be nominative as a subject, since it is an indefinite noun described by a qualifier, and its predicate is ﴿to those with whom you made a covenant﴾.

Isa ibn Umar read *bara'atan* (بَراءَةً) with the accusative, on the assumed meaning "hear a disavowal," or "adhere to a disavowal," because it carries the sense of an incitement (*al-ighra'*). The *min* (مِنَ) in His words ﴿from Allah﴾ indicates the starting point (*ibtida' al-ghaya*) and is attached to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier: "conveyed from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made a covenant."

Rawh and Zayd read *Rasulihi* (رَسُولِهِ) with the accusative. The rest read it with the nominative.

*Al-'ahd* (العَهْد) is a binding contract confirmed by oath.

The address in ﴿you made﴾ is to the Muslims. They had made covenants with the polytheists of Makkah and others, by permission from Allah and from the Messenger ﷺ. The meaning is an announcement to the Muslims that Allah and His Messenger have disowned that covenant because of the breach committed by the disbelievers. Thus renouncing their covenant became obligatory for the Muslim covenanters. The disavowal of Allah, glorified is He, means that He authorized the Muslims to renounce the covenant of the polytheists after they breached it. In this there is an obvious magnification of the matter of the disavowal, a strong emphasis on it, and an unmistakable recording against the polytheists of humiliation and disgrace.

His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾. This is a command from Him, glorified is He, to travel after the announcement of that disavowal. *Al-siyaha* (السِّياحَةُ) means travel. It is said: "So-and-so travelled in the land (sa'a fi al-ardi, ساحَ فُلانٌ في الأرْضِ), travels (yasihu) with travel (siyahatan), journeying (suyuhan), and wandering (sayahanan)." From it: "the water flowed over the land (sayaha al-ma')," and "the horses roamed (sayaha al-khayl)." From it is the saying of Tarafa ibn al-'Abd:

*"Had I feared this from you, you would not have reached me, until you see horses before me roaming."*

The meaning of the verse is that Allah, glorified is He, after permitting the renunciation of the covenant with the polytheists, allowed the polytheists to move about the land, go wherever they wished, and prepare for war during these four months. The command to travel is not meant as an obligation imposed on them.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq and others said: The polytheists were of two kinds. One kind had a covenant of less than four months, so it was given the full four months. The other had a covenant longer than that, so it was limited to four months so that it could consider its position; after that it was at war with Allah, His Messenger, and the believers, and would be killed wherever found. The beginning of this term was the Day of the Greater Hajj, and it ended at the tenth of Rabi' al-Akhir. As for one who had no covenant, his term was the expiry of the sacred months, which is fifty days: twenty days of Dhu al-Hijjah and the month of Muharram.

Al-Kalbi said: The four months were only for those who had a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of less than four months. As for one whose covenant was longer than that, it is the one about whom Allah commanded that his covenant be fulfilled, by His words: ﴿So fulfil their covenant to their term﴾ (At-Tawbah: 4). Ibn Jarir and others preferred this view. Later in the discussion, the narrations will clarify the meaning of the verse.

His words: ﴿And know that you cannot escape Allah﴾, meaning: know that this granting of respite is not due to incapacity, but for a purpose, so that whoever repents may repent. In this there is a kind of threat, as if it were said: do in this period everything you can of preparing instruments and tools, for you will not escape Allah, and He will disgrace you, that is, humiliate you in this world by killing and capture, and in the Hereafter by punishment. Placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun indicates that the cause of this disgrace is disbelief. It is also possible that the intended reference is the category of disbelievers, which would include the addressees by primary inclusion (*dukhulan awwaliyyan*).

His words: ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the Day of the Greater Hajj﴾. *Adhanun* (أذانٌ) is nominative either as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a subject whose predicate is what follows it, as explained for the nominative of *bara'atun*. This sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: His words "and a proclamation" are conjoined to his words "a disavowal."

It was objected that if this were so, the proclamation would be described by the first predicate, which is ﴿to those of the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾. This is not correct. Rather, the predicate is "to the people." *Al-adhan* here means *al-iadh*, which is notification, just as *al-aman* and *al-ata'* mean *al-iman* and *al-i'ta'*. The meaning of His words "to the people" is generality in this matter: it is a notification from Allah to all people, not specific to one group over another. So this sentence contains the information that notifying all people is obligatory, while the first sentence contains the information of disavowal addressed specifically to those in covenant. The Day of the Hajj is an adverbial complement of "and a proclamation." He described it as "greater" because the people gather on it, or because most of the rites of Hajj take place on it.

The scholars differed in determining the day mentioned in the verse. A group, including 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abi Awfa, al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, and Mujahid, held that it is the Day of Sacrifice (*yawm al-nahr*). Ibn Jarir preferred this view. Others, including Umar, Ibn Abbas, and Tawus, held that it is the Day of 'Arafah.

The first view is more preferred, because the Prophet ﷺ commanded the one he sent to convey this to the polytheists to deliver it to them on the Day of Sacrifice.

His words: ﴿that Allah is disowned of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾. It was read with *anna* (أنَّ) having a fatha, on the assumed meaning "that Allah is disowned of the polytheists," with the *ba'* (بِأنَّ) omitted for lightness. It was also read with a kasra, because the proclamation carries the sense of speech (*al-qawl*). The nominative of *Rasuluhu* (رَسُولُهُ) is either conjoined to the position of the noun of *inna* (اسْمِ أنَّ), or to the pronoun in *bari'* (بَرِيءٌ), or it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and the assumed meaning is "and His Messenger is disowned of them." Al-Hasan and others read *wa-Rasulahu* (وَرَسُولَهُ) with the accusative, conjoined to the form of the noun of *anna* (لَفْظِ اسْمِ أنَّ).

*Wa-Rasulihi* (وَرَسُولِهِ) was read with the genitive, on the basis that the *waw* is for an oath. This is reported from al-Hasan, but it is a very weak reading, since there is no sense in swearing by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ here, along with what is established of the prohibition against swearing by other than Allah. It was also said that it is genitive by *al-jiwar* (الجِوار), that is, by proximity to the preceding word.

His words: ﴿So if you repent﴾, meaning from disbelief. In it there is an *iltifat* (الالتفات), a shift from the third person (absence) to the second person (address). It was said that the benefit of this shift is an increase in threat. The pronoun in His words ﴿it is better for you﴾ refers to the repentance understood from "you repent," meaning it is better for you than what you are in of disbelief. ﴿And if you turn away﴾, meaning you refuse repentance and remain in disbelief, ﴿then know that you cannot escape Allah﴾, meaning you cannot elude Him. Rather, He will overtake you and requite you for your deeds.

His words: ﴿And give tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment﴾. This is mockery of them, and in it there is a threat that is not hidden.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made a covenant among the polytheists﴾: to the people of covenant, Khuza'ah, Mudlij, and whoever had a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, from Tabuk when he had finished with it and intended Hajj. Then he said: "Polytheists visit this House and circumambulate it naked, so I do not like to perform Hajj until that stops." So he sent Abu Bakr and Ali, and they went around among the people at Dhu al-Majaz and at their marketplaces where they used to trade, or throughout the whole season. They informed the people of the covenant that they would be safe for four months, which are the consecutive sacred months that run out: twenty days from the end of Dhu al-Hijjah to the tenth of Rabi' al-Akhir. After that there was no covenant for them, and he announced to all people war until they die.

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal reported in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, as did Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh, from Ali who said: "When ten verses of 'Bara'ah' were revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, he summoned Abu Bakr to recite them to the people of Makkah." Then he called me and said to me: "Overtake Abu Bakr, and wherever you meet him, take the document from him and recite it to the people of Makkah." So I caught up with him and took the document from him, and Abu Bakr returned and said: "O Messenger of Allah, has something been revealed concerning me?" He said: "No, but Jibril came to me and said: 'None will convey on your behalf except you or a man from you.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh reported a similar account from the hadith of Anas.

Ibn Mardawayh also reported a similar account from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Hurayrah who said: "I was with Ali when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent him to the people of Makkah" with "Bara'ah," and we would proclaim that no one enters Paradise except a believer, no one circumambulates the House naked, and whoever has a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his term and limit is four months. When the four months have passed, Allah is disowned of the polytheists and so is His Messenger, and no polytheist shall perform Hajj to this House after this year.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Abu Hurayrah who said: "Abu Bakr sent me in that Hajj, among the callers whom he sent on the Day of Sacrifice to proclaim at Mina: that no polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, and no one shall circumambulate the House naked. Then the Prophet ﷺ rode behind Ali ibn Abi Talib and commanded him to proclaim 'Bara'ah,' so Ali proclaimed on the Day of Sacrifice with 'Bara'ah': that no polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, and no one shall circumambulate the House naked."

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn Abbas: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Abu Bakr and commanded him to proclaim these words. Then he sent Ali after him and commanded him to proclaim these words. They set out and performed Hajj, and Ali stood during the days of Tashriq and proclaimed: 'Indeed Allah is disowned of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger. So travel freely in the land for four months. No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, no one shall circumambulate the House naked, and no one shall enter Paradise except a believer.'" Ali kept proclaiming, and when he tired, Abu Bakr stood and proclaimed them.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Nahhas, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Zayd ibn Tubay' who said: "I asked Ali: 'With what were you sent together with Abu Bakr for Hajj?' He said: 'I was sent with four things: no soul enters Paradise except a believing soul, no one circumambulates the House naked, no believer and disbeliever gather in the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs, and whoever has a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his covenant is until its term, and whoever has no covenant, his term is four months.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger﴾ and the rest of the verse: "Allah set for those who had covenants with His Messenger a limit of four months in which they may travel wherever they wish. He set the term for one who has no covenant as the expiry of the four sacred months from the Day of Sacrifice until the end of Muharram, fifty nights. When the sacred months expire, He commanded him to put the sword to those with whom he had a covenant if they do not enter Islam, and to break what had been stipulated for them of covenant and pact, and He removed the first condition: ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque﴾ (At-Tawbah: 7), meaning the people of Makkah."

al-Nahhas reported similarly from him, and said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not make a covenant with anyone after this."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Nahhas reported from al-Zuhri, concerning ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾: it was revealed in Shawwal, so the four months are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and Muharram.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd, concerning His words ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger﴾: "It is a notification from Allah and His Messenger."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 3–4 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAli, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the Day of the Greater Hajj, and he said: 'It is the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr).'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tirmidhi and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated it from him, as his own statement.

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and al-Hakim, who graded it authentic, narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Qurt, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The greatest of days before Allah is the Day of Sacrifice, then the Day of Qarr."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abi Awfa, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "This Day of Sacrifice is the Day of the Greater Hajj."

Al-Bukhari, in a suspended narration (taʿliq), Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Hilya narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood on the Day of Sacrifice between the jamarat in the Hajj he performed, and said: 'What day is this?' They said: 'The Day of Sacrifice.' He said: 'This is the Day of the Greater Hajj.'"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: Abu Bakr dispatched me among those who proclaimed on the Day of Sacrifice at Mina: "No polytheist may perform Hajj after this year, and no one may circumambulate the House naked. The Day of the Greater Hajj is the Day of Sacrifice, and the Greater Hajj is the Hajj." The word "greater" was used only because of people's saying "the Lesser Hajj." Abu Bakr then renounced (the treaties) to the people in that year, so no polytheist performed Hajj in the year of the Farewell Hajj in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed Hajj. And in the year in which Abu Bakr renounced (the treaties) to the polytheists, Allah revealed: ﴿O you who believe, the polytheists are only impure﴾ (al-Tawbah: 28), and the rest of the verse.

Al-Tabarani narrated from Samurah ibn Jundub that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said at the time of the Conquest: 'Indeed, this is the year of the Greater Hajj,'" and he said: "The Hajj of the Muslims and the Hajj of the polytheists coincided on three consecutive days, and the Christians and the Jews coincided on three consecutive days, so the Hajj of the Muslims, the polytheists, the Christians and the Jews coincided on six consecutive days. This had not occurred since the creation of the heavens and the earth before this year, and it will not occur after this year until the Hour arrives."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that he was asked about the Day of the Greater Hajj and said: "What concern do you have with the Greater Hajj? That was the year in which Abu Bakr performed Hajj, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had appointed as his deputy, so he led the people in Hajj. The Muslims and the polytheists gathered in it, and for this reason it was called the Greater Hajj, and it coincided with the festival of the Jews and Christians."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "The Greater Hajj is the second day after the Day of Sacrifice, for do you not see that the imam delivers the sermon on it?"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "This Day of ʿArafah is the Day of the Greater Hajj."

Ibn Saʿd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "The Greater Hajj is the Day of ʿArafah."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu al-Sahba' al-Bakri, who said: "I asked ʿAli ibn Abi Talib about the Day of the Greater Hajj, and he said: 'It is the Day of ʿArafah.'"

Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Indeed, the Day of ʿArafah is the Day of the Greater Hajj."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Zubayr something similar.

It is not hidden from you that the reports stating that the Day of Sacrifice is the Day of the Greater Hajj are established in the Two Sahihs and elsewhere through multiple chains, so these reports which state explicitly that it is the Day of ʿArafah cannot stand against them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from al-Shaʿbi that he was asked: "This is the Greater Hajj, so what is the Lesser Hajj?" He said: "It is ʿUmrah in Ramadan."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Ibn Ishaq, who said: "I asked ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad about the Greater Hajj, and he said: 'The Greater Hajj is the Day of Sacrifice, and the Lesser Hajj is ʿUmrah.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Masʿud, who said: "Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah was asked about good tidings given in a disliked matter, and he said: 'Have you not heard His saying: ﴿And give tidings of a painful punishment to those who disbelieve﴾?'"

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 3–4 (part 1 of 2):**

His words: ﴿A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger﴾. *Bara'a* (بَرِئْتُ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ أبْرَأُ بَراءَةً): "I disowned the thing, I disown it with *bara'a*, and I am *bari'* (بَرِيءٌ) of it," when you remove it from yourself and cut the cause between you and it. *Bara'atun* (بَراءَةٌ) is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "this is a disavowal." It may also be nominative as a subject, since it is an indefinite noun described by a qualifier, and its predicate is ﴿to those with whom you made a covenant﴾.

Isa ibn Umar read *bara'atan* (بَراءَةً) with the accusative, on the assumed meaning "hear a disavowal," or "adhere to a disavowal," because it carries the sense of an incitement (*al-ighra'*). The *min* (مِنَ) in His words ﴿from Allah﴾ indicates the starting point (*ibtida' al-ghaya*) and is attached to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier: "conveyed from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made a covenant."

Rawh and Zayd read *Rasulihi* (رَسُولِهِ) with the accusative. The rest read it with the nominative.

*Al-'ahd* (العَهْد) is a binding contract confirmed by oath.

The address in ﴿you made﴾ is to the Muslims. They had made covenants with the polytheists of Makkah and others, by permission from Allah and from the Messenger ﷺ. The meaning is an announcement to the Muslims that Allah and His Messenger have disowned that covenant because of the breach committed by the disbelievers. Thus renouncing their covenant became obligatory for the Muslim covenanters. The disavowal of Allah, glorified is He, means that He authorized the Muslims to renounce the covenant of the polytheists after they breached it. In this there is an obvious magnification of the matter of the disavowal, a strong emphasis on it, and an unmistakable recording against the polytheists of humiliation and disgrace.

His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾. This is a command from Him, glorified is He, to travel after the announcement of that disavowal. *Al-siyaha* (السِّياحَةُ) means travel. It is said: "So-and-so travelled in the land (sa'a fi al-ardi, ساحَ فُلانٌ في الأرْضِ), travels (yasihu) with travel (siyahatan), journeying (suyuhan), and wandering (sayahanan)." From it: "the water flowed over the land (sayaha al-ma')," and "the horses roamed (sayaha al-khayl)." From it is the saying of Tarafa ibn al-'Abd:

*"Had I feared this from you, you would not have reached me, until you see horses before me roaming."*

The meaning of the verse is that Allah, glorified is He, after permitting the renunciation of the covenant with the polytheists, allowed the polytheists to move about the land, go wherever they wished, and prepare for war during these four months. The command to travel is not meant as an obligation imposed on them.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq and others said: The polytheists were of two kinds. One kind had a covenant of less than four months, so it was given the full four months. The other had a covenant longer than that, so it was limited to four months so that it could consider its position; after that it was at war with Allah, His Messenger, and the believers, and would be killed wherever found. The beginning of this term was the Day of the Greater Hajj, and it ended at the tenth of Rabi' al-Akhir. As for one who had no covenant, his term was the expiry of the sacred months, which is fifty days: twenty days of Dhu al-Hijjah and the month of Muharram.

Al-Kalbi said: The four months were only for those who had a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of less than four months. As for one whose covenant was longer than that, it is the one about whom Allah commanded that his covenant be fulfilled, by His words: ﴿So fulfil their covenant to their term﴾ (At-Tawbah: 4). Ibn Jarir and others preferred this view. Later in the discussion, the narrations will clarify the meaning of the verse.

His words: ﴿And know that you cannot escape Allah﴾, meaning: know that this granting of respite is not due to incapacity, but for a purpose, so that whoever repents may repent. In this there is a kind of threat, as if it were said: do in this period everything you can of preparing instruments and tools, for you will not escape Allah, and He will disgrace you, that is, humiliate you in this world by killing and capture, and in the Hereafter by punishment. Placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun indicates that the cause of this disgrace is disbelief. It is also possible that the intended reference is the category of disbelievers, which would include the addressees by primary inclusion (*dukhulan awwaliyyan*).

His words: ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the Day of the Greater Hajj﴾. *Adhanun* (أذانٌ) is nominative either as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a subject whose predicate is what follows it, as explained for the nominative of *bara'atun*. This sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: His words "and a proclamation" are conjoined to his words "a disavowal."

It was objected that if this were so, the proclamation would be described by the first predicate, which is ﴿to those of the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾. This is not correct. Rather, the predicate is "to the people." *Al-adhan* here means *al-iadh*, which is notification, just as *al-aman* and *al-ata'* mean *al-iman* and *al-i'ta'*. The meaning of His words "to the people" is generality in this matter: it is a notification from Allah to all people, not specific to one group over another. So this sentence contains the information that notifying all people is obligatory, while the first sentence contains the information of disavowal addressed specifically to those in covenant. The Day of the Hajj is an adverbial complement of "and a proclamation." He described it as "greater" because the people gather on it, or because most of the rites of Hajj take place on it.

The scholars differed in determining the day mentioned in the verse. A group, including 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abi Awfa, al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, and Mujahid, held that it is the Day of Sacrifice (*yawm al-nahr*). Ibn Jarir preferred this view. Others, including Umar, Ibn Abbas, and Tawus, held that it is the Day of 'Arafah.

The first view is more preferred, because the Prophet ﷺ commanded the one he sent to convey this to the polytheists to deliver it to them on the Day of Sacrifice.

His words: ﴿that Allah is disowned of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾. It was read with *anna* (أنَّ) having a fatha, on the assumed meaning "that Allah is disowned of the polytheists," with the *ba'* (بِأنَّ) omitted for lightness. It was also read with a kasra, because the proclamation carries the sense of speech (*al-qawl*). The nominative of *Rasuluhu* (رَسُولُهُ) is either conjoined to the position of the noun of *inna* (اسْمِ أنَّ), or to the pronoun in *bari'* (بَرِيءٌ), or it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and the assumed meaning is "and His Messenger is disowned of them." Al-Hasan and others read *wa-Rasulahu* (وَرَسُولَهُ) with the accusative, conjoined to the form of the noun of *anna* (لَفْظِ اسْمِ أنَّ).

*Wa-Rasulihi* (وَرَسُولِهِ) was read with the genitive, on the basis that the *waw* is for an oath. This is reported from al-Hasan, but it is a very weak reading, since there is no sense in swearing by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ here, along with what is established of the prohibition against swearing by other than Allah. It was also said that it is genitive by *al-jiwar* (الجِوار), that is, by proximity to the preceding word.

His words: ﴿So if you repent﴾, meaning from disbelief. In it there is an *iltifat* (الالتفات), a shift from the third person (absence) to the second person (address). It was said that the benefit of this shift is an increase in threat. The pronoun in His words ﴿it is better for you﴾ refers to the repentance understood from "you repent," meaning it is better for you than what you are in of disbelief. ﴿And if you turn away﴾, meaning you refuse repentance and remain in disbelief, ﴿then know that you cannot escape Allah﴾, meaning you cannot elude Him. Rather, He will overtake you and requite you for your deeds.

His words: ﴿And give tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment﴾. This is mockery of them, and in it there is a threat that is not hidden.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made a covenant among the polytheists﴾: to the people of covenant, Khuza'ah, Mudlij, and whoever had a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, from Tabuk when he had finished with it and intended Hajj. Then he said: "Polytheists visit this House and circumambulate it naked, so I do not like to perform Hajj until that stops." So he sent Abu Bakr and Ali, and they went around among the people at Dhu al-Majaz and at their marketplaces where they used to trade, or throughout the whole season. They informed the people of the covenant that they would be safe for four months, which are the consecutive sacred months that run out: twenty days from the end of Dhu al-Hijjah to the tenth of Rabi' al-Akhir. After that there was no covenant for them, and he announced to all people war until they die.

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal reported in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, as did Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh, from Ali who said: "When ten verses of 'Bara'ah' were revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, he summoned Abu Bakr to recite them to the people of Makkah." Then he called me and said to me: "Overtake Abu Bakr, and wherever you meet him, take the document from him and recite it to the people of Makkah." So I caught up with him and took the document from him, and Abu Bakr returned and said: "O Messenger of Allah, has something been revealed concerning me?" He said: "No, but Jibril came to me and said: 'None will convey on your behalf except you or a man from you.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh reported a similar account from the hadith of Anas.

Ibn Mardawayh also reported a similar account from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Hurayrah who said: "I was with Ali when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent him to the people of Makkah" with "Bara'ah," and we would proclaim that no one enters Paradise except a believer, no one circumambulates the House naked, and whoever has a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his term and limit is four months. When the four months have passed, Allah is disowned of the polytheists and so is His Messenger, and no polytheist shall perform Hajj to this House after this year.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Abu Hurayrah who said: "Abu Bakr sent me in that Hajj, among the callers whom he sent on the Day of Sacrifice to proclaim at Mina: that no polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, and no one shall circumambulate the House naked. Then the Prophet ﷺ rode behind Ali ibn Abi Talib and commanded him to proclaim 'Bara'ah,' so Ali proclaimed on the Day of Sacrifice with 'Bara'ah': that no polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, and no one shall circumambulate the House naked."

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn Abbas: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Abu Bakr and commanded him to proclaim these words. Then he sent Ali after him and commanded him to proclaim these words. They set out and performed Hajj, and Ali stood during the days of Tashriq and proclaimed: 'Indeed Allah is disowned of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger. So travel freely in the land for four months. No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, no one shall circumambulate the House naked, and no one shall enter Paradise except a believer.'" Ali kept proclaiming, and when he tired, Abu Bakr stood and proclaimed them.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Nahhas, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Zayd ibn Tubay' who said: "I asked Ali: 'With what were you sent together with Abu Bakr for Hajj?' He said: 'I was sent with four things: no soul enters Paradise except a believing soul, no one circumambulates the House naked, no believer and disbeliever gather in the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs, and whoever has a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his covenant is until its term, and whoever has no covenant, his term is four months.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger﴾ and the rest of the verse: "Allah set for those who had covenants with His Messenger a limit of four months in which they may travel wherever they wish. He set the term for one who has no covenant as the expiry of the four sacred months from the Day of Sacrifice until the end of Muharram, fifty nights. When the sacred months expire, He commanded him to put the sword to those with whom he had a covenant if they do not enter Islam, and to break what had been stipulated for them of covenant and pact, and He removed the first condition: ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque﴾ (At-Tawbah: 7), meaning the people of Makkah."

al-Nahhas reported similarly from him, and said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not make a covenant with anyone after this."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Nahhas reported from al-Zuhri, concerning ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾: it was revealed in Shawwal, so the four months are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and Muharram.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd, concerning His words ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger﴾: "It is a notification from Allah and His Messenger."

(p. 557) **The exception in His words, ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant﴾.** Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) said: it refers back to His words "a declaration of disavowal," and the sense is: "a declaration of disavowal from Allah and His Messenger to the covenanted polytheists, except those who did not break the covenant with you."

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: it is an exception from His words "so travel freely," and the sense is: "say to them, travel freely, except those with whom you made a covenant and who have not failed you, so fulfil to them their covenant."

He said: the exception is in the sense of *istidrak* (a qualifying correction, "but"), as if it were said: "after they were commanded regarding those who break their oaths, but those who have not broken them, fulfil to them their covenant and do not treat them as such."

It has been objected that a separation has intervened between the exception and what it excepts from, namely ﴿and a proclamation from Allah﴾, and so on. It was answered that this does not harm, because it is not foreign (to the matter). It has also been said that the exception is from the polytheists mentioned before it, so it would be a connected (*muttasil*) exception, but this is weak.

His words, **"﴿then they have not fallen short of you in anything﴾,"** meaning: no shortfall at all occurred from them, even a slight one. ʿIkrimah and ʿAta' ibn Yasar read *yanqudukum* with the dotted *ḍād*, meaning: "they did not break your covenant." In this there is evidence that among the people of the covenant there were those who were treacherous with their pact and those who remained steadfast. So Allah, glorified is He, permitted His Prophet ﷺ to annul the covenant of whoever broke it, and to keep faith with whoever did not break it until its term. ﴿And they have not supported anyone against you﴾: *al-muzaharah* means assistance; that is, they did not assist any of your enemies against you. ﴿So fulfil to them their covenant﴾: that is, render to them their covenant complete, without deficiency, ﴿until their term﴾ which you agreed with them, even if it was more than four months. And do not treat them as those who break their oaths by fighting after the passing of the aforementioned term, which was previously four months or fifty days, according to the earlier disagreement.

His words: **﴿So when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾.** *Inslakh* of a month means its completion part by part until it ends, like the stripping of a skin from what it covers. It likens the departure of that which is in time from its time to the separation of what is in a place from its place. Its origin is the stripping that occurs between an animal and its hide, and it was borrowed for the ending of months. It is said: "I stripped the month (*salakhtu al-shahr*), you strip it, *salkhan* and *sulukhan*," meaning "I came out of it." From this is the words of the poet:

*When I strip off the month and begin its like,*
*the stripping of months and my beginning them suffice as a killer.*

It is also said: "the woman stripped her garment," meaning she took it off. In the revelation: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ (Yasin 36:37).

The scholars differed in identifying the sacred months mentioned here. It was said: they are the well-known sacred months, which are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and Muharram (three consecutive) and Rajab (a single one separately).

According to this, the meaning of the verse is the obligation to refrain from fighting those polytheists who have no covenant during these sacred months.

The proclamation and the repudiation of covenants to the polytheists took place on the Day of Sacrifice (*yawm al-nahr*), so the remainder of the sacred months, the three consecutive ones, was fifty days, which end with the end of the month of Muharram. Then Allah commanded them to kill the polytheists wherever they are found. This was the view of a group of scholars, including al-Dahhak, al-Baqir, and it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jarir chose it.

It was also said: what is meant by them are the months of the covenant indicated by His words: ﴿So fulfil to them their covenant until their term﴾. They were called sacred because Allah, glorified is He, forbade the Muslims during them the blood of the polytheists and attacking them. This was the view of a group of scholars, including Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Zayd, and ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb. It was also said: they are the months mentioned in His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ (9:2).

This has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and a group, and Ibn Kathir preferred it, and related it from Mujahid, ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, Muhammad ibn Ishaq, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam. The explanation of the ruling on fighting in the sacred months, which recur every year, will come in this surah, God willing.

The meaning of **﴿wherever you find them﴾** is: in whatever place you find them, whether in the non-sacred area (*ḥill*) or the sacred precinct (*ḥaram*).

The meaning of **"take them"** is captive, for the *akhidh* is the captive.

The meaning of **"besiege them"** is preventing them from moving about in the lands of the Muslims except with their permission. *Al-marṣad* is the place where the enemy is watched. It is said: "I ambushed so-and-so, I watch him," that is, I observed him. That is, sit in wait for them in the places where you lie in ambush for them. ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl said:

*And indeed you know, though I do not think you know,*
*that death for a youth is at the place of ambush.*

And al-Nabighah said:

*O blamer, indeed ignorance is part of a youth's pleasure,*
*and indeed deaths lie in wait for souls.*

The word **"every"** in **﴿every ambush﴾** is in the accusative as an adverb of place (*ẓarfiyyah*), and this is al-Zajjaj's choice. It was also said that it is accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning "in every ambush." Abu ʿAli al-Farisi declared al-Zajjaj wrong in making it an adverb.

This verse abrogated every verse that mentions turning away from the polytheists and patience over their harm.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: rather, it abrogates His words: ﴿Then either grace after that or ransom﴾, and that it is not permissible regarding the captives among the polytheists except killing.

Ibn Zayd said: the two verses are *muhkamatan* (clear, not abrogated).

Al-Qurtubi said: this is the correct view, because grace, killing, and ransom have not ceased to be part of the ruling of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ regarding them since the first battle in which he brought them, which was the Day of Badr.

His words: **﴿But if they repent and establish prayer and give zakah﴾**: that is, they repent from polytheism, which is the cause of killing, and they fulfil repentance by doing what is among the greatest pillars of Islam, which is the establishment of prayer. This pillar suffices to indicate the bodily acts of worship, because it is their head. And he suffices with the other pillar concerning wealth, which is the giving of zakah, for all acts of worship relating to wealth, because it is the greatest of them. **﴿Then let them go their way﴾**: that is, leave them and their affairs; do not take them captive, do not besiege them, and do not kill them. **﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving﴾** toward them, **Merciful** to them.

His words: **﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection﴾**. It is said: "*istajarta* so-and-so," meaning I asked him to be a protector (*jar*), that is, a defender and guardian (p. 558) from anyone who might wrong me or attack me. *Ahad* (anyone) is in the nominative by a verb implied and explained by what follows it: that is, "if anyone seeks your protection, he seeks your protection." The grammarians disliked combining the explained element and the explainer. The meaning is: if any of the polytheists whom you have been commanded to fight seeks your protection, then grant him protection, that is, be a protector for him, a believing defender. **﴿Until he hears the words of Allah﴾** from you and reflects on them as they should be reflected upon, and comes to know the truth of what you call to. **﴿Then deliver him to his place of safety﴾**: that is, to the land in which he is secure after he has heard the words of Allah, if he has not become Muslim. Then, after you have delivered him to his place of safety, fight him, for he has left your protection and returned to his former state of having his blood permitted and being obliged to be killed wherever he is found. The reference of **"that"** in His words is to what preceded of the command to grant protection and what follows it. **﴿That is because they are a people who do not know﴾**: that is, because of their lack of beneficial knowledge that distinguishes between good and evil in present and final outcome.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words **﴿except those with whom you made a covenant﴾**, that he said: "They are the Quraysh."

He also related from Qatadah, who said: "They are the polytheists of Quraysh with whom the Prophet of Allah made a covenant at the time of al-Hudaybiyah, and four months of their term remained after the Day of Sacrifice. So he commanded his Prophet to fulfil to them this covenant until their term."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Muhammad ibn ʿAbbad ibn Jaʿfar regarding His words **﴿except those with whom you made a covenant﴾**, that he said: "They are the Banu Jadhimah ibn ʿAmir of the Banu Bakr ibn Kinanah."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding His words **﴿So fulfil to them their covenant until their term﴾**, that he said: "A covenant remained for the Banu Madhhij and Khuzaʿah, and it is this about which Allah said: ﴿So fulfil to them their covenant until their term﴾."

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding His words **﴿except those with whom you made a covenant among the polytheists﴾**, that he said: "These are the Banu Damrah and the Banu Mudlij of the Banu Kinanah, who were allies of the Prophet ﷺ at the expedition of al-ʿAshirah, from the valley of Yanbuʿ." **﴿Then they have not fallen short of you in anything﴾**: then they did not break their covenant with you by treachery. **﴿And they have not supported anyone against you﴾**: he said: "they did not support your enemy against you." **﴿So fulfil to them their covenant until their term﴾**: he says: "their appointed time which you stipulated for them." **﴿Indeed Allah loves the righteous﴾**: he says: "those who fear Allah regarding what is forbidden to them, and so they fulfil the covenant."

He said: "The Prophet ﷺ did not make a covenant with anyone after these verses."

I say: al-Suddi's meaning is that these months are called sacred because securing the covenanted during them entails the prohibition of fighting; not that they are the well-known sacred months.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid that he said: "They are the four months of which He said: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah something similar to al-Suddi's earlier view.

**His saying: ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with Allah and with His Messenger?﴾** The interrogative (*istifhām*) here is for astonishment that implies denial. *"ʿAhd"* (covenant) is the subject of *yakūnu* (be/have). The predicate of *yakūnu* has three possible analyses:

First: the predicate is *kayfa* (how), which is placed first because it is an interrogative.
Second: the predicate is *lil-mushrikīn* (for the polytheists), and *ʿinda* (with) on these two readings is an adverb of place modifying *al-ʿahd*, or modifying *yakūnu*, or it is an adjective of *al-ʿahd*.
Third: the predicate is *ʿinda Allāh* (with Allah), and there is an ellipsis (*iḍmār*) in the verse.

The meaning is: how can the polytheists have a covenant with Allah by which they would be secure from His punishment? It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is: it is impossible that a covenant should be established for these people, when they are your enemies who harbour treachery, so let them not aspire to that, nor let them entertain it in their souls. Then He makes an exception, saying: ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque﴾, that is: but those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque, who have not breached it and have not broken it, so do not fight them. As long as they remain upright toward you in the covenant between you and them, then remain upright toward them. It has been said that they are the Banū Bakr, and it has been said that they are the Banū Kinānah and the Banū Ḍamrah. Regarding *mā* (what) there are two possibilities: one, that it is a temporal *maṣdariyyah* (verbal particle indicating a duration); the other, that it is a conditional (*shartiyyah*). His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the God-fearing﴾ indicates that fulfilling the covenant and remaining upright in it are among the deeds of the God-fearing, so this serves as a reason (*taʿlīl*) for the command to remain upright.

**His saying: ﴿How, when if they prevail over you﴾** He repeats the astonishing interrogative for emphasis and affirmation. The implied sense is: how can they have a covenant with Allah and with His Messenger, when, if they gain the upper hand over you by victory, they do not observe regarding you *illan* (kinship), that is, they do not respect regarding you any covenant, *"nor any obligation (dhimmah)"*.

(p. 559) He said in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: *al-Ill* means covenant and kinship. From this is the saying of Ḥassān:

*By your life, your kinship (illaka) with Quraysh*
*is like the kinship of the young camel with the ostrich chick.*

Then He described them with His saying: ﴿They have sold the signs of Allah for a small price﴾, that is, they exchanged the verses of the Qur'an, among which is the command to fulfil covenants, for a small, worthless price, which is what they preferred of the transient goods of this world. ﴿So they have barred [others] from His way﴾, that is, they deviated and turned away from the way of truth, or they diverted others from it.

**His saying: ﴿They do not observe regarding you kinship or obligation﴾.** Al-Naḥḥās said: this is not a repetition. Rather, the first refers to all the polytheists, and the second refers specifically to the Jews.

The evidence for this is ﴿They have sold the signs of Allah for a small price﴾, meaning the Jews. It has also been said that this (the second) involves respecting the rights of believers in general, while the first involves respecting the rights of a particular group of believers. ﴿And those are the transgressors﴾, that is, those who go beyond what is lawful to what is forbidden by breaking the covenant, or who carry evil and rebellion to its utmost extreme.

**Then if they repent** from polytheism and adhere to the rulings of Islam, ﴿then they are your brothers﴾, that is, they are your brothers in religion, namely in the religion of Islam. ﴿And We detail the signs﴾, that is, We explain and clarify them, ﴿for a people who know﴾ their rulings and comprehend them. He specified people of knowledge because they are the ones who benefit from them. The "signs" here means what has passed of the verses concerning the circumstances of the polytheists in their various kinds.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), regarding His saying ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque﴾, that he said: they are Quraysh.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn Zayd something similar.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Muqātil, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) had made a covenant with some people from the Banū Ḍamrah, the Banū Bakr and Kinānah specifically. He made the covenant with them at the Sacred Mosque and made their term four months. These are the ones Allah mentioned in ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque, so as long as they remain upright toward you, remain upright toward them﴾. He means: as long as they fulfil the covenant to you, fulfil it to them.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Suddī, who said: they are the Banū Jadhīmah.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Qatādah, regarding His saying ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque﴾, that he said: it is the day of al-Ḥudaybiyah.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying ﴿nor any obligation﴾, that he said: *al-Ill* is kinship, and *al-Dhimmah* is covenant.

al-Firyābī, Abū ʿUbayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Mujāhid, who said: *al-Ill* is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from ʿIkrimah something similar.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Mujāhid, regarding His saying ﴿They have sold the signs of Allah for a small price﴾, that he said: Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb fed his allies and abandoned the allies of Muḥammad (ﷺ).

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah, regarding His saying ﴿Then if they repent﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: if they abandon al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā, and testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, then they are your brothers in religion.

Ibn Jarīr and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: this verse made forbidden the fighting against, or the shedding of the blood of, the people of prayer (*ahl al-ṣalāh*).

**His saying: ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with Allah and with His Messenger?﴾** The interrogative (*istifhām*) here is for astonishment that implies denial. *"ʿAhd"* (covenant) is the subject of *yakūnu* (be/have). The predicate of *yakūnu* has three possible analyses:

First: the predicate is *kayfa* (how), which is placed first because it is an interrogative.
Second: the predicate is *lil-mushrikīn* (for the polytheists), and *ʿinda* (with) on these two readings is an adverb of place modifying *al-ʿahd*, or modifying *yakūnu*, or it is an adjective of *al-ʿahd*.
Third: the predicate is *ʿinda Allāh* (with Allah), and there is an ellipsis (*iḍmār*) in the verse.

The meaning is: how can the polytheists have a covenant with Allah by which they would be secure from His punishment? It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is: it is impossible that a covenant should be established for these people, when they are your enemies who harbour treachery, so let them not aspire to that, nor let them entertain it in their souls. Then He makes an exception, saying: ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque﴾, that is: but those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque, who have not breached it and have not broken it, so do not fight them. As long as they remain upright toward you in the covenant between you and them, then remain upright toward them. It has been said that they are the Banū Bakr, and it has been said that they are the Banū Kinānah and the Banū Ḍamrah. Regarding *mā* (what) there are two possibilities: one, that it is a temporal *maṣdariyyah* (verbal particle indicating a duration); the other, that it is a conditional (*shartiyyah*). His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the God-fearing﴾ indicates that fulfilling the covenant and remaining upright in it are among the deeds of the God-fearing, so this serves as a reason (*taʿlīl*) for the command to remain upright.

**His saying: ﴿How, when if they prevail over you﴾** He repeats the astonishing interrogative for emphasis and affirmation. The implied sense is: how can they have a covenant with Allah and with His Messenger, when, if they gain the upper hand over you by victory, they do not observe regarding you *illan* (kinship), that is, they do not respect regarding you any covenant, *"nor any obligation (dhimmah)"*.

(p. 559) He said in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: *al-Ill* means covenant and kinship. From this is the saying of Ḥassān:

*By your life, your kinship (illaka) with Quraysh*
*is like the kinship of the young camel with the ostrich chick.*

Al-Zajjāj said: *al-Ill*, in my view, according to what the language requires, revolves around the meaning of sharpness. From it comes *al-illah*, the spearhead, and from it comes *udhun muʾallalah*, meaning a sharpened ear. From it is the saying of Ṭarafah ibn al-ʿAbd describing the two ears of his she-camel as sharp and erect:

*Two sharpened ears, by which the neck is recognised,*
*like the two ears of a lone sheep at Ḥawmal.*

Abū ʿUbaydah said: *al-Ill* is covenant, obligation (*dhimmah*), and close companion (*nadīm*).

al-Zuhrī said: it is a name of Allah in Hebrew, and its origin is from *al-alīl*, which is brightness. It is said: *allat lawnuhu yaʾullu illan*, meaning his colour became pure and gleamed. *Al-Dhimmah* is covenant, and its plural is *dhimam*. So whoever interprets *al-ill* as covenant, the repetition is for emphasis, with the two words differing.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verse 12–16:

His saying: "وإنْ نَكَثُوا" ("But if they break their oaths") is coordinated with "فَإنْ تابُوا" ("then if they repent"). Al-nakth (breaking) means nAqḍ (undoing), and its original sense is undoing a thread after it has been twisted; then it was used for every kind of undoing, and from it comes the breaking of oaths and covenants, by way of metaphor (isti'arah).

The meaning of "مِن بَعْدِ عَهْدِهِمْ" ("after their covenant") is: after they had made a covenant with you.

The meaning is: if the disbelievers break the covenants with which they bound themselves to the Muslims and by which they gave them assurance, and add to that the defaming of the religion of Islam and disparaging it, then it has become obligatory upon the Muslims to fight them. "أئِمَّةُ الكُفْرِ" (the leaders of disbelief): the plural of imam, and what is meant is the chieftains of the polytheists, and those in leadership among them in general. Hamzah recited "أإمَةَ".

Most of the grammarians hold that this is a solecism (laḥn), because it involves the joining of two hamzahs in one word.

The majority recited it by making the second hamzah between-between (bayn bayn, i.e. between the point of articulation of the hamzah and that of the yā'). It was also recited with the yā' made pure, and that is a solecism, as az-Zamakhshari said.

His saying: ﴿إنَّهم لا أيْمانَ لَهُمْ﴾ ("Indeed, they have no oaths") — this sentence is a causal explanation of what precedes it. "al-Aymān" is the plural of yamīn in the recitation of the majority.

Ibn 'Amir recited "لا إيمانَ لَهم" with a kasrah on the hamzah.

The meaning according to the recitation of the majority: the oaths of the disbelievers, although in form they are oaths, are in reality not oaths. According to the second recitation: these breakers of oaths who slander the religion are not among the people of faith in God, so as to deserve the protection of their blood and property; therefore fighting them is obligatory upon the Muslims.

His saying: "لَعَلَّهم يَنْتَهُونَ" ("so that they may desist") means: from their disbelief, their breaking of covenants, and their defaming of the religion of Islam.

The meaning is: their fighting is to be carried on until the goal, which is their ceasing from that.

This verse has been cited as evidence that a dhimmi who defames the religion is not killed until he breaks the covenant, as Abu Hanifah said, because God only commanded their killing on two conditions: one of them is breaking the covenant, and the second is defaming the religion. Malik, al-Shafi'i and others held that if he defames the religion he is killed, because by that his covenant is broken. They said: likewise, if a dhimmi commits mere breaking of the covenant alone, without defaming the religion, he is killed.

His saying: ﴿ألا تُقاتِلُونَ قَوْمًا نَكَثُوا أيْمانَهم﴾ ("Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths?") — the hamzah entering upon the negative particle is an interrogative of rebuke, together with what is derived from it of urging to fighting and emphasis on its realization. The meaning: whoever is in the condition of these people, in breaking the covenant, expelling the Messenger from Makkah, and initiating the fighting, is deserving that his fighting not be abandoned, and that whoever neglected that be rebuked. Then he increased the rebuke and said: "أتَخْشَوْنَهم" ("Do you fear them?"). This interrogative is for rebuke and reproach: that is, do you fear that some harm will befall you from them, so that you abandon fighting them out of this fear? Then he explained what the matter must be: ﴿فاللَّهُ أحَقُّ أنْ تَخْشَوْهُ إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("God has more right that you fear Him, if you are believers"), that is, He has more right to be feared by you, for He is the true Harmer and Benefactor; and from your fear of Him is that you fight those whom He has commanded you to fight, for the requirement of faith makes that obligatory upon you.

Then he increased the emphasis on the command to fight and said: "قاتِلُوهم" ("Fight them"), and upon this command he arranged several benefits. The first: God's punishment of the disbelievers by the hands of the believers, through killing and capture. The second: their humiliation; it was said: by capture, and it was said: by the abasement and disgrace that befell them. The third: the victory of the Muslims over them and their overcoming them. The fourth: that God heals with fighting the hearts (ṣudūr) of a people of believers from among those who did not witness the fighting nor were present at it. The fifth: that He, glorified is He, removes by fighting the rage (ghayẓ) of the hearts of the believers, which had befallen them because of what the disbelievers had done of matters that bring rage and constriction of the breast.

If it is said: the healing of hearts (ṣudūr) and the removal of the rage of hearts are both of one meaning, so it would be a repetition. It is answered: the heart (qalb) is more specific than the breast (ṣadr). It was also said: the healing of the breasts is an allusion to the promise of conquest, and there is no doubt that waiting for the fulfilment of the promise with confidence in it is a healing for the breasts in both cases; and that the removal of the rage of hearts is an allusion to the occurrence of the conquest. These matters have all come to pass for the believers, and to God be praise.

Then he said: ﴿ويَتُوبُ اللَّهُ عَلى مَن يَشاءُ﴾ ("And God accepts repentance from whom He wills"). This is a new statement that includes information about what will come to be, namely that some of the disbelievers will repent of their disbelief, as happened with some of the people of Makkah on the day of the Conquest; they embraced Islam and their Islam was sound. This is on the recitation of the nominative in "يَتُوبُ", which is the recitation of the majority. It was recited with the accusative "يَتُوبَ" by the implicit "أنْ", and the entry of repentance into the category of what the command is answered with is by way of meaning.

This was recited by Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa ath-Thaqafi, and al-A'raj.

If it is said: how can repentance come as a consequence of fighting? It is answered: fighting may be a cause of it when it comes from the side of the disbelievers; as for when it comes from the side of the Muslims, its aspect is that victory and triumph from God becomes a cause for the purity of intention and repentance from sins.

His saying: ﴿أمْ حَسِبْتُمْ أنْ تُتْرَكُوا﴾ ("Or did you suppose that you would be left alone?"). This "am" here is the disjunctive one which has the meaning of "bal" (rather), and the hamzah and interrogation are for rebuke, and the particle of turning away is to indicate the transition from one speech to another.

The meaning: how could supposing come from you that you would be left as you are? The phrase "أنْ تُتْرَكُوا" stands in the position of the two objects of "ḥasiba" according to Sibawayh.

Al-Mubarrad said: the second object is omitted, and the estimate is: "Or did you suppose that you would be left without being tested by that which makes manifest the believer and the hypocrite, the manifestation that deserves reward and punishment?" The clause ﴿ولَمّا يَعْلَمِ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ جاهَدُوا مِنكُمْ﴾ ("while God has not yet known those of you who strove") is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl). The denial of knowledge here means the denial of the thing known; the meaning is: how do you suppose that you will be left while God has not yet made clear, among you, the sincere in his struggle from the non-sincere? The clause "ولَمْ يَتَّخِذُوا" ("and did not take") is coordinated with "جاهَدُوا", and is included with it under the ruling of negation, and falls within the scope of the relative clause. The "walījah" comes from "wulūj", which is entering; "walaja yalij wulūjan" means "he entered"; so the walījah is the intruder.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: everything you have introduced into something that is not of it is a walījah.

Aban ibn Tha'labah said:

"Evil is the intimate of the fleers, and the transgressors, and the people of doubt."

Al-Farra' said: the walījah is the inner confidant from among the polytheists; the meaning is one: that is, how do you take an intruder or an inner confidant from among the polytheists, to whom you disclose your secrets and make known your affairs, apart from God? ﴿واللَّهُ خَبِيرٌ بِما تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("And God is Aware of what you do"), that is, of all your deeds.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿وإنْ نَكَثُوا أيْمانَهُمْ﴾, that he said: "their covenant."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, that he said: God says to His Prophet: "And if they break the covenant between you and them, then fight them, for they are the leaders of disbelief."

'Abd ar-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu ash-Shaykh reported from Qatadah regarding His saying "أئِمَّةَ الكُفْرِ" that he said: Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, and Suhayl ibn 'Amr, and they are the ones who broke the covenant of God and resolved to expel the Messenger from Makkah.

Ibn 'Asakir reported the like of it from Malik ibn Anas.

Abu ash-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿فَقاتِلُوا أئِمَّةَ الكُفْرِ﴾, that he said: the heads of Quraysh.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu ash-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Umar that he said: Abu Sufyan ibn Harb was among them.

Abu ash-Shaykh reported from al-Hasan that they were the Daylam.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu ash-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Hudhayfah that they mentioned, at this verse, and said: "None of the people of this verse has been fought yet."

Ibn Mardawayh reported the like of it from 'Ali.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Hudhayfah that he said: "None remains of the people of this verse except three, and none of the hypocrites except four." A Bedouin said: "You, companions of Muhammad, tell us we do not know. So what about those who scratch our houses and steal our valuables?" He said: "Those are the wicked. Yes, none of them remains except four, one of them an old shaykh who, if he drank cold water, would not find its coldness."

The preferable view is that the verse is general concerning all the leaders of the disbelievers, without restriction to a specific time or a specific group, relying on the generality of the wording and not the specific occasion of revelation. Among what supports this is what Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Abd ar-Rahman ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr, that during the time of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, when he directed the people to Syria, he said: "You will find a people whose heads are hollowed out (i.e. empty of understanding); so strike the seats of Satan among them with swords. By God, for me to kill one man of them is dearer to me than to kill seventy of others." That is because God says: ﴿فَقاتِلُوا أئِمَّةَ الكُفْرِ﴾.

Abu ash-Shaykh reported from Hudhayfah concerning ﴿لا أيْمانَ لَهُمْ﴾ that he said: "They have no covenants."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported the like of it from 'Ammar.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu ash-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿ألا تُقاتِلُونَ قَوْمًا نَكَثُوا أيْمانَهم﴾ that he said: "It is the fighting of the Quraysh, allies of the Prophet ﷺ, and their intention to expel the Messenger."

It is claimed that this was in the year of the Prophet's ﷺ 'Umrah in the year following al-Hudaybiyah: Quraysh broke the covenant of al-Hudaybiyah, and they resolved in themselves that when they entered Makkah they would expel him from it; that was their intention to expel him. Khuza'ah did not follow them in that; when the Prophet ﷺ left Makkah, Quraysh said to Khuza'ah: "You blinded us from his expulsion," and they fought them and killed some men of them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu ash-Shaykh reported from 'Ikrimah that he said: the verse "قاتِلُوهم يُعَذِّبْهُمُ اللَّهُ بِأيْدِيكم ويُخْزِهِمْ" was revealed concerning Khuza'ah.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu ash-Shaykh reported the like of it from Mujahid.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu ash-Shaykh reported the like of it from as-Suddi.

Abu ash-Shaykh reported the like of it from Qatadah as well. Ibn Ishaq related the story in his Sirah, and included in it the verses which Khuza'ah sent to the Prophet ﷺ, the beginning of which is:

"O Lord, I call upon Muhammad to keep the alliance of our father and his father of old."

Al-Bayhaqi related the story in ad-Dala'il.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu ash-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the walījah is the inner confidant from outside their religion.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatadah, who said: walījah means treachery.

Most of the grammarians hold that this is a solecism (laḥn), because it involves the joining of two hamzahs in one word.

The majority recited it by making the second hamzah between-between (bayn bayn, i.e. between the point of articulation of the hamzah and that of the yā'). It was also recited with the yā' made pure, and that is a solecism, as az-Zamakhshari said.

According to the second recitation: these breakers of oaths who slander the religion are not among the people of faith in God, so as to deserve the protection of their blood and property; therefore fighting them is obligatory upon the Muslims.

His saying: "لَعَلَّهم يَنْتَهُونَ" ("so that they may desist") means: from their disbelief, their breaking of covenants, and their defaming of the religion of Islam.

The meaning is: their fighting is to be carried on until the goal, which is their ceasing from that.

This verse has been cited as evidence that a dhimmi who defames the religion is not killed until he breaks the covenant, as Abu Hanifah said, because God only commanded their killing on two conditions: one of them is breaking the covenant, and the second is defaming the religion. Malik, al-Shafi'i and others held that if he defames the religion he is killed, because by that his covenant is broken. They said: likewise, if a dhimmi commits mere breaking of the covenant alone, without defaming the religion, he is killed.

The meaning: whoever is in the condition of these people, in breaking the covenant, expelling the Messenger from Makkah, and initiating the fighting, is deserving that his fighting not be abandoned, and that whoever neglected that be rebuked. Then he increased the rebuke and said: "أتَخْشَوْنَهم" ("Do you fear them?"). This interrogative is for rebuke and reproach: that is, do you fear that some harm will befall you from them, so that you abandon fighting them out of this fear? Then he explained what the matter must be: ﴿فاللَّهُ أحَقُّ أنْ تَخْشَوْهُ إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("God has more right that you fear Him, if you are believers"), that is, He has more right to be feared by you, for He is the true Harmer and Benefactor; and from your fear of Him is that you fight those whom He has commanded you to fight, for the requirement of faith makes that obligatory upon you.

Then he increased the emphasis on the command to fight and said: "قاتِلُوهم" ("Fight them"), and upon this command he arranged several benefits. The first: God's punishment of the disbelievers by the hands of the believers, through killing and capture. The second: their humiliation; it was said: by capture, and it was said: by the abasement and disgrace that befell them. The third: the victory of the Muslims over them and their overcoming them. The fourth: that God heals with fighting the hearts (ṣudūr) of a people of believers from among those who did not witness the fighting nor were present at it. The fifth: that He, glorified is He, removes by fighting the rage (ghayẓ) of the hearts of the believers, which had befallen them because of what the disbelievers had done of matters that bring rage and constriction of the breast.

It is answered: the heart (qalb) is more specific than the breast (ṣadr).
