Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu ash-Shaykh reported the like of it from as-Suddi.

Abu ash-Shaykh reported the like of it from Qatadah as well. Ibn Ishaq related the story in his Sirah, and included in it the verses which Khuza'ah sent to the Prophet ﷺ, the beginning of which is:

"O Lord, I call upon Muhammad to keep the alliance of our father and his father of old."

Al-Bayhaqi related the story in ad-Dala'il.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu ash-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the walījah is the inner confidant from outside their religion.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatadah, who said: walījah means treachery.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 17–22:

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read "يَعْمُرُوا" (ya'muru) with a fatha on the present-tense letter and a damma on the mim, from ʿamara, yaʿmuru.

Ibn al-Sumaifiʿ read it with a damma on the present-tense letter, from aʿmara, yuʿmiru, meaning: they appoint someone to maintain it (yajʿalūna lahā man yaʿmuruhā).

Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Muhaysin, Sahm and Yaʿqub read "مَسْجِدَ اللَّهِ" (masjid Allah) in the singular.

The remaining readers read "مَسَاجِدَ" (masajid) in the plural. Abu ʿUbayda preferred this reading.

Al-Nahhas said: because it is more general, and the specific falls under the general.

It is also possible that the plural is intended to mean only the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram). This is permissible in the case of generic nouns (asmaʾ al-ajnas), as one says, "So-and-so rides horses," even if he has ridden only one horse.

He said: They have agreed on the plural in His words: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah﴾. It is also narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that He said "masajid" (mosques) while meaning the Sacred Mosque, because it is the qiblah of all mosques and their leader (imam), so its maintainer is like the maintainer of all the mosques.

Al-Farraʾ said: The Arabs sometimes place the singular in place of the plural, as in their saying, "So-and-so has much dirham (money)," and vice versa, as in their saying, "So-and-so sits with kings," though he may have sat with only one king.

The meaning of "ʿimara" (maintenance) is either its literal sense or its figurative sense, which is persistent attendance (mulazamah) at it and worship in it. Neither of these belongs to the polytheists. As for the first: it would imply a favour upon the Muslims by maintaining their mosques. As for the second: the unbelievers have no worship, given that they are forbidden from approaching the Sacred Mosque.

The meaning of ﴿It is not for the polytheists﴾ is: it is not valid or proper for them to do that.

﴿Bearing witness against themselves to disbelief﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: it is not for them to do that while they bear witness against themselves to disbelief, by displaying what is disbelief, namely setting up idols, worshipping them and taking them as gods. This is a testimony from them against themselves to disbelief, even if they deny it with their tongues. So how can they combine two contrary matters: the maintenance of mosques, which is the business of the believers, and the testimony against themselves to disbelief, which is not the business of one who seeks nearness to Allah by maintaining His mosques?

It was said: the meaning of this testimony is their saying during their circumambulation: "Here I am, O Allah, no partner have You, except a partner who is Yours, You possess him and what he possesses." It was also said: their testimony against themselves to disbelief is that the Jew says, "He is a Jew"; the Christian says, "He is a Christian"; the Sabian says, "He is a Sabian"; and the polytheist says, "He is a polytheist."

﴿Those, their deeds have become void﴾ — the deeds in which they take pride and which they suppose to be deeds of goodness. That is: they have been nullified and no trace of them remains.

﴿And in the Fire they will abide eternally﴾. In this nominal sentence, together with the fronting of the adverbial phrase that is attached to the predicate, there is an emphasis on its content.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear who is worthy of maintaining the mosque, saying: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾, and performs what is among the necessities of faith, namely establishing prayer, giving zakah, and not fearing anyone except Allah. Whoever combines these attributes is the one worthy of maintaining the mosques, not one who is devoid of them or of some of them. He limited the mention to prayer, zakah and fear (khashyah) as a reminder of what is among the greatest matters of religion, over what is other than them of what Allah has made obligatory upon His servants, because all of that is among the necessities of faith.

The discussion of the reason for the plural of "masajid" and of the explanation of the reality of "ʿimara" has already preceded. Whoever permits combining the literal and the figurative sense understands "ʿimara" here as both.

In His words: ﴿Perhaps those will be among the guided﴾, there is a cutting off of the hopes of the unbelievers of benefiting from their deeds. For if the guidance of those who possess these attributes is only hoped for, how about the unbelievers, who did not possess any of these attributes?

(p-562) It was said: "ʿasā" (perhaps) from Allah is binding (wājibah). It was said: it means "khalīq" (fitting, likely): that is, it is fitting that they will be among the guided. It was also said: the hope returns to the servants.

The interrogative in ﴿Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque﴾ is for denial (inkar). "Siqayah" (giving drink) and "ʿimarah" (maintenance) are verbal nouns (masdar), like "saʿayah" and "himayah." In the sentence there is an omission, and the estimate is: "Have you made the people of the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the mosque, or its people, like one who believes?" so that the subject and predicate agree. Or the estimate in the predicate is: "Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque like the deed of one who believes, or like the faith of one who believes?"

Ibn Abi Wajza al-Saʿdi, Ibn al-Zubayr and Saʿid ibn Jubayr read: "أَجَعَلْتُمْ سُقَاةَ الحَاجِّ وَعَمَرَةَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرَامِ" (ajaʿaltum suqat al-hajj wa-ʿamarat al-masjid al-haram), with "suqat" as the plural of "saqin" (one who gives drink) and "ʿamarat" as the plural of "ʿamir" (maintainer). On this reading no omitted element is needed. The meaning is that Allah denied them equating what the Jahiliyyah used to do, of deeds that took on the appearance of goodness even though they did not benefit from them, with the faith and jihad of the believers in the way of Allah. The polytheists used to take pride in the giving of drink and the maintenance, and prefer them over the deeds of the Muslims, so Allah denied this against them. Then He, glorified is He, explicitly stated the preference between the two groups, their differing, and their non-equality, saying: ﴿They are not equal in the sight of Allah﴾, meaning: that disbelieving group which gives drink to the pilgrims and maintains the Sacred Mosque is not equal to this believing group, which believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in His way.

By the negation of equality, He, glorified is He, indicated the negation of the virtue which the polytheists claim, meaning: if the deeds of the unbelievers do not reach the point of being equal to the deeds of the Muslims, how could they be superior to them as they claim? Then He judged them to be wrongdoers, and that, along with their wrongdoing in what they are engaged in of polytheism, they do not deserve guidance from Allah, glorified is He. In this there is an allusion to the (other) group.

Then He explicitly named the excellent group, saying: ﴿Those who believed...﴾ to the end of the verse, meaning those who combine faith, emigration (hijrah) and jihad with their wealth and their selves: ﴿They are greater in rank in the sight of Allah﴾, and more deserving of what is with Him of good than that polytheistic group, which takes pride in its deeds which are nullified and false. In His words, "in the sight of Allah" there is a great honouring of the believers. The reference in His words "those" to those characterised by the aforementioned attributes is: ﴿they are the triumphant﴾, that is, those specifically reserved for success in the sight of Allah.

Then He explained the success with His words: ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him, and approval, and gardens for them wherein is enduring bliss﴾. The indefiniteness in "mercy," "approval," and "gardens" is for magnification, and the meaning is that they are beyond the description of describers and the imagination of imaginers.

"Al-naʿim al-muqim" (enduring bliss) is that which is lasting and continuous and does not leave its possessor.

The mention of "abadan" (forever) after "khulud" (abiding) is an emphasis on it. The clause ﴿Indeed, with Allah is a great reward﴾ confirms what precedes it while also including a reason: that is, Allah, glorified is He, has given them these great rewards because the reward which is with Him is great, and He gives of it whatever He wills to whomever He wills, and He is the Lord of great bounty.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾, and He said: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾. So He negated the polytheists from the mosque. ﴿Who believes in Allah﴾: that is, who affirms the oneness of Allah and believes in what Allah has sent down, and establishes prayer, meaning the five prayers, ﴿and does not fear anyone except Allah﴾: that is, does not worship anyone except Allah. ﴿Perhaps those will be...﴾: that is, those are the guided, like His saying to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ (al-Isra, 79), meaning: your Lord will surely raise you to a praiseworthy station, which is the intercession. And every "ʿasā" (perhaps) in the Qur'an is binding.

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you see a man frequenting the mosques, then bear witness to him of faith." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾.

Many hadiths have been narrated concerning the recommendation of constant attendance at the mosques, maintaining them, and frequenting them for acts of obedience.

Muslim, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir, who said: "I was near the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among a group of his Companions. A man among them said: 'I do not care if I do no deed for Allah after Islam except that I give drink to the pilgrims.' Another said: 'Rather, the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque.' Another said: 'Rather, jihad in the way of Allah is better than what you have said.' ʿUmar rebuked them and said: 'Do not raise your voices near the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that is on Friday. But when I have prayed the Friday prayer, I will enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and ask him for a ruling concerning what you have disputed about.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims...﴾ up to His words: ﴿Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims﴾, the verse, and that is because the polytheists said: "The maintenance of the House of Allah and the custody of the giving of drink is better than one who believes and strives." So they used to boast of the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) and be arrogant with it, because they were its people and its maintainers. So Allah, glorified is He, mentioned their arrogance and their turning away, and He said to the polytheists of the Sacred Precinct: ﴿My verses were recited to you, but you used to turn back on your heels﴾, ﴿being arrogant regarding it, conversing by night, speaking nonsense﴾ (al-Muminun, 66–67). That is, they were arrogant about the Haram. And His words "sāmiran" (conversing by night): they used to converse about it in the night and revile the Qur'an and the Prophet (ﷺ). So the faith in Allah and the jihad alongside the Prophet of Allah are better than the polytheists' prosperity of the House and their custody of the giving of drink, and it would not benefit them with Allah while they associate partners with Him, even if they maintained His House and served it. Allah said: ﴿They are not equal in the sight of Allah, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning those who claimed that they were the people of maintenance. So He named them wrongdoers because of their polytheism, and thus the maintenance did not avail them anything. Al-ʿAwfi, who is weak, is in its chain of transmission.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: al-ʿAbbas said when he was taken captive on the day of Badr: "If you preceded us in Islam, emigration and jihad, we used to maintain the Sacred Mosque, give drink to the pilgrims and ransom the captive." So Allah revealed: ﴿Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims...﴾, the verse. Meaning: that was in polytheism, so I do not accept what was done in polytheism.

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him (Ibn ʿAbbas), concerning the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and al-ʿAbbas.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Shaʿbi, who said: ʿAli, al-ʿAbbas and Shayba boasted about the giving of drink and the custody of the key (al-hijabah). So Allah revealed: ﴿Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims...﴾, the verse. The meaning of this has been narrated through several chains.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read "يَعْمُرُوا" (ya'muru) with a fatha on the present-tense letter and a damma on the mim, from ʿamara, yaʿmuru.

Ibn al-Sumaifiʿ read it with a damma on the present-tense letter, from aʿmara, yuʿmiru, meaning: they appoint someone to maintain it (yajʿalūna lahā man yaʿmuruhā).

Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Muhaysin, Sahm and Yaʿqub read "مَسْجِدَ اللَّهِ" (masjid Allah) in the singular.

The remaining readers read "مَسَاجِدَ" (masajid) in the plural. Abu ʿUbayda preferred this reading.

Al-Nahhas said: because it is more general, and the specific falls under the general.

It is also possible that the plural is intended to mean only the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram). This is permissible in the case of generic nouns (asmaʾ al-ajnas), as one says, "So-and-so rides horses," even if he has ridden only one horse.

He said: They have agreed on the plural in His words: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah﴾. It is also narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that He said "masajid" (mosques) while meaning the Sacred Mosque, because it is the qiblah of all mosques and their leader (imam), so its maintainer is like the maintainer of all the mosques.

Al-Farraʾ said: The Arabs sometimes place the singular in place of the plural, as in their saying, "So-and-so has much dirham (money)," and vice versa, as in their saying, "So-and-so sits with kings," though he may have sat with only one king.

The meaning of "ʿimara" (maintenance) is either its literal sense or its figurative sense, which is persistent attendance (mulazamah) at it and worship in it. Neither of these belongs to the polytheists. As for the first: it would imply a favour upon the Muslims by maintaining their mosques. As for the second: the unbelievers have no worship, given that they are forbidden from approaching the Sacred Mosque.

The meaning of ﴿It is not for the polytheists﴾ is: it is not valid or proper for them to do that.

﴿Bearing witness against themselves to disbelief﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: it is not for them to do that while they bear witness against themselves to disbelief, by displaying what is disbelief, namely setting up idols, worshipping them and taking them as gods. This is a testimony from them against themselves to disbelief, even if they deny it with their tongues. So how can they combine two contrary matters: the maintenance of mosques, which is the business of the believers, and the testimony against themselves to disbelief, which is not the business of one who seeks nearness to Allah by maintaining His mosques?

It was said: the meaning of this testimony is their saying during their circumambulation: "Here I am, O Allah, no partner have You, except a partner who is Yours, You possess him and what he possesses." It was also said: their testimony against themselves to disbelief is that the Jew says, "He is a Jew"; the Christian says, "He is a Christian"; the Sabian says, "He is a Sabian"; and the polytheist says, "He is a polytheist."

﴿Those, their deeds have become void﴾ — the deeds in which they take pride and which they suppose to be deeds of goodness. That is: they have been nullified and no trace of them remains.

﴿And in the Fire they will abide eternally﴾. In this nominal sentence, together with the fronting of the adverbial phrase that is attached to the predicate, there is an emphasis on its content.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear who is worthy of maintaining the mosque, saying: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾, and performs what is among the necessities of faith, namely establishing prayer, giving zakah, and not fearing anyone except Allah. Whoever combines these attributes is the one worthy of maintaining the mosques, not one who is devoid of them or of some of them. He limited the mention to prayer, zakah and fear (khashyah) as a reminder of what is among the greatest matters of religion, over what is other than them of what Allah has made obligatory upon His servants, because all of that is among the necessities of faith.

The discussion of the reason for the plural of "masajid" and of the explanation of the reality of "ʿimara" has already preceded. Whoever permits combining the literal and the figurative sense understands "ʿimara" here as both.

In His words: ﴿Perhaps those will be among the guided﴾, there is a cutting off of the hopes of the unbelievers of benefiting from their deeds. For if the guidance of those who possess these attributes is only hoped for, how about the unbelievers, who did not possess any of these attributes?

(p-562) It was said: "ʿasā" (perhaps) from Allah is binding (wājibah). It was said: it means "khalīq" (fitting, likely): that is, it is fitting that they will be among the guided. It was also said: the hope returns to the servants.

The interrogative in ﴿Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque﴾ is for denial (inkar). "Siqayah" (giving drink) and "ʿimarah" (maintenance) are verbal nouns (masdar), like "saʿayah" and "himayah." In the sentence there is an omission, and the estimate is: "Have you made the people of the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the mosque, or its people, like one who believes?" so that the subject and predicate agree. Or the estimate in the predicate is: "Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque like the deed of one who believes, or like the faith of one who believes?"

Ibn Abi Wajza al-Saʿdi, Ibn al-Zubayr and Saʿid ibn Jubayr read: "أَجَعَلْتُمْ سُقَاةَ الحَاجِّ وَعَمَرَةَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرَامِ" (ajaʿaltum suqat al-hajj wa-ʿamarat al-masjid al-haram), with "suqat" as the plural of "saqin" (one who gives drink) and "ʿamarat" as the plural of "ʿamir" (maintainer). On this reading no omitted element is needed. The meaning is that Allah denied them equating what the Jahiliyyah used to do, of deeds that took on the appearance of goodness even though they did not benefit from them, with the faith and jihad of the believers in the way of Allah. The polytheists used to take pride in the giving of drink and the maintenance, and prefer them over the deeds of the Muslims, so Allah denied this against them. Then He, glorified is He, explicitly stated the preference between the two groups, their differing, and their non-equality, saying: ﴿They are not equal in the sight of Allah﴾, meaning: that disbelieving group which gives drink to the pilgrims and maintains the Sacred Mosque is not equal to this believing group, which believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in His way.

By the negation of equality, He, glorified is He, indicated the negation of the virtue which the polytheists claim, meaning: if the deeds of the unbelievers do not reach the point of being equal to the deeds of the Muslims, how could they be superior to them as they claim? Then He judged them to be wrongdoers, and that, along with their wrongdoing in what they are engaged in of polytheism, they do not deserve guidance from Allah, glorified is He. In this there is an allusion to the (other) group.

In His words, "in the sight of Allah" there is a great honouring of the believers. The reference in His words "those" to those characterised by the aforementioned attributes is: ﴿they are the triumphant﴾, that is, those specifically reserved for success in the sight of Allah.

Then He explained the success with His words: ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him, and approval, and gardens for them wherein is enduring bliss﴾. The indefiniteness in "mercy," "approval," and "gardens" is for magnification, and the meaning is that they are beyond the description of describers and the imagination of imaginers.

"Al-naʿim al-muqim" (enduring bliss) is that which is lasting and continuous and does not leave its possessor.

The mention of "abadan" (forever) after "khulud" (abiding) is an emphasis on it. The clause ﴿Indeed, with Allah is a great reward﴾ confirms what precedes it while also including a reason: that is, Allah, glorified is He, has given them these great rewards because the reward which is with Him is great, and He gives of it whatever He wills to whomever He wills, and He is the Lord of great bounty.

So He negated the polytheists from the mosque. ﴿Who believes in Allah﴾: that is, who affirms the oneness of Allah and believes in what Allah has sent down, and establishes prayer, meaning the five prayers, ﴿and does not fear anyone except Allah﴾: that is, does not worship anyone except Allah. ﴿Perhaps those will be...﴾: that is, those are the guided, like His saying to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ (al-Isra, 79), meaning: your Lord will surely raise you to a praiseworthy station, which is the intercession. And every "ʿasā" (perhaps) in the Qur'an is binding.

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you see a man frequenting the mosques, then bear witness to him of faith." Many hadiths have been narrated concerning the recommendation of constant attendance at the mosques, maintaining them, and frequenting them for acts of obedience.

The remaining readers read "مَسَاجِدَ" (masajid) in the plural. Abu ʿUbayda preferred this reading.

Al-Nahhas said: because it is more general, and the specific falls under the general.

It is also possible that the plural is intended to mean only the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram). This is permissible in the case of generic nouns (asmaʾ al-ajnas), as one says, "So-and-so rides horses," even if he has ridden only one horse.

He said: They have agreed on the plural in His words: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah﴾. It is also narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that He said "masajid" (mosques) while meaning the Sacred Mosque, because it is the qiblah of all mosques and their leader (imam), so its maintainer is like the maintainer of all the mosques.

Al-Farraʾ said: The Arabs sometimes place the singular in place of the plural, as in their saying, "So-and-so has much dirham (money)," and vice versa, as in their saying, "So-and-so sits with kings," though he may have sat with only one king.

The meaning of "ʿimara" (maintenance) is either its literal sense or its figurative sense, which is persistent attendance (mulazamah) at it and worship in it. Neither of these belongs to the polytheists. As for the first: it would imply a favour upon the Muslims by maintaining their mosques. As for the second: the unbelievers have no worship, given that they are forbidden from approaching the Sacred Mosque.

The meaning of ﴿It is not for the polytheists﴾ is: it is not valid or proper for them to do that.

﴿Bearing witness against themselves to disbelief﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: it is not for them to do that while they bear witness against themselves to disbelief, by displaying what is disbelief, namely setting up idols, worshipping them and taking them as gods. This is a testimony from them against themselves to disbelief, even if they deny it with their tongues. So how can they combine two contrary matters: the maintenance of mosques, which is the business of the believers, and the testimony against themselves to disbelief, which is not the business of one who seeks nearness to Allah by maintaining His mosques?

It was said: the meaning of this testimony is their saying during their circumambulation: "Here I am, O Allah, no partner have You, except a partner who is Yours, You possess him and what he possesses." It was also said: their testimony against themselves to disbelief is that the Jew says, "He is a Jew"; the Christian says, "He is a Christian"; the Sabian says, "He is a Sabian"; and the polytheist says, "He is a polytheist."

﴿Those, their deeds have become void﴾ — the deeds in which they take pride and which they suppose to be deeds of goodness. That is: they have been nullified and no trace of them remains.

﴿And in the Fire they will abide eternally﴾. In this nominal sentence, together with the fronting of the adverbial phrase that is attached to the predicate, there is an emphasis on its content.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear who is worthy of maintaining the mosque, saying: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾, and performs what is among the necessities of faith, namely establishing prayer, giving zakah, and not fearing anyone except Allah. Whoever combines these attributes is the one worthy of maintaining the mosques, not one who is devoid of them or of some of them. He limited the mention to prayer, zakah and fear (khashyah) as a reminder of what is among the greatest matters of religion, over what is other than them of what Allah has made obligatory upon His servants, because all of that is among the necessities of faith.

The discussion of the reason for the plural of "masajid" and of the explanation of the reality of "ʿimara" has already preceded. Whoever permits combining the literal and the figurative sense understands "ʿimara" here as both.

In His words: ﴿Perhaps those will be among the guided﴾, there is a cutting off of the hopes of the unbelievers of benefiting from their deeds. For if the guidance of those who possess these attributes is only hoped for, how about the unbelievers, who did not possess any of these attributes?

(p-562) It was said: "ʿasā" (perhaps) from Allah is binding (wājibah). It was said: it means "khalīq" (fitting, likely): that is, it is fitting that they will be among the guided. It was also said: the hope returns to the servants.

The interrogative in ﴿Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque﴾ is for denial (inkar). "Siqayah" (giving drink) and "ʿimarah" (maintenance) are verbal nouns (masdar), like "saʿayah" and "himayah." In the sentence there is an omission, and the estimate is: "Have you made the people of the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the mosque, or its people, like one who believes?" so that the subject and predicate agree. Or the estimate in the predicate is: "Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque like the deed of one who believes, or like the faith of one who believes?"

Ibn Abi Wajza al-Saʿdi, Ibn al-Zubayr and Saʿid ibn Jubayr read: "أَجَعَلْتُمْ سُقَاةَ الحَاجِّ وَعَمَرَةَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرَامِ" (ajaʿaltum suqat al-hajj wa-ʿamarat al-masjid al-haram), with "suqat" as the plural of "saqin" (one who gives drink) and "ʿamarat" as the plural of "ʿamir" (maintainer). On this reading no omitted element is needed. The meaning is that Allah denied them equating what the Jahiliyyah used to do, of deeds that took on the appearance of goodness even though they did not benefit from them, with the faith and jihad of the believers in the way of Allah. The polytheists used to take pride in the giving of drink and the maintenance, and prefer them over the deeds of the Muslims, so Allah denied this against them. Then He, glorified is He, explicitly stated the preference between the two groups, their differing, and their non-equality, saying: ﴿They are not equal in the sight of Allah﴾, meaning: that disbelieving group which gives drink to the pilgrims and maintains the Sacred Mosque is not equal to this believing group, which believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in His way.

By the negation of equality, He, glorified is He, indicated the negation of the virtue which the polytheists claim, meaning: if the deeds of the unbelievers do not reach the point of being equal to the deeds of the Muslims, how could they be superior to them as they claim? Then He judged them to be wrongdoers, and that, along with their wrongdoing in what they are engaged in of polytheism, they do not deserve guidance from Allah, glorified is He. In this there is an allusion to the (other) group.

Then He explicitly named the excellent group, saying: ﴿Those who believed...﴾ to the end of the verse, meaning those who combine faith, emigration (hijrah) and jihad with their wealth and their selves: ﴿They are greater in rank in the sight of Allah﴾, and more deserving of what is with Him of good than that polytheistic group, which takes pride in its deeds which are nullified and false. In His words, "in the sight of Allah" there is a great honouring of the believers. The reference in His words "those" to those characterised by the aforementioned attributes is: ﴿they are the triumphant﴾, that is, those specifically reserved for success in the sight of Allah.

Then He explained the success with His words: ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him, and approval, and gardens for them wherein is enduring bliss﴾. The indefiniteness in "mercy," "approval," and "gardens" is for magnification, and the meaning is that they are beyond the description of describers and the imagination of imaginers.

"Al-naʿim al-muqim" (enduring bliss) is that which is lasting and continuous and does not leave its possessor.

The mention of "abadan" (forever) after "khulud" (abiding) is an emphasis on it. The clause ﴿Indeed, with Allah is a great reward﴾ confirms what precedes it while also including a reason: that is, Allah, glorified is He, has given them these great rewards because the reward which is with Him is great, and He gives of it whatever He wills to whomever He wills, and He is the Lord of great bounty.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾, and He said: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾. So He negated the polytheists from the mosque. ﴿Who believes in Allah﴾: that is, who affirms the oneness of Allah and believes in what Allah has sent down, and establishes prayer, meaning the five prayers, ﴿and does not fear anyone except Allah﴾: that is, does not worship anyone except Allah. ﴿Perhaps those will be...﴾: that is, those are the guided, like His saying to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ (al-Isra, 79), meaning: your Lord will surely raise you to a praiseworthy station, which is the intercession. And every "ʿasā" (perhaps) in the Qur'an is binding.

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Darimi, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you see a man frequenting the mosques, then bear witness to him of faith." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾.

Many hadiths have been narrated concerning the recommendation of constant attendance at the mosques, maintaining them, and frequenting them for acts of obedience.

Muslim, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir, who said: "I was near the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among a group of his Companions. A man among them said: 'I do not care if I do no deed for Allah after Islam except that I give drink to the pilgrims.' Another said: 'Rather, the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque.' Another said: 'Rather, jihad in the way of Allah is better than what you have said.' ʿUmar rebuked them and said: 'Do not raise your voices near the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that is on Friday. But when I have prayed the Friday prayer, I will enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and ask him for a ruling concerning what you have disputed about.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims...﴾ up to His words: ﴿Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims﴾, the verse, and that is because the polytheists said: "The maintenance of the House of Allah and the custody of the giving of drink is better than one who believes and strives." So they used to boast of the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) and be arrogant with it, because they were its people and its maintainers. So Allah, glorified is He, mentioned their arrogance and their turning away, and He said to the polytheists of the Sacred Precinct: ﴿My verses were recited to you, but you used to turn back on your heels﴾, ﴿being arrogant regarding it, conversing by night, speaking nonsense﴾ (al-Muminun, 66–67). That is, they were arrogant about the Haram. And His words "sāmiran" (conversing by night): they used to converse about it in the night and revile the Qur'an and the Prophet (ﷺ). So the faith in Allah and the jihad alongside the Prophet of Allah are better than the polytheists' prosperity of the House and their custody of the giving of drink, and it would not benefit them with Allah while they associate partners with Him, even if they maintained His House and served it. Allah said: ﴿They are not equal in the sight of Allah, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning those who claimed that they were the people of maintenance. So He named them wrongdoers because of their polytheism, and thus the maintenance did not avail them anything. Al-ʿAwfi, who is weak, is in its chain of transmission.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: al-ʿAbbas said when he was taken captive on the day of Badr: "If you preceded us in Islam, emigration and jihad, we used to maintain the Sacred Mosque, give drink to the pilgrims and ransom the captive." So Allah revealed: ﴿Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims...﴾, the verse. Meaning: that was in polytheism, so I do not accept what was done in polytheism.

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him (Ibn ʿAbbas), concerning the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and al-ʿAbbas.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Shaʿbi, who said: ʿAli, al-ʿAbbas and Shayba boasted about the giving of drink and the custody of the key (al-hijabah). So Allah revealed: ﴿Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims...﴾, the verse. The meaning of this has been narrated through several chains.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verse 23–24:

The address is to the believers in general, and it is a ruling that remains in force until the Day of Resurrection, indicating the severing of loyalty (wilayah) between believers and disbelievers. A group of the people of knowledge (ahl al-ilm) said: it was revealed to urge emigration (hijrah) and to renounce the lands of disbelief. In that case the address is to those believers who were in Makkah and other lands of the Arabs. They were forbidden to take as allies their fathers and brothers, lest they follow them in settling in lands of disbelief.

"In-istahabbu" (if they prefer): that is, if they love, just as it is said istajaba (to respond) in the sense of ajaba (to answer). Originally it means seeking love. The detailed discussion of this matter has already been given in Surah al-Ma'idah in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 51). Then He judged that whoever takes as ally those who prefer disbelief over faith, from among fathers and brothers, is a wrongdoer (zalim). This indicates that taking such people as allies is among the greatest and most severe of sins.

Then Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to say to them: ﴿If your fathers﴾ to the end of the verse. The ashirah (kin group) is the group that traces back to a single ancestor, and the ashirah of a man are his nearest relatives, those who associate with him closely. It is a collective noun (ism jam').

Abu Bakr and Hammad read "ashiratukum" in the plural.

Al-Akhfash said: the Arabs hardly pluralize ashirah as ashirat; rather they pluralize it as ashair.

Its original sense is detaching a thing from its place, and the root revolves around nearness: the earner brings a thing near himself and brings it under his possession. Al-kasad (slackness of trade) means the lack of demand, because the time for selling them has passed through emigration and leaving homelands.

Among the strange interpretations is what is narrated from Ibn al-Mubarak, that he said: the intended meaning of "trade" in this verse is daughters and sisters who, when they become unmarried (kasadna) in the house, find no suitor for them. He cited in support of this the words of the poet:

"They remained unmarried among their people because of poverty, and my standing (among them) has only increased their unmarried state."

Although this line uses kasad for the absence of a suitor for them, there is no permission in it to apply the name of "trade" to them. By "the dwellings they are pleased with" is meant the homes that please them and to which their souls incline, and they see residing in them as more beloved to them than emigrating to Allah and His Messenger. It has been said: the intended meaning of Allah's command, glorified is He, is fighting. Then it was revealed: ﴿Do not take your fathers and your brothers﴾, the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil concerning this verse that he said: it is about emigration.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verse 23–24:

The address is to the believers in general, and it is a ruling that remains in force until the Day of Resurrection, indicating the severing of loyalty (wilayah) between believers and disbelievers. A group of the people of knowledge (ahl al-ilm) said: it was revealed to urge emigration (hijrah) and to renounce the lands of disbelief. In that case the address is to those believers who were in Makkah and other lands of the Arabs. They were forbidden to take as allies their fathers and brothers, lest they follow them in settling in lands of disbelief.

"In-istahabbu" (if they prefer): that is, if they love, just as it is said istajaba (to respond) in the sense of ajaba (to answer). Originally it means seeking love. The detailed discussion of this matter has already been given in Surah al-Ma'idah in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 51). Then He judged that whoever takes as ally those who prefer disbelief over faith, from among fathers and brothers, is a wrongdoer (zalim). This indicates that taking such people as allies is among the greatest and most severe of sins.

Then Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to say to them: ﴿If your fathers﴾ to the end of the verse. The ashirah (kin group) is the group that traces back to a single ancestor, and the ashirah of a man are his nearest relatives, those who associate with him closely. It is a collective noun (ism jam').

The places of battle are plural of "mawtin" (station, position), and the places of battle are its stations. The places in which Allah gave victory to the Muslims are the Day of Badr and what came after it of the places in which Allah gave the Muslims victory over the disbelievers before the Day of Hunayn. ﴿And the Day of Hunayn﴾ is in the conjunctive relation to "mawatin" with an elided noun, either at the first, the meaning being "in the days of places," or at the second, the meaning being "and the place of the Day of Hunayn," lest time be conjoined to place.

It was answered that there is no improbability in conjoining time to place, so no elision is needed. It was also said that "the Day of Hunayn" is in the accusative by a verb understood and conjoined to "nasarakum" (He gave you victory), meaning "and He gave you victory on the Day of Hunayn." The author of al-Kashshaf preferred this, saying: what necessitates it is that His saying "when your number pleased you" (idh a'jabat-kum) is an apposition to "the Day of Hunayn," so if it were made to govern the verb, this apparent reading would not be valid, because their numbers did not please them in all those places, nor were they numerous in all of them.

It was answered that conjunction does not require that the conjoined items share in everything that is established for the first item, as you say: "Zayd and 'Amr came to me with his people," or "in his clothes," or "on his horse." It was also said that ﴿when your great number pleased you﴾ is not an apposition to "the Day of Hunayn," but is in the accusative by a verb understood: i.e., remember when your great number pleased you. Hunayn is a valley between Makkah and al-Ta'if; it is treated as diptote (not taking tanwin) on the basis that it is the name of a place, while some Arabs treat it as triptote on the basis that it is the name of a locality. From this is the poet's saying:

"They gave victory to their Prophet and strengthened his support at Hunayn, the day the champions called upon one another."

The reason those Muslims who were pleased by their numbers were pleased is that they were twelve thousand; it was also said eleven thousand, and it was also said sixteen thousand. Some of them said: "We will not be defeated today for lack of numbers." So they were left to this statement, and the great number availed them nothing; rather they fled, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood firm, and with him stood a small group of them, including his uncle al-'Abbas and Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith. Then the Muslims returned, and there was victory and triumph.

"Al-ighna'" (sufficing) means giving what removes need: i.e., the great number gave you nothing that removes your need and did not benefit you.

His saying "bima rahubat" — "ruhb" with a damma on the ra' means breadth, and "rahb" with a fatha on the ra' means a wide place. The ba' is in the sense of "ma'a" (with), and "ma" is masdariyya (verbal), and the place of the prepositional phrase is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

The meaning: the earth, despite being broad in its expanses, became constricted for them because of the fear and dread that befell them. It was also said that the ba' is in the sense of "ala" (upon): i.e., upon its breadth. ﴿Then you turned back, retreating﴾: i.e., you were routed while retreating, turning your backs and making your direction toward your enemy.

His saying: ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾: they are those who did not flee; it was also said: those who fled. The apparent meaning is all who were present among them, because they stood firm after that, fought, and were victorious.

His saying: ﴿and sent down hosts you did not see﴾ — they are the angels.

Their number has been disputed in several reports: it was said five thousand, it was said eight thousand, it was said sixteen thousand, and it was said other than that. This is not known except through prophetic transmission.

They also differed on whether the angels fought on this day or not. It has already been mentioned that the angels did not fight except on the Day of Badr, and that they were present on other occasions only to strengthen the hearts of the believers and to cast terror into the hearts of the polytheists. ﴿And He punished those who disbelieved﴾ by what befell them of killing, capture, seizure of property, and taking of women and children captive. The reference in His saying "That" (dhalika) is to the punishment implied by "punished." What befell them of punishment on this day was called "recompense" although it is not sufficient, rather the punishment of the Hereafter is also necessary, as an exaggeration in describing what befell them and magnifying it.

﴿Then Allah turns in repentance after that to whom He wills﴾: i.e., after this punishment, to whom He wills of those He guided to Islam. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving﴾: He forgives whoever sins and repents. ﴿Merciful﴾ to His servants, bestowing upon them forgiveness for what they committed.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah, who said: Hunayn is what lies between Makkah and al-Ta'if. The Prophet of Allah fought Hawazin and Thaqif; over Hawazin was Malik ibn 'Awf, and over Thaqif was 'Abd Yalil ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Hasan, who said: "When the people of Makkah and the people of Madinah gathered, they said: Now we will fight since we have gathered. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked what they said and what their great number pleased them with. They met and were routed, until no one stood over anyone, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ began calling out to the tribes of the Arabs: 'To me, to me!' By Allah, no one turned toward him until his place was emptied. He turned to the Ansar, who were on one side, and called out to them: 'O Ansar of Allah and Ansar of His Messenger, to me, servants of Allah, I am the Messenger of Allah!' They knelt weeping and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, by the Lord of the Ka'bah, we come to you, by Allah!' They lowered their heads weeping, and advanced their swords, striking before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, until Allah granted them victory."

al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from al-Rabi': "A man said on the Day of Hunayn: 'We will not be defeated for lack of numbers,' which grieved the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so Allah sent down: ﴿And on the Day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you﴾." al-Rabi' said: They were twelve thousand, of whom two thousand were from the people of Makkah.

al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the Day of Hunayn. The people turned away from him, and I remained with him with eighty men of the Muhajirun and the Ansar. We stood on our feet about eighty paces, and we did not turn our backs to them. They are the ones upon whom Allah sent down tranquillity. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was on his white mule, moving forward. He said: 'Hand me a handful of dust.' I handed it to him, and he struck with it at their faces, and their eyes were filled with dust, and the polytheists turned their backs."

The battle of Hunayn is mentioned in the books of biography and hadith with its full length and details, so we will not lengthen with that.

What befell them of punishment on this day was called "recompense" although it is not sufficient, rather the punishment of the Hereafter is also necessary, as an exaggeration in describing what befell them and magnifying it.

﴿Then Allah turns in repentance after that to whom He wills﴾: i.e., after this punishment, to whom He wills of those He guided to Islam. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving﴾: He forgives whoever sins and repents. ﴿Merciful﴾ to His servants, bestowing upon them forgiveness for what they committed.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah, who said: Hunayn is what lies between Makkah and al-Ta'if. The Prophet of Allah fought Hawazin and Thaqif; over Hawazin was Malik ibn 'Awf, and over Thaqif was 'Abd Yalil ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Hasan, who said: "When the people of Makkah and the people of Madinah gathered, they said: Now we will fight since we have gathered. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked what they said and what their great number pleased them with. They met and were routed, until no one stood over anyone, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ began calling out to the tribes of the Arabs: 'To me, to me!' By Allah, no one turned toward him until his place was emptied. He turned to the Ansar, who were on one side, and called out to them: 'O Ansar of Allah and Ansar of His Messenger, to me, servants of Allah, I am the Messenger of Allah!' They knelt weeping and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, by the Lord of the Ka'bah, we come to you, by Allah!' They lowered their heads weeping, and advanced their swords, striking before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, until Allah granted them victory."

al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from al-Rabi': "A man said on the Day of Hunayn: 'We will not be defeated for lack of numbers,' which grieved the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so Allah sent down: ﴿And on the Day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you﴾." al-Rabi' said: They were twelve thousand, of whom two thousand were from the people of Makkah.

al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the Day of Hunayn. The people turned away from him, and I remained with him with eighty men of the Muhajirun and the Ansar. We stood on our feet about eighty paces, and we did not turn our backs to them. They are the ones upon whom Allah sent down tranquillity. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was on his white mule, moving forward. He said: 'Hand me a handful of dust.' I handed it to him, and he struck with it at their faces, and their eyes were filled with dust, and the polytheists turned their backs."

The battle of Hunayn is mentioned in the books of biography and hadith with its full length and details, so we will not lengthen with that.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿and sent down hosts you did not see﴾: they are the angels. ﴿And He punished those who disbelieved﴾: he killed them by the sword.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: On the Day of Hunayn, Allah aided His Messenger with five thousand angels, marked (musawwimin), and on that day Allah named the Ansar "believers." He said: So He sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, who said: "Before the defeat of the people, while the people were fighting, I saw something like a black cloak descend from the sky until it fell between the people. I looked, and there were black ants spread out that filled the valley. I had no doubt that they were the angels, and there was nothing but the people's defeat."

The noun *najas* (ritual impurity) is a verbal noun that is not made dual or plural. One says *rajulun najasun* (a man who is impure), *imra'atun najasun* (a woman who is impure), *rajulani najasun*, *imra'atani najasun*, *rijalun najasun*, and *nisa'un najisun*. It is also said *najisun* and *najusun* (with the jim vowelled with kasra and with damma), and *nijsun* (with the nun vowelled with kasra and the jim sukun), which is a lightened form of the vowelled one. It has been said that this form is used only when *rijs* (filth) is mentioned with it, and it has been said that this is a general tendency rather than an absolute rule. (p. 565)

*Al-mushrikun* (the polytheists) is the subject, and its predicate is the verbal noun *najas*, as an intensification in describing them with it, to the point that they are as if they were the very embodiment of impurity. Or it is by way of an implied genitive construction: *dhawu najasin* (those possessing impurity), because *shirk* (associating partners with God) is with them, and it is in the position of impurity.

Qatada and Ma'mar and others said: they were described with this because they do not purify themselves, do not perform ritual bathing, and do not avoid impurities.

The verse has been used as evidence by those who say that the polytheist is impure in his very essence, as the Zahiris (literalist school) and some Zaydis (followers of Zayd ibn Ali) held. This is also reported from al-Hasan al-Basri, and it is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The majority of the early and later scholars, including the followers of the four legal schools, held that the disbeliever is not impure in essence, because God, glorified is He, made their food lawful, and there is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ in this matter, in his deeds and his words, what indicates that their persons are not impure. He ate from their vessels, drank from them, performed ablution in them, and lodged them in his mosque.

His saying: ﴿So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque﴾. The *fa'* is for consequence: their not approaching the Sacred Mosque is a consequence of their impurity.

By "the Sacred Mosque" is meant the whole Sacred Precinct (*al-Haram*). This was reported from 'Ata', so they are prevented from the entire Sacred Precinct. Others among the scholars held that what is meant is the Sacred Mosque itself, so the polytheist is not prevented from entering the rest of the Sacred Precinct.

The scholars differed concerning the polytheist's entering mosques other than the Sacred Mosque. The people of Medina held that every polytheist is prevented from every mosque.

Al-Shafi'i said: the verse is general concerning all polytheists, but specific to the Sacred Mosque, so they are not prevented from entering other mosques.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is rigid adherence on his part to the apparent wording, because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are impure﴾ is an indication of the cause, namely shirk and impurity. It may be answered that this analogy is rejected by the Prophet's ﷺ lodging Thumama ibn Uthal in his mosque, and by his lodging the delegation of Thaqif in it.

It is reported from Abu Hanifa the same as the view of al-Shafi'i, and he added that it is permissible for the dhimmi (protected non-Muslim) to enter all mosques without need. Al-Shafi'i restricted it to necessity. Qatada said: this is permitted for the dhimmi but not for the polytheist.

It is also reported from Abu Hanifa that it is permissible for them to enter the Sacred Precinct, the Sacred Mosque, and all other mosques. The prohibition on the polytheists approaching the Sacred Mosque is a prohibition to the Muslims against enabling them to do so, and it is of the type of their saying: "I will not see you here."

His saying: ﴿after this year of theirs﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: it is the year nine (AH), the year in which Abu Bakr performed the pilgrimage at the season.

The second: it is the year ten, as Qatada said. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is the correct view that the wording indicates. It is strange to say that it is the year nine, which is the year in which the proclamation occurred. If a man's slave entered his house one day, and his master said to him: "Do not enter this house after your day," the intended meaning would not be the day on which he entered. End of quotation.

It may be answered that what the wording indicates is contrary to what he claimed, for the reference in His saying ﴿after this year of theirs﴾ is to the year mentioned before the demonstrative, which is the year of the proclamation. Likewise in the example he gave, the intended meaning is the prohibition of entering after the day of entry that is the subject of the address. The matter is evident and not hidden. Perhaps he intended the explanation of what follows the *mudaf* (the noun in the construct phrase) "their year", and there is no doubt that it is the year ten. As for the explanation of the year referred to by "this", there is no doubt whatsoever that it is the year nine. On this basis Qatada's statement is to be understood.

Those who held that the polytheists are permitted to enter the Sacred Mosque and other mosques have argued from this qualifier, namely His saying ﴿after this year of theirs﴾, saying that the prohibition is specific to the time of the Hajj and 'Umra, so they are prohibited only from Hajj and 'Umra and not from entering in general.

It may be answered that the apparent meaning of the prohibition of approaching after this year indicates a prohibition on approaching at every time that comes after it, and specifying some of these times as permissible requires a specifier.

His saying: ﴿And if you fear poverty, God will enrich you from His bounty﴾. *'Ayla* is poverty. One says: 'ala al-rajulu ya'ilu, when he becomes poor. The poet said:

*"The poor man does not know when his wealth will come, and the rich man does not know when he will become poor."*

'Alqama and others among the companions of Ibn Mas'ud read *'ayilatan*, which is a verbal noun like *qa'ila*, *'afiya* and *'aqiba*. It has been said that its meaning is a difficult matter. One says: 'alani al-amr ya'ulunI, meaning the matter was hard and severe upon me.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari related that one says 'ala ya'ulu, when he became poor. When the Muslims prevented the polytheists from the season, and they used to bring foodstuffs and merchandise to it, Satan cast into their hearts the fear of poverty, and they said: "From where shall we live?" So God promised them that He would enrich them from His bounty.

Al-Dahhak said: then God opened to them the gate of the jizya (poll tax) from the People of the Dhimma, by His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in God﴾, the verse.

'Ikrima said: He enriched them by the abundance of rain and vegetation and the fertility of the land, and the Arabs embraced Islam, and they carried to Mecca what God had enriched them with.

It has been said: He enriched them by the *fay'* (spoils acquired without battle). The purpose of the qualification by "if God wills" is to teach the servants to say it in everything they speak about that relates to the future, and so that they do not slacken in supplication and entreaty. God is All-Knowing of your conditions, All-Wise in His giving and His withholding. What He wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be.

His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in God﴾, the verse. In it is the command to fight those who combine these attributes.

Abu al-Wafa' ibn 'Aqil said: His saying "fight" is a command to punishment. Then He said: ﴿those who do not believe in God﴾, thereby specifying the sin that makes the punishment obligatory. Then He said: ﴿nor in the Last Day﴾, emphasizing the sin on the side of belief. Then He said: ﴿nor do they forbid what God and His Messenger have forbidden﴾, which adds to the sin in violating deeds. Then He said: ﴿nor do they adopt the religion of truth﴾, which indicates the emphasis of disobedience through deviation, obstinacy and aversion to submission. Then He said: ﴿from among those who were given the Scripture﴾, which is emphasis of the proof against them, for they used to find it written among them in the Torah and the Gospel. Then He said: ﴿until they give the jizya﴾, thereby specifying the limit to which the punishment extends. End of quotation.

His saying: ﴿from among those who were given the Scripture﴾ is an explanation of the relative pronoun together with what is in its clause, and they are the people of the Torah and the Gospel.

His saying: ﴿until they give the jizya with willing submission (*'an yadin*)﴾. The *jizya* is on the pattern *fi'la*, from *jaza, yajzi*, when one repays for what was done to him. So it is as if they gave it as repayment for what they were granted of security. It has been said: it was named *jizya* because it is a portion of what the People of the Dhimma must repay, that is, pay off. In the Sharia it is what the mu'ahid (one under treaty) gives for his covenant. And *'an yadin* is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

The meaning is: with a willing hand, not refusing. It has been said: its meaning is that they give it with their own hands, not appointing anyone to deliver it on their behalf. It has been said: its meaning is ready cash, not deferred. It has been said: by compulsion. It has been said: its meaning is as a favour from you to them, because taking it from them is a kind of favour to them. It has been said: its meaning is "disgraced."

A group of the scholars, including al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri and Abu Thawr, held that the jizya is not accepted except from the People of the Book.

Al-Awza'i and Malik said that the jizya is taken from all kinds of disbelievers, whoever they may be, and according to the first view the Magians are included among the People of the Book.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: I know of no disagreement that the jizya is taken from them.

The scholars differed concerning the amount of the jizya. 'Ata' said: there is no fixed amount for it; it is taken according to what they agreed upon in a settlement. Yahya ibn Adam, Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn Jarir also said this, except that the latter said: the least of it is one dinar, and its maximum has no limit.

Al-Shafi'i said: one dinar on the rich and the poor among free adult males, from which nothing is reduced. Abu Thawr also said this.

Al-Shafi'i said: and if they agree to more than one dinar, it is permitted, and if they increase it and their hearts are content with that, it is accepted from them.

Malik said: it is four dinars for the people of gold, and forty dirhams for the people of silver; the rich and the poor are equal, and even if he is a Magian it is neither increased nor decreased.

Abu Hanifa and his companions, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: twelve, twenty-four, and forty-eight (dirhams, according to the three classes of wealth).

The discussion of the jizya is established in its proper places, and the truth among these views we have established in our commentary on *al-Muntaqa* and in others of our works.

His saying: ﴿and they are humbled (*sagharun*)﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, and *al-saghar* is abasement.

The meaning is: the dhimmi gives the jizya while in a state of humiliation. It has been said: this is that he brings it himself, on foot, not riding, and hands it over while standing, while the one receiving it is seated.

In sum, the one collecting the jizya should make the one handing it over, at the time of its collection, humbled and abased.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are impure﴾, the verse, that he said: except for a slave or one of the People of the Dhimma. It has also been reported as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report by another route.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir, who said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "No polytheist shall enter this mosque of ours after this year of ours, except the people of the covenant and your servants."

Ibn Kathir said: Ahmad alone transmitted it as marfu', and the mawquf (traced only to a companion) version is more authentic.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the polytheists used to come to the House, bringing food with them, trading with it. When they were forbidden to come to the House, the Muslims said: "From where will we get food?" So God revealed: ﴿And if you fear poverty, God will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills﴾. He said: so God sent down rain upon them, and their good increased when the polytheists departed from them.

Ibn Mardawayh related from him, who said: so God enriched them from His bounty, and commanded them to fight the People of the Book.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrima concerning His saying: ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾, that he said: it is destitution.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿then God will enrich you from His bounty﴾, that he said: through the jizya.

Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Dahhak something similar.

'Abd al-Razzaq related something similar from Qatada.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are impure﴾, that he said: filth (*qadhar*).

Abu al-Shaykh also related from him, who said: whoever shakes hands with them, let him perform ablution.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever shakes hands with a polytheist, let him perform ablution or wash his palms."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in God﴾, that he said: this verse was revealed when Muhammad ﷺ and his companions were commanded to the expedition of Tabuk.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Shihab, who said: it was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitna﴾, and it was revealed concerning the People of the Book: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in God﴾, the verse, up to His saying: ﴿until they give the jizya﴾. The first to give the jizya were the people of Najran.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verse 28–29 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His words: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah﴾, meaning: those who do not affirm the Oneness of Allah; ﴿nor do they forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden﴾, meaning wine and silk; ﴿nor do they adopt the religion of truth﴾, meaning the religion of Islam; ﴿from among those who were given the Scripture, until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled﴾, meaning: subjugated.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words: "willingly" (ʿan yadin), he said: "under compulsion" (ʿan qahrin).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, regarding His words: "willingly" (ʿan yadin), he said: "from his own hand, and he should not send it through anyone else."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Sinan, regarding His words: "willingly" (ʿan yadin), he said: "from a position of power" (ʿan qudrah).

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿while they are humbled﴾, he said: "they walk with it swaying from side to side" (mutaltilīn).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, he said: "they are pushed/struck on the neck" (yulkazūn).

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Salman regarding the verse, he said: "not praiseworthy" (ghayru mahmudayn).
