There is no obstacle to carrying the verse upon all these meanings, because the meaning of the verse is: go forth, whether movement becomes easy for you or heavy.

It was said: this verse is abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak or upon the sick﴾ (at-Tawbah: 91). It was said: its abrogator is His saying: ﴿Why should not a group from every division of them go forth [to acquire knowledge]?﴾ (at-Tawbah: 122), and so on. It was said: it is *muhkam* (not abrogated), and the exclusion of the blind and the lame is by His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾ (an-Nur: 61), and the exclusion of the weak and the sick is by His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak or upon the sick﴾ (at-Tawbah: 91), which is by way of specification (*takhsis*), not by way of abrogation (*naskh*), on the supposition that these people fall under His saying "light or heavy." The apparent view is that they do not fall under the generality.

His saying: ﴿and strive with your wealth and your lives in the way of Allah﴾ In it is the command to strive with lives and wealth, and its obligation upon the servants. So the poor strive with their lives, and the wealthy with their wealth and their lives.

Jihad is among the most emphatic and greatest of obligations, and it is a collective obligation (*fard kifayah*) so long as some are carrying out the fight against the enemy and repelling it. But if the enemy cannot be confronted except by all the Muslims in one region of the earth, or in several regions, then it becomes obligatory upon them as an individual obligation (*fard 'ayn*).

The reference in His saying: ﴿That is] ‑ "that" ‑ better for you﴾ is to what preceded of the command to mobilize and the command to strive. ﴿Better for you﴾ That is: a great good in itself, and better than tranquility and ease, if you know that and recognize the excellent things and distinguish them from the inferior.

His saying: ﴿Had it been a near gain and a moderate journey, they would have followed you﴾

Az-Zajjaj said: "Had it been [the thing] called to," and it was elided because of what preceded it as an indication. *Al-'Arad* is what presents itself of the benefits of this world.

The meaning: a spoil that is near, not distant. ﴿And a moderate journey﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, that is: a journey intermediate between nearness and distance. Everything intermediate between excess and deficiency is *qāṣid* (moderate). ﴿But the distance seemed long to them﴾

Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: *al-shuqqah* is a journey to a far land, and it is said of it: *shuqqah shāqqah* (a laborious distance).

Al-Jawhari said: *al-shuqqah* with a *ḍamma* is [a piece] of cloth, and *al-shuqqah* also means a long journey; and they sometimes say it with a *kasra*. What is intended by this is the expedition of Tabuk, for it was a long and arduous journey.

Ibn 'Umar's son 'Isa recited *ba'idat 'alayhimu al-shiqqah* with a *kasra* on the *'ayn* and the *shīn*.

His saying: ﴿And they will swear by Allah﴾ That is: those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk, while you are saying: ﴿If we had been able, we would have gone out with you.﴾ That is: if we had been capable of going out and had found what we need for it, of what is indispensable, we would have gone out with you. This sentence stands in place of the answer of the oath and the conditional.

His saying: ﴿They destroy themselves﴾ It is a substitute for *sa-yaḥlifūna* (they will swear), because whoever swears falsely has destroyed himself. Or it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), that is: destroying themselves, placing it in the position of destruction. ﴿And Allah knows that they are liars﴾ in their oath, which they will swear to you.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu ash-Shaykh have related, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿O you who believe, what is [the matter] with you when you are told, "Go forth"?﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: this was when they were commanded to the expedition of Tabuk after the Conquest, and when he commanded them to mobilize in the summer, and when the dates dried and the fruits ripened and they desired shade, and departure was hard upon them. So Allah revealed: ﴿Go forth, light or heavy﴾.

(p-574) Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu ash-Shaykh, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, have related, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called upon a tribe from among the tribes of the Arabs to go forth, and they were slow to respond to him, so Allah revealed this verse, and He withheld the rain from them, and that was their punishment."

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from 'Ikrimah, that he said: When the verse was revealed, ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾, some people had stayed behind in the desert to instruct their people in religion. The believers said: "Some people remain in the deserts," and they said: "The people of the deserts have perished." So the verse was revealed: ﴿And it is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ (at-Tawbah: 122).

Abu Dawud, Ibn Abi Hatim, an-Nahhas, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, have related, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿If you do not go forth﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: it was abrogated by ﴿And it is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ (at-Tawbah: 122).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu ash-Shaykh have related, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿If you do not support him, Allah has already supported him﴾, that he said: He mentioned what happened at the beginning of his affair when he was sent, saying: "So I shall do that for him, and support him as I supported him at that time, when he was the second of two."

Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi in *ad-Dala'il* have related, from Ibn Shihab and 'Urwah, that: "They rode in every direction, meaning the polytheists, seeking the Prophet (ﷺ). They sent to the people of the watering places, ordering them, and making for them a great reward. They came to Thawr, the mountain in which was the cave, and in which was the Prophet (ﷺ), until they climbed above it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr heard their voices, so Abu Bakr became fearful, and worry and fear overcame him. At that point the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) supplicated, and tranquility from Allah descended upon him: ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾, the verse."

Ibn Shahin, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Habashi ibn Junadah, who said: "Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if any one of the polytheists were to lift his foot, he would see us.' He (ﷺ) said: 'O Abu Bakr, do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Zuhri, regarding His words ﴿when they were both in the cave﴾, that he said: "It is the cave that is in the mountain called Thawr."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and Ibn 'Asakir in his History narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿then Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾, that he said: "Upon Abu Bakr, because the Prophet (ﷺ) always had tranquility with him."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr entered the cave of Hira'. Abu Bakr said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'If one of them were to look at the place of his foot, he would see me and you.' He (ﷺ) said: 'What do you think of two whose third is Allah, O Abu Bakr? Indeed Allah has sent down His tranquility upon you, and has strengthened me with hosts you did not see.'"

al-Khatib in his History narrated from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, regarding ﴿then Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾, that he said: "Upon Abu Bakr. As for the Prophet (ﷺ), tranquility was already upon him."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest﴾, that he said: "It is shirk (associating partners with Allah)." ﴿And the word of Allah is the highest﴾: he said: "There is no god but Allah."

al-Firyabi and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu al-Duha, who said: "The first part of Bara'ah (al-Tawbah) to be revealed was ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾, then its beginning and end were revealed."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Malik something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿light and heavy﴾, that he said: "Eager and not eager."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hakam regarding the verse, that he said: "Busy and not busy."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "In hardship and in ease."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "Young men and elderly men."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: "Youths and old men."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, who said: "They said: 'Among us are the heavy, those with needs, those with dependents, and those preoccupied.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾, and He refused to excuse them unless they went forth, light and heavy, and in whatever state they were."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "A man came, whom they claimed was al-Miqdad, and he was large and heavy. He complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him for permission to stay behind, but he refused. So ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ was revealed. When this verse was revealed, its matter weighed heavily upon the people, so Allah abrogated it (nasakha, i.e., abrogated) and said: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak or upon the sick﴾" (At-Tawbah: 91), the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Will you not raid the Banu al-Asfar (the Romans)? Perhaps you will obtain the daughter of the great man of the Romans.' Two men said: 'You know, O Messenger of Allah, that women are a trial, so do not tempt us with them; give us permission.' So he gave them permission. When we set out, one of them said: 'It is nothing but a morsel for the first to eat.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proceeded, and nothing had been revealed to him about that. When they were part of the way, he descended upon him while he was at some of al-Manah: ﴿Had it been a near gain and a moderate journey, they would have followed you﴾ and there was revealed to him: ﴿Allah pardon you; why did you give them permission?﴾ (At-Tawbah: 43) and there was revealed to him: ﴿Only those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day ask your permission﴾ (At-Tawbah: 45) and there was revealed to him: ﴿Indeed they are defilement, and their refuge is Hell as recompense for what they used to earn﴾ (At-Tawbah: 95)."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿Had it been a near gain﴾, he said: "a near booty," ﴿but the distance seemed long to them﴾, he said: "the journey."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿and Allah knows that they are liars﴾, that he said: "They were certainly able to go out, but it was a holding back from their own selves and a disinclination toward jihad."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 38–42 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿O you who believe, what is [the matter] with you?﴾ When he (Allah) had explained the faults of those disbelievers, He returned to encouraging the believers to fight them. The interrogative in "what is [the matter] with you?" is for denunciation and reproach, meaning: what prevents you from that? There is no disagreement that this verse was revealed as a rebuke to those who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk, which took place in the ninth year after the Hijrah, one year after the Conquest. The *nafr* (mobilization) is moving swiftly from one place to another for a matter that has arisen.

His saying: ﴿you cling heavily to the earth﴾ The original form is *tathaqaltum*, and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *tha'* (*idgham*) because they are close in articulation. The connecting *alif* (*alif al-wasl*) was brought so that one could reach the pronunciation of the unvocalized consonant. Similar to it are *idda'arakū*, *iṭṭayyartum*, and *iṭṭayyarū*. Al-Kisa'i recited:

*Tawālā al-ḍajī'u idhā mā ishtāqahā ḥaḍaran* ‑ *'adhbu al-madhāqi idhā mā ittābaʿa al-qubalā*

(The bedfellow who is near her, whenever he longs for her, follows [her kisses]; sweet of taste, whenever he follows kisses.)

Al-A'mash recited *tathaqaltum* in its original form. Its meaning is *tabāṭa'tum* (you were slow and sluggish). It is construed with *ilā* (to) because it includes the meaning of inclination and adherence. It was also said that its meaning is: you inclined to remaining in your land and staying in it. It was recited *ā-thāqaltum* as an interrogative, and its meaning is reproach. The element governing the adverbial phrase is *mā* in "what is [the matter] with you?", in the sense of the verb, as if it were said: what prevents you, or what do you do, when it is said to you? And *ilā al-arḍ* (to the earth) is connected to *ithāqaltum* as previously mentioned.

His saying: ﴿Are you satisfied with the life of this world?﴾ That is, with its pleasures, in place of the Hereafter, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We willed, We would have made from you angels upon the earth succeeding [you]﴾ (az-Zukhruf: 60), meaning, in place of you. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

*Qalabat lanā min mā'i Zamzama shurbatan* ‑ *mubarradatan bātat ʿalā ṭahayān*

(She turned for us, from the water of Zamzam, a drink, cooled, that spent the night upon *ṭahayān*.)

That is, in place of the water of Zamzam. *Al-ṭahayān* is a piece of wood set up in a corner of the house for the air, on which water is hung so that it becomes cool. The meaning of "in the Hereafter" is: in comparison to the Hereafter, and in exchange for it. "Except a little" means: except a meager enjoyment that is not valued. It is permissible that by "the little" is meant nothing, since there is no ratio between the finite, perishing thing and the infinite, enduring thing. Apparently this clinging did not come from all of them, for it is unlikely that they would all agree upon sluggishness and heaviness. Rather, it is from the category of attributing what occurs from some to all, and this is common and widespread.

His saying: ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you﴾ This is a severe threat and an emphatic warning to whoever abandons going forth with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾ That is, He will destroy you with a severe, painful punishment. It was said: it is in this world only; and it was said: it is more general than that.

His saying: ﴿and will replace you with another people﴾ That is, He will make them, for His messengers, a replacement for you, from those who are not slow when they are needed.

It has been differed concerning who these people are. It was said: the people of Yemen; and it was said: the people of Persia. There is no basis for specifying them without evidence.

His saying: ﴿and you will not harm Him at all﴾ It is conjoined to *yastabdil* (He will replace). The pronoun refers, it was said, to Allah; and it was said, to the Prophet (ﷺ). That is: you will not harm Allah by abandoning compliance with His command to mobilize, at all; or you will not harm the Messenger of Allah by abandoning his support and going forth with him, at all. ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾, and among the things He is capable of is punishing you and replacing you. (p-573)

His saying: ﴿If you do not support him, Allah has already supported him﴾ That is: if you abandon supporting him, Allah is responsible for him. He has already supported him in times of few numbers, and made him prevail over his enemy by overpowering and subduing. Or: He will support him who supported him when he had with him none but one man, at the time when those who disbelieved expelled him, the second of two, that is, one of two: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

It was recited with the *yā'* (in *thāniya*) vocalized as sukūn.

Ibn Jinni said: Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' related it, and its basis is that the *yā'* is made quiescent by analogy with the *alif*.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is like the recitation of al-Hasan, ﴿what remains of interest﴾ (al-Baqarah: 278), and like the saying of Jarir:

*Huwa al-khalīfatu fa'rḍū mā raḍiyahu lakum* ‑ *māḍī al-ʿazīmati mā fī ḥukmihi janafu*

(He is the caliph, so be pleased with what he is pleased with for you; he who carries out his resolve, in whose judgment there is no bias.)

His saying: ﴿when they were both in the cave﴾ It is a substitute for *idh akhrajahu* (when they expelled him), a partial substitution (*badal al-ba'd*). The cave (*al-ghar*) is a hole in the mountain called *Thawr*, and it is well known as the Cave of Thawr. It is a mountain near Makkah. The story of his (ﷺ) leaving Makkah for Madinah, he and Abu Bakr, and their entering the cave, is well known and mentioned in the books of biography (*siyar*) and hadith.

His saying: ﴿when he said to his companion﴾ It is a second substitution, that is: at the time of his saying to Abu Bakr: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us﴾. That is: leave off grief, for Allah, with His victory, help and support, is with us. Whoever Allah is with will never be overcome, and whoever is not overcome is entitled not to grieve.

His saying: ﴿So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾ *Al-sakīnah* is the calming of his heart and the granting of security to him, until his fear departed and safety was attained for him. This is on the basis that the pronoun in *'alayhi* refers to Abu Bakr. It was said: it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the tranquility sent down upon him would mean his being protected from the occurrence of any cause of fear for him. What supports the pronoun in *'alayhi* referring to the Prophet (ﷺ) is the pronoun in ﴿and supported him with soldiers you did not see﴾, for it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), because he is the one supported with these soldiers, who are the angels, as was the case on the day of Badr. It was also said: there is no objection to the pronoun returning from *'alayhi* to Abu Bakr and from *ayyadahu* to the Prophet (ﷺ), for that is common in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs.

﴿And He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest﴾ That is, the word of shirk, which is their call to it and their invocation of the idols. ﴿And the word of Allah is the highest﴾.

Al-A'mash and Ya'qub recited *kalimatan* in the accusative, taking it as governed by *ja'ala* (made). The rest recited it in the nominative, as a resumption (*isti'naf*).

Al-Farra' and Abu Hatim considered the accusative recitation weak. The pronoun of separation (*ḍamīr al-faṣl*), I mean *hiya*, is an emphasis on the excellence of His word in elevation, and that it is specific to Him and not to anything else. "The word of Allah" is the word of monotheism and the call to Islam. ﴿And Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise﴾ That is: Overpowering and Subduing, who does nothing except what contains wisdom and correctness.

Then, when He had threatened those who do not go forth with the Messenger (ﷺ), and had set forth the examples He mentioned, He followed this with a categorical command, saying: ﴿Go forth, light or heavy﴾ That is: while you are light or heavy. It was said: the meaning is those going out alone or in groups; it was said: energetic and not energetic; it was said: poor and wealthy; it was said: young and old; it was said: men and cavalry; it was said: those who have no dependents and those who have dependents; it was said: those who advance to war like the vanguard, and those who lag behind like the army; and it was said: other than that.

There is no obstacle to carrying the verse upon all these meanings, because the meaning of the verse is: go forth, whether movement becomes easy for you or heavy.

It was said: this verse is abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak or upon the sick﴾ (at-Tawbah: 91). It was said: its abrogator is His saying: ﴿Why should not a group from every division of them go forth [to acquire knowledge]?﴾ (at-Tawbah: 122), and so on. It was said: it is *muhkam* (not abrogated), and the exclusion of the blind and the lame is by His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾ (an-Nur: 61), and the exclusion of the weak and the sick is by His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak or upon the sick﴾ (at-Tawbah: 91), which is by way of specification (*takhsis*), not by way of abrogation (*naskh*), on the supposition that these people fall under His saying "light or heavy." The apparent view is that they do not fall under the generality.

His saying: ﴿and strive with your wealth and your lives in the way of Allah﴾ In it is the command to strive with lives and wealth, and its obligation upon the servants. So the poor strive with their lives, and the wealthy with their wealth and their lives.

Jihad is among the most emphatic and greatest of obligations, and it is a collective obligation (*fard kifayah*) so long as some are carrying out the fight against the enemy and repelling it. But if the enemy cannot be confronted except by all the Muslims in one region of the earth, or in several regions, then it becomes obligatory upon them as an individual obligation (*fard 'ayn*).

Az-Zajjaj said: "Had it been [the thing] called to," and it was elided because of what preceded it as an indication. *Al-'Arad* is what presents itself of the benefits of this world.

Ibn 'Umar's son 'Isa recited *ba'idat 'alayhimu al-shiqqah* with a *kasra* on the *'ayn* and the *shīn*.

His saying: ﴿And they will swear by Allah﴾ That is: those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk, while you are saying: ﴿If we had been able, we would have gone out with you.﴾ That is: if we had been capable of going out and had found what we need for it, of what is indispensable, we would have gone out with you. This sentence stands in place of the answer of the oath and the conditional.

Or it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), that is: destroying themselves, placing it in the position of destruction. ﴿And Allah knows that they are liars﴾ in their oath, which they will swear to you.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) supplicated, and tranquility from Allah descended upon him: ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾, the verse."

Ibn Shahin, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Habashi ibn Junadah, who said: "Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if any one of the polytheists were to lift his foot, he would see us.' He (ﷺ) said: 'O Abu Bakr, do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Zuhri, regarding His words ﴿when they were both in the cave﴾, that he said: "It is the cave that is in the mountain called Thawr."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and Ibn 'Asakir in his History narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿then Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾, that he said: "Upon Abu Bakr, because the Prophet (ﷺ) always had tranquility with him."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr entered the cave of Hira'. Abu Bakr said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'If one of them were to look at the place of his foot, he would see me and you.' He (ﷺ) said: 'What do you think of two whose third is Allah, O Abu Bakr? Indeed Allah has sent down His tranquility upon you, and has strengthened me with hosts you did not see.'"

al-Khatib in his History narrated from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, regarding ﴿then Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾, that he said: "Upon Abu Bakr. As for the Prophet (ﷺ), tranquility was already upon him."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest﴾, that he said: "It is shirk (associating partners with Allah)." ﴿And the word of Allah is the highest﴾: he said: "There is no god but Allah."

al-Firyabi and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu al-Duha, who said: "The first part of Bara'ah (al-Tawbah) to be revealed was ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾, then its beginning and end were revealed."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Malik something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿light and heavy﴾, that he said: "Eager and not eager."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hakam regarding the verse, that he said: "Busy and not busy."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "In hardship and in ease."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "Young men and elderly men."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: "Youths and old men."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, who said: "They said: 'Among us are the heavy, those with needs, those with dependents, and those preoccupied.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾, and He refused to excuse them unless they went forth, light and heavy, and in whatever state they were."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "A man came, whom they claimed was al-Miqdad, and he was large and heavy. He complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him for permission to stay behind, but he refused. So ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ was revealed. When this verse was revealed, its matter weighed heavily upon the people, so Allah abrogated it (nasakha, i.e., abrogated) and said: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak or upon the sick﴾" (At-Tawbah: 91), the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Will you not raid the Banu al-Asfar (the Romans)? Perhaps you will obtain the daughter of the great man of the Romans.' Two men said: 'You know, O Messenger of Allah, that women are a trial, so do not tempt us with them; give us permission.' So he gave them permission. When we set out, one of them said: 'It is nothing but a morsel for the first to eat.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proceeded, and nothing had been revealed to him about that. When they were part of the way, he descended upon him while he was at some of al-Manah: ﴿Had it been a near gain and a moderate journey, they would have followed you﴾ and there was revealed to him: ﴿Allah pardon you; why did you give them permission?﴾ (At-Tawbah: 43) and there was revealed to him: ﴿Only those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day ask your permission﴾ (At-Tawbah: 45) and there was revealed to him: ﴿Indeed they are defilement, and their refuge is Hell as recompense for what they used to earn﴾ (At-Tawbah: 95)."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿Had it been a near gain﴾, he said: "a near booty," ﴿but the distance seemed long to them﴾, he said: "the journey."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿and Allah knows that they are liars﴾, that he said: "They were certainly able to go out, but it was a holding back from their own selves and a disinclination toward jihad."

(p. 575) The interrogative in ﴿*'Afa Allāhu 'anka, lima adhinta lahum*﴾ ("God pardon you! Why did you grant them leave?") expresses disapproval from God, exalted is He, toward His Messenger (ﷺ), because he granted permission to those who asked to stay behind before it had become clear who among them was truthful in the excuse he offered and who was lying in it.

Mentioning God's pardon of him (ﷺ) indicates that this permission he granted was contrary to what was preferable (*khilaf al-awla*). In this there is a gentle rebuke from God, glorified is He. It has also been said that this is a rebuke to him (ﷺ) for granting permission to the hypocrites to go out with him, not for granting them permission to stay back from going out. The first interpretation is the better one.

God, exalted is He, had already given him a concession in Surat al-Nur with His saying: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whomever you will among them﴾ (al-Nur 24:62). The two verses can be reconciled by saying that the rebuke here is directed at granting permission before verification (*istithbat*), until the truthful is distinguished from the liar, while the permission there is directed at granting it after verification. And God knows best.

It has also been said that His saying ﴿'Afa Allāhu 'anka﴾ is an opening of speech, as when you say, "May God make you prosperous, strengthen you, and have mercy on you, how did you do such-and-such?" This is related by Makki, al-Nahhas, and al-Mahdawi. According to this interpretation, it is good to pause at ﴿'Afa Allāhu 'anka﴾, whereas according to the first interpretation it is not good.

It is not hidden from you that the first interpretation is the one that corresponds to what the wording requires according to the Arabic language, and there is no basis for removing it from its Arabic meaning.

The verse contains evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning, personal judgment) on the part of the Prophet (ﷺ). The question is recorded in the books of usul al-fiqh (legal theory). It also contains evidence for the legislated character of guarding against haste and against being deceived by the outward appearances of matters.

As for ﴿*hattā yatabayyana laka alladhīna ṣadaqū*﴾ ("until those who were truthful became clear to you"), *ḥattā* here indicates a limit (*li-al-ghāya*), as if it were said: "Why did you rush to grant them permission? Why did you not take your time until the truthfulness of the one among them who was truthful in the excuse he presented became clear to you, and the lying of the one among them who was lying in that became clear?"

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that it is not the custom of the believers to ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission to stay back from jihad. Rather, it was their custom that when he (ﷺ) granted permission to one of them to stay behind, this weighed heavily upon him. So He said: ﴿Those who believe in God and the Last Day do not ask your permission to strive with their wealth and their selves﴾ (al-Tawba 9:44). This is according to the view that the meaning of the verse is "that they not strive," with the negative particle deleted. It has also been said that the meaning is: "The believers do not ask your permission to stay behind out of dislike for jihad." And it has been said that the meaning of seeking permission for something is disliking it. But according to what the apparent wording requires, the meaning is: the believers do not ask your permission regarding jihad; rather, their habit is to hasten toward it without hesitation or waiting for your permission to come, let alone asking you permission to stay behind.

Al-Zajjaj said: *an yujāhidū* is in a position of accusative (*naṣb*) by the implied preposition *fī*, meaning "in that they strive." ﴿And God knows the pious﴾, and they are those who did not ask permission.

It is only those who ask your permission to stay back from jihad and to remain behind from it ﴿who do not believe in God and the Last Day﴾, and they are the hypocrites. He mentioned belief in God first and belief in the Last Day second in both places, because these are the two motives for striving in the path of God.

His saying ﴿*wa-artābat qulūbuhum*﴾ ("and their hearts are in doubt") is coordinated with His saying ﴿who do not believe﴾. The past tense is used to indicate the certainty of doubt (*rayb*) in their hearts, and *rayb* is suspicion.

His saying ﴿*fa-hum fī raybihim yataraddadūn*﴾ ("so they are wavering in their doubt") means: in their doubt that has settled in their hearts they are bewildered, and *taraddud* is bewilderment.

The meaning is: those who ask your permission are not believers, but rather doubters, bewildered, not guided to the path of rightness, and not knowing the truth.

His saying ﴿*wa-law arādū al-khurūja la-a'addū lahu 'uddatan*﴾ ("And if they had intended to go out, they would have prepared for it some preparation") means: if they had been truthful in what they claim and what they inform you of, that they intend to strive with you, but they had not with them the equipment for jihad that is needed, they would not have neglected to prepare and gather the equipment before the time of jihad, as believers prepare for it. So the meaning of this statement is that they do not intend to go out at all, nor have they made any preparation for the campaign.

*'Udda* is what the striver needs of provisions, mount, and weapons.

His saying ﴿*wa-lākin karaha Allāhu inbi'āthahum*﴾ ("But God disliked their being sent forth") means: but God disliked their going out, so they were held back from going out. The meaning is: they did not go out, but they were restrained, because God's disliking of their being sent forth necessitates their being held back from going out. *Inbi'āth* is going out. That is, God held them back from going out with you and forsook them. For they said: "If permission is not given to us to sit back, we will corrupt and incite against the believers." It has also been said that the meaning is: "If they had intended to go out, they would have prepared for it some preparation, but they did not intend it because God disliked it."

His saying ﴿*wa-qīla 'quʿudū ma'a al-qā'idīn*﴾ ("And it was said: 'Sit with those who sit'") — it has been said that the one who said this to them was Satan through the whisperings he cast into them. It has also been said that some of them said it to others. It has also been said that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said it in anger at them. And it has been said that it is an expression of abandonment (*khidhlān*): that is, God placed sitting back in their hearts as abandonment of them.

The meaning of ﴿with those who sit﴾ is: with those of the disabled, the blind, the sick, the women, and the children. In this there is blame for them, belittlement of them, and disparagement of them, which is not hidden.

His saying ﴿*law kharajū fīkum mā zādūkum illā khabālan*﴾ ("Had they gone out among you, they would not have increased you except in corruption") is a consolation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers for the hypocrites' staying back.

*Khabāl* is corruption, slander, the sowing of discord, and the spreading of false rumors.

It has been said: this exception is disjunctive (*munqaṭi'*), meaning: "they would not have increased you in strength, but they sought corruption." It has been said: the meaning is: "they would not have increased you in the matter about which you were hesitating in opinion except in corruption," and thus it is connected (*muttaṣil*). It has also been said: it is an exception from the more general category (*istithnā' min a'amm al-'amm*), meaning: "they would not have increased you in anything except in corruption," so the exception is of the connected type, because *khabāl* is among the things that the word "thing" truly applies to.

His saying ﴿*wa-la-awḍa'ū khilālakum*﴾ ("and they would have hastened between you") — *īḍā'* is swiftness of travel. From it is the saying of Waraqa ibn Nawfal:

*"Would that I were in it as a young camel, / I would gallop in it and hasten."*

It is said: *awḍa'a al-ba'īr* when the camel hastened its pace. It has also been said that *īḍā'* is the gait of *khabab* (a fast trot). *Khalal* is the gap between two things, and its plural is *khilāl*, that is, the openings that are between the rows.

The meaning is: they would have run about among you with corruption, by means of the lies they fabricate, which include spreading false rumors and slander, which cause the corruption of relations among you.

His saying ﴿*yabghūnakumu al-fitnata*﴾ ("seeking to cause you discord"): it is said *baghaytuhu kadhā* meaning "I sought it for him," and *abghaytuhu kadhā* meaning "I helped him in seeking it."

The meaning is: they seek discord for you in your relations with one another by means of their incitement and corruption. It has also been said that *fitna* here means *shirk* (polytheism).

The clause ﴿*wa-fīkum sammā'ūna lahum*﴾ ("and among you are those who listen to them") is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: while among you are those who listen to what they say of falsehood and then convey it to you, so that discord among you is affected by that, and corruption spreads to your brethren. ﴿And God is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, and of what would have occurred from them had they gone out with you. Therefore His perfect wisdom required that they not go out with you, and He disliked their being sent forth with you. And their condition in this does not contradict the earlier rebuke to him (ﷺ) for granting them permission to stay back, because he hastened to grant them permission and had not known of their conditions that if they went out they would do these deeds. So he (ﷺ) was rebuked for his haste to grant them permission before it became clear to him which of them was truthful in his excuse and which was lying. For this reason God, glorified is He, said later in this surah: ﴿So if God returns you to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, say: "You will never go out with me, ever"﴾ (al-Tawba 9:83), and He said in Surat al-Fath: ﴿Those who stayed behind will say, when you set out to take spoils: "Let us follow you." They wish to change God's word. Say: "You will never follow us"﴾ (al-Fath 48:15).

His saying ﴿*laqadi ibtaghawu al-fitnata min qablu*﴾ ("They had already sought discord before") means: they had sought corruption, the spreading of disunity among the believers, and the scattering of their unity, before this campaign from which they stayed back, as happened from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and others. ﴿And God refuses except to perfect His light, though the disbelievers dislike it﴾ (al-Tawba 9:32).

His saying ﴿*wa-qallabū laka al-umūr*﴾ ("and they turned matters over for you") means: they changed them from one matter to another and devised for you tricks and schemes. From this is the Arabs' saying *ḥawwal qullab* ("a changeable, shrewd man") when he is constantly engaged in plots and tricks, turning the opinion over in them and reflecting upon them.

It is read *wa-qalabū* with the light pronunciation. ﴿*Ḥattā jā'a al-ḥaqq*﴾ ("until the truth came") means: up to a limit which is the coming of the truth, which is victory for you, support, and the manifestation of God's command by the exaltation of His religion, the making known of His law, and the subjugation of His enemies. It has also been said that *al-ḥaqq* is the Qur'an. ﴿*wa-hum kārihūn*﴾ ("while they were averse") means: while they were averse to the coming of the truth and the manifestation of God's command, but it happened in spite of them.

"And among them" means: among the hypocrites is one who says to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Grant me permission" to stay behind from jihad, "and do not tempt me," meaning: do not put me into temptation, that is, into sin, if you do not grant me permission and I stay behind without your permission. It has also been said that its meaning is: do not put me into destruction by going out. ﴿Surely in temptation they have fallen﴾, meaning: into temptation itself they have fallen, and this temptation is the temptation of staying behind from jihad and of false excuse.

The meaning is: they thought that by going out, or by your not granting them permission, they would fall into temptation, while by this staying back they have fallen into the great temptation.

In the expression "fallen" there is an indication that they fell into it as one who falls from a height to a lower place, and that is more severe than merely entering into temptation. Then He threatened them for this, saying: ﴿And indeed Hell is encompassing of the disbelievers﴾, meaning: encircling them from all sides, so that they find no escape from it, and are not able to get out of it in any condition.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq in *al-Muṣannaf*, and Ibn Jarir, related from ʿAmr ibn Maymun, who said: "Two things the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did, concerning which he was not commanded with anything: his granting permission to the hypocrites, and his taking ransom from the captives. Then God revealed: ʿAfā Allāhu ʿanka, lima adhinta lahum."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: "Have you heard of a rebuke more gentle than this? He began with pardon before the rebuke, saying: ʿAfā Allāhu ʿanka, lima adhinta lahum."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿ʿAfā Allāhu ʿanka﴾ and the verse, that he said: "Some people said: 'Ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) permission: if he grants you permission, sit back; and if he does not grant you permission, sit back.'"

Al-Nahhas related in his *Nāsikh* from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying ﴿ʿAfā Allāhu ʿanka, lima adhinta lahum﴾ — the three verses — that he said: "It abrogated them: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whomever you will among them﴾" (al-Nur 24:62).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Nahhas in his *Nāsikh* related from him concerning His saying ﴿Those who believe in God do not ask your permission﴾ and the verse, that he said: "This is a reproach to the hypocrites when they asked permission to sit back from jihad without an excuse, and God gave excuse to the believers, saying: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whomever you will among them﴾" (al-Nur 24:62).

Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from him also, concerning His saying: "Those who do not ask your permission..." the two verses, that he said: "They were abrogated by the verse in Surat al-Nur: ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in God and His Messenger﴾ until ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (al-Nur 24:62). So God made the Prophet (ﷺ) the one with the better of the two views in this matter: whoever went out, went out for a virtue, and whoever stayed back, stayed back without blame, God willing."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Dahhak concerning His saying ﴿But God disliked their being sent forth﴾, that he said: "Their going out."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying ﴿*fa-thabbaṭahum*﴾ ("so He held them back"), that he said: "He detained them."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Zayd concerning His saying ﴿Had they gone out among you, they would not have increased you except in corruption﴾, that he said: "These are the hypocrites in the campaign of Tabuk."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿*wa-la-awḍa'ū khilālakum*﴾, that he said: "They would have hastened among you."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verse 43–49 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿And they would have hastened between you﴾, that he said: "They would have fled." "﴿Seeking to cause you fitnah﴾": they would have slowed you down. ʿAbd Allah ibn Nabtal, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Rifaʿah ibn Tabut, and Aws ibn Qayzi. "﴿And among you are listeners for them﴾": those who relay your narrations to them, though they are not hypocrites, and they are spies for the hypocrites.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Maʿrifah related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) intended to set out for the expedition of Tabuk, he said to Jadd ibn Qays: 'O Jadd ibn Qays, what do you say about fighting the Banu al-Asfar (the Byzantines)?' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I am a man fond of women, and whenever I see the women of the Banu al-Asfar I will be tempted. So grant me permission and do not tempt me.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And among them is he who says, 'Grant me permission and do not tempt me.'﴾ [the verse]."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related similar to this from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah.

Ibn Mardawayh related similar to this from ʿA'ishah as well.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿And do not tempt me﴾, that he said: "Do not make me go out." ﴿Surely, in fitnah they have fallen﴾: meaning, in going out.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿And do not tempt me﴾, that he said: "Do not make me sinful." ﴿Surely, in fitnah﴾: he said: "Surely, in sin." The story of Tabuk is recorded in the books of hadith and biography, so we will not lengthen it by mentioning it.

His saying ﴿*wa-lākin karaha Allāhu inbi'āthahum*﴾ ("But God disliked their being sent forth") means: but God disliked their going out, so they were held back from going out. The meaning is: they did not go out, but they were restrained, because God's disliking of their being sent forth necessitates their being held back from going out. *Inbi'āth* is going out. That is, God held them back from going out with you and forsook them. For they said: "If permission is not given to us to sit back, we will corrupt and incite against the believers." It has also been said that the meaning is: "If they had intended to go out, they would have prepared for it some preparation, but they did not intend it because God disliked it."

His saying ﴿*wa-qīla 'quʿudū ma'a al-qā'idīn*﴾ ("And it was said: 'Sit with those who sit'") — it has been said that the one who said this to them was Satan through the whisperings he cast into them. It has also been said that some of them said it to others. It has also been said that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said it in anger at them. And it has been said that it is an expression of abandonment (*khidhlān*): that is, God placed sitting back in their hearts as abandonment of them.

The meaning of ﴿with those who sit﴾ is: with those of the disabled, the blind, the sick, the women, and the children. In this there is blame for them, belittlement of them, and disparagement of them, which is not hidden.

His saying ﴿*law kharajū fīkum mā zādūkum illā khabālan*﴾ ("Had they gone out among you, they would not have increased you except in corruption") is a consolation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers for the hypocrites' staying back.

*Khabāl* is corruption, slander, the sowing of discord, and the spreading of false rumors.

It has been said: this exception is disjunctive (*munqaṭi'*), meaning: "they would not have increased you in strength, but they sought corruption." It has been said: the meaning is: "they would not have increased you in the matter about which you were hesitating in opinion except in corruption," and thus it is connected (*muttaṣil*). It has also been said: it is an exception from the more general category (*istithnā' min a'amm al-'amm*), meaning: "they would not have increased you in anything except in corruption," so the exception is of the connected type, because *khabāl* is among the things that the word "thing" truly applies to.

His saying ﴿*wa-la-awḍa'ū khilālakum*﴾ ("and they would have hastened between you") — *īḍā'* is swiftness of travel. From it is the saying of Waraqa ibn Nawfal:

*"Would that I were in it as a young camel, / I would gallop in it and hasten."*

It is said: *awḍa'a al-ba'īr* when the camel hastened its pace. It has also been said that *īḍā'* is the gait of *khabab* (a fast trot). *Khalal* is the gap between two things, and its plural is *khilāl*, that is, the openings that are between the rows.

The meaning is: they would have run about among you with corruption, by means of the lies they fabricate, which include spreading false rumors and slander, which cause the corruption of relations among you.

His saying ﴿*yabghūnakumu al-fitnata*﴾ ("seeking to cause you discord"): it is said *baghaytuhu kadhā* meaning "I sought it for him," and *abghaytuhu kadhā* meaning "I helped him in seeking it."

The meaning is: they seek discord for you in your relations with one another by means of their incitement and corruption. It has also been said that *fitna* here means *shirk* (polytheism).

The clause ﴿*wa-fīkum sammā'ūna lahum*﴾ ("and among you are those who listen to them") is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: while among you are those who listen to what they say of falsehood and then convey it to you, so that discord among you is affected by that, and corruption spreads to your brethren. ﴿And God is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, and of what would have occurred from them had they gone out with you. Therefore His perfect wisdom required that they not go out with you, and He disliked their being sent forth with you. And their condition in this does not contradict the earlier rebuke to him (ﷺ) for granting them permission to stay back, because he hastened to grant them permission and had not known of their conditions that if they went out they would do these deeds. So he (ﷺ) was rebuked for his haste to grant them permission before it became clear to him which of them was truthful in his excuse and which was lying. For this reason God, glorified is He, said later in this surah: ﴿So if God returns you to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, say: "You will never go out with me, ever"﴾ (al-Tawba 9:83), and He said in Surat al-Fath: ﴿Those who stayed behind will say, when you set out to take spoils: "Let us follow you." From this is the Arabs' saying *ḥawwal qullab* ("a changeable, shrewd man") when he is constantly engaged in plots and tricks, turning the opinion over in them and reflecting upon them.

It is read *wa-qalabū* with the light pronunciation. ﴿*Ḥattā jā'a al-ḥaqq*﴾ ("until the truth came") means: up to a limit which is the coming of the truth, which is victory for you, support, and the manifestation of God's command by the exaltation of His religion, the making known of His law, and the subjugation of His enemies. It has also been said that *al-ḥaqq* is the Qur'an. ﴿*wa-hum kārihūn*﴾ ("while they were averse") means: while they were averse to the coming of the truth and the manifestation of God's command, but it happened in spite of them.

"And among them" means: among the hypocrites is one who says to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Grant me permission" to stay behind from jihad, "and do not tempt me," meaning: do not put me into temptation, that is, into sin, if you do not grant me permission and I stay behind without your permission. It has also been said that its meaning is: do not put me into destruction by going out. ﴿Surely in temptation they have fallen﴾, meaning: into temptation itself they have fallen, and this temptation is the temptation of staying behind from jihad and of false excuse.

The meaning is: they thought that by going out, or by your not granting them permission, they would fall into temptation, while by this staying back they have fallen into the great temptation.

In the expression "fallen" there is an indication that they fell into it as one who falls from a height to a lower place, and that is more severe than merely entering into temptation. Then He threatened them for this, saying: ﴿And indeed Hell is encompassing of the disbelievers﴾, meaning: encircling them from all sides, so that they find no escape from it, and are not able to get out of it in any condition.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿*wa-la-awḍa'ū khilālakum*﴾, that he said: "They would have hastened among you."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verse 43–49 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿And they would have hastened between you﴾, that he said: "They would have fled." "﴿Seeking to cause you fitnah﴾": they would have slowed you down. ʿAbd Allah ibn Nabtal, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Rifaʿah ibn Tabut, and Aws ibn Qayzi. "﴿And among you are listeners for them﴾": those who relay your narrations to them, though they are not hypocrites, and they are spies for the hypocrites.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Maʿrifah related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) intended to set out for the expedition of Tabuk, he said to Jadd ibn Qays: 'O Jadd ibn Qays, what do you say about fighting the Banu al-Asfar (the Byzantines)?' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I am a man fond of women, and whenever I see the women of the Banu al-Asfar I will be tempted. So grant me permission and do not tempt me.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And among them is he who says, 'Grant me permission and do not tempt me.'﴾ [the verse]."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related similar to this from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah.

Ibn Mardawayh related similar to this from ʿA'ishah as well.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿And do not tempt me﴾, that he said: "Do not make me go out." ﴿Surely, in fitnah they have fallen﴾: meaning, in going out.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿And do not tempt me﴾, that he said: "Do not make me sinful." ﴿Surely, in fitnah﴾: he said: "Surely, in sin." The story of Tabuk is recorded in the books of hadith and biography, so we will not lengthen it by mentioning it.

(p. 575) The interrogative in ﴿*'Afa Allāhu 'anka, lima adhinta lahum*﴾ ("God pardon you! Why did you grant them leave?") expresses disapproval from God, exalted is He, toward His Messenger (ﷺ), because he granted permission to those who asked to stay behind before it had become clear who among them was truthful in the excuse he offered and who was lying in it.

Mentioning God's pardon of him (ﷺ) indicates that this permission he granted was contrary to what was preferable (*khilaf al-awla*). In this there is a gentle rebuke from God, glorified is He. It has also been said that this is a rebuke to him (ﷺ) for granting permission to the hypocrites to go out with him, not for granting them permission to stay back from going out. The first interpretation is the better one.

God, exalted is He, had already given him a concession in Surat al-Nur with His saying: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whomever you will among them﴾ (al-Nur 24:62). The two verses can be reconciled by saying that the rebuke here is directed at granting permission before verification (*istithbat*), until the truthful is distinguished from the liar, while the permission there is directed at granting it after verification. And God knows best.

It has also been said that His saying ﴿'Afa Allāhu 'anka﴾ is an opening of speech, as when you say, "May God make you prosperous, strengthen you, and have mercy on you, how did you do such-and-such?" This is related by Makki, al-Nahhas, and al-Mahdawi. According to this interpretation, it is good to pause at ﴿'Afa Allāhu 'anka﴾, whereas according to the first interpretation it is not good.

It is not hidden from you that the first interpretation is the one that corresponds to what the wording requires according to the Arabic language, and there is no basis for removing it from its Arabic meaning.

The verse contains evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning, personal judgment) on the part of the Prophet (ﷺ). The question is recorded in the books of usul al-fiqh (legal theory). It also contains evidence for the legislated character of guarding against haste and against being deceived by the outward appearances of matters.

As for ﴿*hattā yatabayyana laka alladhīna ṣadaqū*﴾ ("until those who were truthful became clear to you"), *ḥattā* here indicates a limit (*li-al-ghāya*), as if it were said: "Why did you rush to grant them permission? Why did you not take your time until the truthfulness of the one among them who was truthful in the excuse he presented became clear to you, and the lying of the one among them who was lying in that became clear?"

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that it is not the custom of the believers to ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission to stay back from jihad. Rather, it was their custom that when he (ﷺ) granted permission to one of them to stay behind, this weighed heavily upon him. So He said: ﴿Those who believe in God and the Last Day do not ask your permission to strive with their wealth and their selves﴾ (al-Tawba 9:44). This is according to the view that the meaning of the verse is "that they not strive," with the negative particle deleted. It has also been said that the meaning is: "The believers do not ask your permission to stay behind out of dislike for jihad." And it has been said that the meaning of seeking permission for something is disliking it. But according to what the apparent wording requires, the meaning is: the believers do not ask your permission regarding jihad; rather, their habit is to hasten toward it without hesitation or waiting for your permission to come, let alone asking you permission to stay behind.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verse 43–49 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿And they would have hastened between you﴾, that he said: "They would have fled." "﴿Seeking to cause you fitnah﴾": they would have slowed you down. ʿAbd Allah ibn Nabtal, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Rifaʿah ibn Tabut, and Aws ibn Qayzi. "﴿And among you are listeners for them﴾": those who relay your narrations to them, though they are not hypocrites, and they are spies for the hypocrites.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Maʿrifah related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) intended to set out for the expedition of Tabuk, he said to Jadd ibn Qays: 'O Jadd ibn Qays, what do you say about fighting the Banu al-Asfar (the Byzantines)?' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I am a man fond of women, and whenever I see the women of the Banu al-Asfar I will be tempted. So grant me permission and do not tempt me.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And among them is he who says, 'Grant me permission and do not tempt me.'﴾ [the verse]."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related similar to this from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah.

Ibn Mardawayh related similar to this from ʿA'ishah as well.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿And do not tempt me﴾, that he said: "Do not make me go out." ﴿Surely, in fitnah they have fallen﴾: meaning, in going out.

The story of Tabuk is recorded in the books of hadith and biography, so we will not lengthen it by mentioning it.

(p. 575) The interrogative in ﴿*'Afa Allāhu 'anka, lima adhinta lahum*﴾ ("God pardon you! Why did you grant them leave?") expresses disapproval from God, exalted is He, toward His Messenger (ﷺ), because he granted permission to those who asked to stay behind before it had become clear who among them was truthful in the excuse he offered and who was lying in it.

Mentioning God's pardon of him (ﷺ) indicates that this permission he granted was contrary to what was preferable (*khilaf al-awla*). In this there is a gentle rebuke from God, glorified is He. It has also been said that this is a rebuke to him (ﷺ) for granting permission to the hypocrites to go out with him, not for granting them permission to stay back from going out. The first interpretation is the better one.

God, exalted is He, had already given him a concession in Surat al-Nur with His saying: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whomever you will among them﴾ (al-Nur 24:62). The two verses can be reconciled by saying that the rebuke here is directed at granting permission before verification (*istithbat*), until the truthful is distinguished from the liar, while the permission there is directed at granting it after verification. And God knows best.

It has also been said that His saying ﴿'Afa Allāhu 'anka﴾ is an opening of speech, as when you say, "May God make you prosperous, strengthen you, and have mercy on you, how did you do such-and-such?" This is related by Makki, al-Nahhas, and al-Mahdawi. According to this interpretation, it is good to pause at ﴿'Afa Allāhu 'anka﴾, whereas according to the first interpretation it is not good.

It is not hidden from you that the first interpretation is the one that corresponds to what the wording requires according to the Arabic language, and there is no basis for removing it from its Arabic meaning.

The verse contains evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning, personal judgment) on the part of the Prophet (ﷺ). The question is recorded in the books of usul al-fiqh (legal theory). It also contains evidence for the legislated character of guarding against haste and against being deceived by the outward appearances of matters.

As for ﴿*hattā yatabayyana laka alladhīna ṣadaqū*﴾ ("until those who were truthful became clear to you"), *ḥattā* here indicates a limit (*li-al-ghāya*), as if it were said: "Why did you rush to grant them permission? Why did you not take your time until the truthfulness of the one among them who was truthful in the excuse he presented became clear to you, and the lying of the one among them who was lying in that became clear?"

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that it is not the custom of the believers to ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission to stay back from jihad. Rather, it was their custom that when he (ﷺ) granted permission to one of them to stay behind, this weighed heavily upon him. So He said: ﴿Those who believe in God and the Last Day do not ask your permission to strive with their wealth and their selves﴾ (al-Tawba 9:44). This is according to the view that the meaning of the verse is "that they not strive," with the negative particle deleted. It has also been said that the meaning is: "The believers do not ask your permission to stay behind out of dislike for jihad." And it has been said that the meaning of seeking permission for something is disliking it. But according to what the apparent wording requires, the meaning is: the believers do not ask your permission regarding jihad; rather, their habit is to hasten toward it without hesitation or waiting for your permission to come, let alone asking you permission to stay behind.

Al-Zajjaj said: *an yujāhidū* is in a position of accusative (*naṣb*) by the implied preposition *fī*, meaning "in that they strive." ﴿And God knows the pious﴾, and they are those who did not ask permission.

It is only those who ask your permission to stay back from jihad and to remain behind from it ﴿who do not believe in God and the Last Day﴾, and they are the hypocrites. He mentioned belief in God first and belief in the Last Day second in both places, because these are the two motives for striving in the path of God.

His saying ﴿*wa-artābat qulūbuhum*﴾ ("and their hearts are in doubt") is coordinated with His saying ﴿who do not believe﴾. The past tense is used to indicate the certainty of doubt (*rayb*) in their hearts, and *rayb* is suspicion.

His saying ﴿*fa-hum fī raybihim yataraddadūn*﴾ ("so they are wavering in their doubt") means: in their doubt that has settled in their hearts they are bewildered, and *taraddud* is bewilderment.

The meaning is: those who ask your permission are not believers, but rather doubters, bewildered, not guided to the path of rightness, and not knowing the truth.

His saying ﴿*wa-law arādū al-khurūja la-a'addū lahu 'uddatan*﴾ ("And if they had intended to go out, they would have prepared for it some preparation") means: if they had been truthful in what they claim and what they inform you of, that they intend to strive with you, but they had not with them the equipment for jihad that is needed, they would not have neglected to prepare and gather the equipment before the time of jihad, as believers prepare for it. So the meaning of this statement is that they do not intend to go out at all, nor have they made any preparation for the campaign.

*'Udda* is what the striver needs of provisions, mount, and weapons.

His saying ﴿*wa-lākin karaha Allāhu inbi'āthahum*﴾ ("But God disliked their being sent forth") means: but God disliked their going out, so they were held back from going out. The meaning is: they did not go out, but they were restrained, because God's disliking of their being sent forth necessitates their being held back from going out. *Inbi'āth* is going out. That is, God held them back from going out with you and forsook them. For they said: "If permission is not given to us to sit back, we will corrupt and incite against the believers." It has also been said that the meaning is: "If they had intended to go out, they would have prepared for it some preparation, but they did not intend it because God disliked it."

His saying ﴿*wa-qīla 'quʿudū ma'a al-qā'idīn*﴾ ("And it was said: 'Sit with those who sit'") — it has been said that the one who said this to them was Satan through the whisperings he cast into them. It has also been said that some of them said it to others. It has also been said that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said it in anger at them. And it has been said that it is an expression of abandonment (*khidhlān*): that is, God placed sitting back in their hearts as abandonment of them.

The meaning of ﴿with those who sit﴾ is: with those of the disabled, the blind, the sick, the women, and the children. In this there is blame for them, belittlement of them, and disparagement of them, which is not hidden.

His saying ﴿*law kharajū fīkum mā zādūkum illā khabālan*﴾ ("Had they gone out among you, they would not have increased you except in corruption") is a consolation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers for the hypocrites' staying back.

*Khabāl* is corruption, slander, the sowing of discord, and the spreading of false rumors.

It has been said: this exception is disjunctive (*munqaṭi'*), meaning: "they would not have increased you in strength, but they sought corruption." It has been said: the meaning is: "they would not have increased you in the matter about which you were hesitating in opinion except in corruption," and thus it is connected (*muttaṣil*). It has also been said: it is an exception from the more general category (*istithnā' min a'amm al-'amm*), meaning: "they would not have increased you in anything except in corruption," so the exception is of the connected type, because *khabāl* is among the things that the word "thing" truly applies to.

His saying ﴿*wa-la-awḍa'ū khilālakum*﴾ ("and they would have hastened between you") — *īḍā'* is swiftness of travel. From it is the saying of Waraqa ibn Nawfal:

*"Would that I were in it as a young camel, / I would gallop in it and hasten."*

It is said: *awḍa'a al-ba'īr* when the camel hastened its pace. It has also been said that *īḍā'* is the gait of *khabab* (a fast trot). *Khalal* is the gap between two things, and its plural is *khilāl*, that is, the openings that are between the rows.

The meaning is: they would have run about among you with corruption, by means of the lies they fabricate, which include spreading false rumors and slander, which cause the corruption of relations among you.

His saying ﴿*yabghūnakumu al-fitnata*﴾ ("seeking to cause you discord"): it is said *baghaytuhu kadhā* meaning "I sought it for him," and *abghaytuhu kadhā* meaning "I helped him in seeking it."

The meaning is: they seek discord for you in your relations with one another by means of their incitement and corruption. It has also been said that *fitna* here means *shirk* (polytheism).

The clause ﴿*wa-fīkum sammā'ūna lahum*﴾ ("and among you are those who listen to them") is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: while among you are those who listen to what they say of falsehood and then convey it to you, so that discord among you is affected by that, and corruption spreads to your brethren. ﴿And God is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, and of what would have occurred from them had they gone out with you. Therefore His perfect wisdom required that they not go out with you, and He disliked their being sent forth with you. And their condition in this does not contradict the earlier rebuke to him (ﷺ) for granting them permission to stay back, because he hastened to grant them permission and had not known of their conditions that if they went out they would do these deeds. So he (ﷺ) was rebuked for his haste to grant them permission before it became clear to him which of them was truthful in his excuse and which was lying. For this reason God, glorified is He, said later in this surah: ﴿So if God returns you to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, say: "You will never go out with me, ever"﴾ (al-Tawba 9:83), and He said in Surat al-Fath: ﴿Those who stayed behind will say, when you set out to take spoils: "Let us follow you." They wish to change God's word. Say: "You will never follow us"﴾ (al-Fath 48:15).

His saying ﴿*laqadi ibtaghawu al-fitnata min qablu*﴾ ("They had already sought discord before") means: they had sought corruption, the spreading of disunity among the believers, and the scattering of their unity, before this campaign from which they stayed back, as happened from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and others. ﴿And God refuses except to perfect His light, though the disbelievers dislike it﴾ (al-Tawba 9:32).

His saying ﴿*wa-qallabū laka al-umūr*﴾ ("and they turned matters over for you") means: they changed them from one matter to another and devised for you tricks and schemes. From this is the Arabs' saying *ḥawwal qullab* ("a changeable, shrewd man") when he is constantly engaged in plots and tricks, turning the opinion over in them and reflecting upon them.

It is read *wa-qalabū* with the light pronunciation. ﴿*Ḥattā jā'a al-ḥaqq*﴾ ("until the truth came") means: up to a limit which is the coming of the truth, which is victory for you, support, and the manifestation of God's command by the exaltation of His religion, the making known of His law, and the subjugation of His enemies. It has also been said that *al-ḥaqq* is the Qur'an. ﴿*wa-hum kārihūn*﴾ ("while they were averse") means: while they were averse to the coming of the truth and the manifestation of God's command, but it happened in spite of them.

"And among them" means: among the hypocrites is one who says to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Grant me permission" to stay behind from jihad, "and do not tempt me," meaning: do not put me into temptation, that is, into sin, if you do not grant me permission and I stay behind without your permission. It has also been said that its meaning is: do not put me into destruction by going out. ﴿Surely in temptation they have fallen﴾, meaning: into temptation itself they have fallen, and this temptation is the temptation of staying behind from jihad and of false excuse.

The meaning is: they thought that by going out, or by your not granting them permission, they would fall into temptation, while by this staying back they have fallen into the great temptation.

In the expression "fallen" there is an indication that they fell into it as one who falls from a height to a lower place, and that is more severe than merely entering into temptation. Then He threatened them for this, saying: ﴿And indeed Hell is encompassing of the disbelievers﴾, meaning: encircling them from all sides, so that they find no escape from it, and are not able to get out of it in any condition.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq in *al-Muṣannaf*, and Ibn Jarir, related from ʿAmr ibn Maymun, who said: "Two things the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did, concerning which he was not commanded with anything: his granting permission to the hypocrites, and his taking ransom from the captives. Then God revealed: ʿAfā Allāhu ʿanka, lima adhinta lahum."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: "Have you heard of a rebuke more gentle than this? He began with pardon before the rebuke, saying: ʿAfā Allāhu ʿanka, lima adhinta lahum."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿ʿAfā Allāhu ʿanka﴾ and the verse, that he said: "Some people said: 'Ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) permission: if he grants you permission, sit back; and if he does not grant you permission, sit back.'"

Al-Nahhas related in his *Nāsikh* from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying ﴿ʿAfā Allāhu ʿanka, lima adhinta lahum﴾ — the three verses — that he said: "It abrogated them: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whomever you will among them﴾" (al-Nur 24:62).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Nahhas in his *Nāsikh* related from him concerning His saying ﴿Those who believe in God do not ask your permission﴾ and the verse, that he said: "This is a reproach to the hypocrites when they asked permission to sit back from jihad without an excuse, and God gave excuse to the believers, saying: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whomever you will among them﴾" (al-Nur 24:62).

Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from him also, concerning His saying: "Those who do not ask your permission..." the two verses, that he said: "They were abrogated by the verse in Surat al-Nur: ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in God and His Messenger﴾ until ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (al-Nur 24:62). So God made the Prophet (ﷺ) the one with the better of the two views in this matter: whoever went out, went out for a virtue, and whoever stayed back, stayed back without blame, God willing."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Dahhak concerning His saying ﴿But God disliked their being sent forth﴾, that he said: "Their going out."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying ﴿*fa-thabbaṭahum*﴾ ("so He held them back"), that he said: "He detained them."
