Being displeased by good and rejoicing at misfortune are among the strongest indications that they have reached the extreme of enmity. The meaning of ﴿they turn away﴾ is that they return to their people, away from gatherings and places of conversation, while rejoicing at the misfortune that struck the believers. The meaning of their words, ﴿We had already taken our precaution beforehand﴾, is that we took care of ourselves and acted with caution, so we did not go out to fight as the believers went out, until what befell them befell them.

Then, when they said this, Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to answer them with His words, ﴿Nothing will befall us except what Allah has decreed for us﴾, that is, in the Preserved Tablet, or in His Book revealed to us. Reliance upon Allah (tawakkul) is entrusting affairs to Him. The meaning is that it is incumbent upon the believers to make their reliance exclusively upon Allah, Glorified is He, and not to rely upon anyone else.

It is like His words, ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80], and in this is an indication of the equality of the two in non-acceptance. The accusative of ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾ is as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl); the two are verbal nouns in the place of the participles: that is, spend willingly without a command from Allah and His Messenger, or unwillingly by a command from them both.

The command from them both is called compulsion because they are hypocrites who do not obey commands, so they were, by their command which they do not obey, like those compelled to spend. Or: willingly, without compulsion from your leaders, or unwillingly from them. The clause ﴿Indeed you have been a defiantly disobedient people﴾ gives the reason for the non-acceptance of their spending.

Fisq (defiant disobedience) is rebellion and insolence, and its meaning linguistically and legally has already been explained.

Then Allah, Glorified is He, explained the cause that prevents their expenditures from being accepted, and said: ﴿Nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾. That is, their disbelief in Allah and His Messenger made the barriers to acceptance three matters. The first: disbelief. The second: they do not pray in any state except in a state of laziness and sluggishness, because they do not hope for reward nor fear punishment, so their prayer is only for show before people and a pretence of Islam while they conceal the opposite. The third: they do not spend their wealth except while unwilling, and they do not spend it willingly, because they consider spending it to be wasting it, due to their lack of faith in what Allah and His Messenger promised.

His words: ﴿So do not let their wealth or their children impress you﴾. To be impressed by something is to be pleased with it with the pleasure of one who is satisfied with it, marvelling at its beauty. It was said: along with a kind of boasting and the belief that no one else has anything equal to it. The meaning: do not regard as fine what they have of wealth and children. ﴿Allah only intends to punish them by them in this worldly life﴾ through the grief and sorrow that come to them when the Muslims take the spoils and seize them from their hands by force, even though they are the adornment of their life and the coolness of their eyes. Likewise in the Hereafter He will punish them with the punishment of the Fire, because of their ingratitude to their Lord who gave them that, and their neglect of what is obligatory upon them of zakat concerning it, and of giving charity with what is due to be given in charity. It was also said: there is an inversion in the speech, and the meaning is: "So do not let their wealth or their children impress you in this worldly life. Allah only intends to punish them by them in the Hereafter, because they are hypocrites, so they spend unwillingly and so they are punished by what they spend."

His words: ﴿And their souls depart while they are disbelievers﴾. Zuhūq is departing with difficulty. The meaning: Allah intends that their souls depart and their spirits leave while they are in a state of disbelief, because they did not accept what the prophets brought and what the messengers were sent with, and because of their persistence in disbelief and their continuing in misguidance.

Then Allah, Glorified is He, mentioned another kind of the hypocrites' ugly traits and said: ﴿They swear by Allah that they are surely of you﴾, that is, of your community in the religion of Islam and in submission to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to the Book of Allah, Glorified is He. ﴿But they are not of you﴾ in that, except in their outward appearance only, not in their inner selves. ﴿But they are a people who are fearful﴾, that is, they fear that what befell the polytheists of killing and captivity may befall them, so they show you Islam out of taqiyyah (precautionary concealment of belief) from them, not out of genuine conviction.

﴿If they could find a refuge﴾ where they could take shelter and protect their selves from you, a fortress or something else, ﴿or caves﴾, plural of maghārah, from ghāra yaghīru. Al-Akhfash said: it may also be from aghāra yughīru. The maghārāt are caverns and underground passages, which are the places in which one hides. From it comes "the water sank" (ghāra al-māʾ) and "the spring sank" (ghārat al-ʿayn). The meaning: if they found places in which to hide their persons, fleeing from you, ﴿or a place of entry﴾, from "entering", that is, a place they could enter among places that are not caves.

Al-Naḥḥās said: the original form of it is mutadakhal, the tā' was changed into dāl. It was also said: its original form is mudtakhal.

Ubayy recited "mutadakhkhalan" (with a doubled dāl), and it is narrated from him that he recited "mundakhalan" with a nūn.

Al-Ḥasan, Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Ibn Muḥaysin recited "aw madkhalan" with a fatḥah on the mīm and sukūn on the dāl.

Al-Zajjāj said: it is also read "aw mudkhalan" with a ḍammah on the mīm and sukūn on the dāl.

The rest recited with a shaddah on the dāl and a ḍammah on the mīm. ﴿They would turn to it﴾, that is, they would take refuge in it and enter themselves into it, ﴿while they rush headlong﴾, that is, they hasten with a speed that nothing can check, from "jamaḥa al-faras" (the horse bolted), when the bridle does not restrain it. From this is the poet's saying:

"Swift and unrestrainable, and its charging is like the crackling of a lit palm frond."

The meaning: if they found any of these things mentioned, they would turn towards it hastening, fleeing from the Muslims.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh who said: The hypocrites who stayed behind in Medina began to report bad news about the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "Muḥammad and his companions have been exhausted in their journey and have perished." Then the falsity of their report reached them, along with the well-being of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, and that displeased them. So Allah revealed: ﴿If good befalls you, it displeases them﴾, the verse.

Sunayd and Ibn Jarīr reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿If good befalls you, it displeases them﴾: that is, if good befalls you on this journey, the expedition to Tabūk, which displeases them. He said: "They are al-Jadd and his companions," meaning al-Jadd ibn Qays.

Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddī regarding ﴿Say: Nothing will befall us except what Allah has written for us﴾: "except what Allah has decreed for us."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes?﴾: "Conquest or martyrdom."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words ﴿or by our hands﴾: "Killing by swords."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: Al-Jadd ibn Qays said: "Indeed, when I see women I cannot restrain myself until I am tempted. But I will help you with my wealth." So regarding him was revealed: ﴿Say: Spend willingly or unwillingly﴾, the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah regarding His words ﴿So do not let their wealth impress you﴾: "This is one of the inversions of speech. He says: 'Do not let their wealth or their children impress you in this worldly life.' Allah only intends to punish them by them in the Hereafter."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: "Allah only intends to punish them by them in the Hereafter."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from al-Suddī regarding His words ﴿and their souls depart while they are disbelievers﴾: "Their souls depart in this worldly life, ﴿while they are disbelievers﴾." He said: "This is a verse in which there is an inversion."

Abū Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding His words ﴿So do not let [them] impress you﴾: "Do not let them deceive you." And "and depart": "their souls leave," he said, "in this world, ﴿while they are disbelievers﴾."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿If they could find a refuge﴾, the verse. He said: "The refuge is a stronghold in the mountains; the maghārāt are caverns; and the mudkhal is a hole."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddī regarding ﴿and they rush headlong﴾: "They hasten."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 58–60 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you﴾ This is a mention of another type of their ugly conduct. It is said: *yalmizuhu* (he finds fault with him) when he defames him.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-lamz* is defamation. Its origin is signalling with the eye or the like. One says *lamazahu, yalmazuhu* and *yalmizuhu*, and a man is *lammaz* (a habitual defamer), and *lumaza* (a great defamer), meaning one who defames often.

Al-Zajjaj said: "*Lamaztu al-rajula, almizuhu* and *almuzuhu*" with the *mim* vowelled with kasra or damma, meaning: when I defamed the man. Likewise *hamaztuhu*.

The meaning of the verse: "Among the hypocrites are those who find fault with you concerning the *sadaqat* (alms), that is, concerning their distribution and division."

It is narrated from Mujahid that he said: the meaning of ﴿yalmizuka﴾ is "he takes from you and asks you." However, according to the lexicographers the first meaning is the correct one, as al-Nahhas said.

It has been read *yalmuzuka* with a damma on the *mim*, and *yulammizuka* with a kasra and shaddah.

The majority read it with a kasra and without shaddah. ﴿If they are given from them﴾, that is, from the alms, an amount that they desire, they are content with what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave and they do not find fault with him. This is because their only aim is the trappings of this world, and they have nothing to do with religion. ﴿But if they are not given from them﴾, that is, from the alms, what they wish for and seek, ﴿then behold, they become angry﴾, that is, if they are not given, they suddenly show anger. The benefit of the sudden *idha* (idha al-fujaʼiyya) is that the condition comes suddenly upon the consequence and attacks it. The sudden *idha* has taken the place of the *fa'* of the consequence.

﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them﴾, that is, what Allah prescribed for them and what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave them of the alms. The answer to *law* (if only) is omitted, meaning: it would have been better for them, for in what He gave them there is good, both immediate and deferred. ﴿And they said: "Allah is sufficient for us; Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. To Allah we turn in hope"﴾. That is, they said this statement when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave them what was theirs: Allah suffices us; He will give us of His bounty, and His Messenger will give us after this what we hope for and aspire to. ﴿To Allah we turn in hope﴾ that He will give us of His bounty what we hope for.

His saying: ﴿The alms are only for the poor﴾. When the hypocrites found fault with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning the division of the alms, Allah made clear to them their destination, to repel their slander and cut off their clamour. *Innama* (only) is one of the forms of restriction (*qasr*). The definite article in *al-sadaqat* is generic: the class of these alms is restricted to these categories mentioned and does not exceed them, but rather they belong to them and not to others.

The scholars differed as to whether it is obligatory to distribute the alms among these eight categories, or whether it is permissible to give them to some and not others according to what the imam or the owner of the alms sees fit. Al-Shafi'i and a group of scholars held the first view, while Malik and Abu Hanifa held the second, and this was also the view of Umar, Huzayfa, Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aliyya, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Maymun ibn Mihran.

Ibn Jarir said, and this is the view of the majority of scholars: The first group relied on the restriction in the verse and on the hadith of Ziyad ibn al-Harith al-Sada'i in Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and pledged allegiance to him. A man came and said: 'Give me from the charity.' He said to him: 'Allah has not been content with the judgment of a prophet or anyone else concerning the alms, until He Himself judged concerning them, and divided them into eight categories. If you are one of those categories, I will give you.'"

The others replied that the restriction in the verse is only to explain the manner of disbursement and the recipients, not to make it obligatory to cover all the categories. They also argued that in the chain of this hadith is ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad ibn Anʿum al-Ifriqi, who is weak.

What supports the view of the others is the saying of the Most High: ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:271]. The term *sadaqa* is applied to the obligatory as well as to the recommended.

It is also authentically reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "I have been commanded to take the charity from your wealthy and return it to your poor."

Malik claimed consensus for the other view. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: He means the consensus of the Companions, for he knows of no dissenter among them.

His saying: *lil-fuqara'* (for the poor): he mentioned them first because, according to the well-known view, they are more in need than the rest, due to the severity of their poverty and need.

The scholars differed concerning the distinction between the *faqir* (poor) and the *miskin* (needy) into several views. Yaqub ibn al-Sikkit, al-Qutaybi and Yunus ibn Habib said: the *faqir* is better off than the *miskin*. They said: the *faqir* is one who has some of what suffices him and sustains him, while the *miskin* has nothing. This was also the view of a group of jurists, among them Abu Hanifa.

Others said the opposite: they made the *miskin* better off than the *faqir*, and they argued from the saying of the Most High: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to needy men﴾ [al-Kahf 18:79]. He informed that they had a boat from the boats of the sea, which may equal a considerable amount of wealth. This is supported by the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeking refuge from poverty, together with his saying: "O Allah, let me live as a *miskin*, let me die as a *miskin*." This was the view of al-Asma'i and other lexicographers, and al-Tahawi reported it from the Kufans. It is one of the two views of al-Shafi'i and of most of his companions.

Others said: the *faqir* and the *miskin* are the same, with no difference between them. This is one of the two views of al-Shafi'i, and Ibn al-Qasim and the rest of Malik's companions held it, as did Abu Yusuf.

Others said: the *faqir* is the one in need who is restrained (in asking), and the *miskin* is the one who asks. This was stated by al-Azhari, preferred by Ibn Sha'ban, and is reported from Ibn Abbas.

Other views besides these have been stated, but multiplying them does not yield any beneficial result.

The most appropriate explanation of the nature of the *miskin* is what was established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The *miskin* is not this wanderer who goes around the people, and a morsel or two, or a date or two, turns him away." They said: "Then who is the *miskin*, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The one who does not find sufficient wealth to suffice him, and who is not noticed so that he may be given charity, and who does not ask people for anything."

His saying: ﴿And those employed to collect them﴾, that is, the agents and collectors whom the imam sends to collect the zakat; they are entitled to a share of it.

It has been disputed as to the amount they take from it. It is said: one-eighth, reported from Mujahid and al-Shafi'i.

It is said: according to the measure of their work in terms of wages, reported from Abu Hanifa and his companions.

It is said: they are given from the public treasury an amount equal to their wage, reported from Malik. But there is no basis for this, for Allah has informed that they have a share of the charity, so how can they be prevented from it and given from something else?

They differed as to whether the collector may be a Hashimite or not. Some prohibited it, and others permitted it, and they said: he is given from other than the charity.

His saying: ﴿And those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾. They are a people who existed in the early period of Islam. It has been said: they are the disbelievers whom the Prophet (ﷺ) would win over so that they might embrace Islam, and they did not enter Islam by force or the sword, but by gifts. It has been said: they are people who professed Islam outwardly but whose Islam was not sound, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would win them over with gifts. It has been said: they are those of the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam. It has been said: they are some of the great polytheists who had followers, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) gave in order to win their followers over to Islam.

The Prophet (ﷺ) gave a number of those who professed Islam outwardly, such as Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, al-Harith ibn Hisham, Suhayl ibn Amr and Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza. He gave each of them one hundred camels, to win them over with this, and he gave others less than these.

The scholars differed as to whether the share of "those whose hearts are to be reconciled" remains after Islam became dominant. Umar, al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi said: this category has been discontinued because of the might of Islam and its ascendancy. This is well known in the school of Malik and the people of opinion (Hanafis). Some Hanafis claimed that the Companions unanimously agreed on this.

A group of scholars said: their share remains, because the imam may sometimes need to win people over to Islam. Umar only discontinued them when he saw how the religion had been strengthened.

Yunus said: I asked al-Zuhri about them, and he said: I do not know of any abrogation (*naskh*, the cancelling of a ruling by a later one) of this. According to the first view, their share goes to the rest of the categories.

His saying: ﴿And for the captives﴾, that is, for the freeing of captives, by buying slaves and then freeing them.

This was reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, and Malik, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq and Abu Ubayd held this view.

Al-Hasan al-Basri, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri and Ibn Zayd said: they are the *mukatabun* (slaves who have contracted to buy their freedom), who are helped from the charity to pay the contract money. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, the people of opinion, and a narration from Malik. The better course is to apply what is in the verse to both views together, since the term "captives" applies both to buying a slave and freeing him, and to helping a *mukatab* with his contract money.

His saying: ﴿And the debtors﴾ are those who are overwhelmed by debts and have no means of repaying them. There is no disagreement about this, except that one who incurred debt through wastefulness is not given from it or from anything else, unless he repents.

The Prophet (ﷺ) helped from the charity one who had taken on a liability (*hamala*), and directed that he be helped from it.

His saying: ﴿And in the way of Allah﴾ are the fighters and those stationed on the frontiers (*al-murabitun*), who are given from the charity what they spend in their campaign and their garrison duty, even if they are wealthy. This is the view of most scholars.

Ibn Umar said: they are the pilgrims and those performing the 'umra. It is reported from Ahmad and Ishaq that they regarded the Hajj as being in the way of Allah.

Abu Hanifa and his two companions said: the fighter is not given (from the charity) unless he is poor and cut off from his means.

His saying: ﴿And the wayfarer﴾. This is the traveller. *Al-sabil* means the road, and the traveller is attributed to it because he constantly keeps to it. The intended meaning is one whose means have been cut off during his journey away from his homeland and place of residence. He is given from it even if he is wealthy in his own land, and even if he finds someone who would lend him money.

Malik said: if he finds someone who would lend him, he is not given.

His saying: ﴿An obligation from Allah﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun (*masdar*), because His saying "The alms are only for the poor" means: Allah has made the alms obligatory for them.

The meaning: that the restriction of the alms to these categories is a binding ruling which Allah has prescribed upon His servants, and He has forbidden them from exceeding it. And Allah is All-Knowing of the conditions of His servants and All-Wise in His actions. It has also been said that *fariḍatan* is in the accusative by an implied verb: that is, Allah prescribed that as an obligation.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: If you ask, why did He change from the preposition *li-* (for) to *fi-* (in) in the last four categories? I say: to signal that they are more firmly entitled to receive charity than those mentioned before. It has also been said that the reason for the change is that the first four categories are given the money so that they may dispose of it as they wish, whereas for the last four the money is not given to them, but is spent on the needs that justify their receiving a share of zakat. So it is said.

Al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was dividing a portion, the son of Dhu al-Khuwaysira al-Tamimi came and said: 'Be just, O Messenger of Allah!' He said: 'Woe to you! Who will be just if I am not just?' Umar ibn al-Khattab said: 'Permit me to strike off his neck.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Leave him, for he has companions, whose prayer one of you will consider insignificant compared to their prayer, and whose fasting you will consider insignificant compared to their fasting. They will pass through the religion as an arrow passes through its game...' [the hadith continues] until he said: 'And concerning them was revealed: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the alms﴾.'"

Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, commentary on Surah 9, verses 58–60 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you﴾ — he said: "yarzuʾuka" means he asks you (for gain).

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah, who said: "yaṭʿanu ʿalayka" means he slanders you.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) distributed the spoils of Hunayn, I heard a man say: 'Indeed, this is a distribution by which Allah was not sought.' So I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him. He said: 'May Allah have mercy on Musa; he was harmed with more than this and was patient.'" And there was revealed: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "This verse abrogated (naskh) every charity mentioned in the Qur'an, namely: ﴿Indeed, the charities are for the poor﴾ — the verse."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Hudhayfah regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, the charities are for the poor﴾ — the verse — he said: "If you wish, you may place it in one category of the eight categories which Allah named, or in two, or in three."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated something similar from Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Hasan, ʿAta', Ibrahim and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The poor (fuqara') are the poor among the Muslims, and the needy (masakin) are the wanderers."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Nahhas and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, who said: "The poor (faqir) is the one who has a disability (zamanah), and the needy (miskin) is the one in need who has no disability."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from ʿUmar regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, the charities are for the poor﴾, he said: "They are the disabled among the People of the Book."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿and those employed to collect them﴾, he said: "They are the collectors (al-sussa'), the officers of the charity."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿and those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾, he said: "They are a people who used to come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after they had embraced Islam, and he would give them a portion from the charities. When he gave them from the charity and they gained some good from it, they said: 'This is a good religion.' But if it was otherwise, they would find fault with it and abandon it."

al-Bukhari, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Saʿid, who said: "ʿAli ibn Abi Talib sent from Yemen to the Prophet (ﷺ) a small gold ore with its earth still in it, and he distributed it among four of those whose hearts are to be reconciled: al-Aqraʿ ibn Habis al-Handhali, ʿAlqamah ibn ʿUlathah al-ʿAmiri, ʿUyaynah ibn Badr al-Fazari, and Zayd al-Khayl al-Ta'i. Then the Quraysh and the Ansar said: 'He distributes among the chiefs of Najd and leaves us out?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I only do so to reconcile their hearts.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Zuhri that he was asked about those whose hearts are to be reconciled. He said: "Whoever embraces Islam from a Jew or a Christian." I said: "Even if he is wealthy?" He said: "Even if he is wealthy."

The same compilers narrated from Abu Jaʿfar, who said: "Today there are no whose hearts are to be reconciled."

The same compilers also narrated from al-Shaʿbi something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil regarding His words: ﴿and for the captives (fi al-riqab)﴾, he said: "They are the mukatabun (slaves who have contracted to buy their freedom)."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Nakhaʿi something similar.

He also narrated from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: "The share of the captives is two halves: half for each mukatab from among those who claim Islam, and the other half is used to buy captives from among those who pray and fast, giving precedence to those who have embraced Islam, male or female, who free them for the sake of Allah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he saw no harm in a man giving from his zakat for Hajj and freeing a slave from it (p-581).

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from al-Zuhri that he was asked about the debtors (al-gharimin). He said: "They are the owners of debts."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Jaʿfar regarding His words: ﴿and the debtors﴾, he said: "He is one who asks (for help) because of blood-money or a calamity that befalls him." ﴿And in the way of Allah﴾, he said: "They are the fighters (al-mujahidun)." ﴿And the wayfarer﴾, he said: "The one cut off from his means, who is given an amount sufficient to bring him to his destination."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The wayfarer is the poor guest who stops among the Muslims."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Charity is not lawful for a rich person except for five: one who collects it, or a man who bought it with his own wealth, or a debtor, or one who fights in the way of Allah, or a needy person to whom charity was given who then gives a gift from it to a wealthy person."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abu Dawud narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Charity is not lawful for a rich person, nor for one who is strong and able to earn."

Ahmad narrated from a man of the Banu Hilal, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAdi ibn al-Khiyar, who said: "Two men informed me that they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during the Farewell Pilgrimage while he was distributing charity, and they asked him for some of it. He looked at us, raising and lowering his gaze, and saw us as strong and sturdy. He said: 'If you wish, I will give you, but there is no share in it for a rich person or for a strong person who earns his living.'"

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 58–60 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you﴾ This is a mention of another type of their ugly conduct. It is said: *yalmizuhu* (he finds fault with him) when he defames him.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-lamz* is defamation. Its origin is signalling with the eye or the like. One says *lamazahu, yalmazuhu* and *yalmizuhu*, and a man is *lammaz* (a habitual defamer), and *lumaza* (a great defamer), meaning one who defames often.

Al-Zajjaj said: "*Lamaztu al-rajula, almizuhu* and *almuzuhu*" with the *mim* vowelled with kasra or damma, meaning: when I defamed the man. Likewise *hamaztuhu*.

The meaning of the verse: "Among the hypocrites are those who find fault with you concerning the *sadaqat* (alms), that is, concerning their distribution and division."

It is narrated from Mujahid that he said: the meaning of ﴿yalmizuka﴾ is "he takes from you and asks you." However, according to the lexicographers the first meaning is the correct one, as al-Nahhas said.

It has been read *yalmuzuka* with a damma on the *mim*, and *yulammizuka* with a kasra and shaddah.

The majority read it with a kasra and without shaddah. ﴿If they are given from them﴾, that is, from the alms, an amount that they desire, they are content with what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave and they do not find fault with him. This is because their only aim is the trappings of this world, and they have nothing to do with religion. ﴿But if they are not given from them﴾, that is, from the alms, what they wish for and seek, ﴿then behold, they become angry﴾, that is, if they are not given, they suddenly show anger. The benefit of the sudden *idha* (idha al-fujaʼiyya) is that the condition comes suddenly upon the consequence and attacks it. The sudden *idha* has taken the place of the *fa'* of the consequence.

﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them﴾, that is, what Allah prescribed for them and what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave them of the alms. The answer to *law* (if only) is omitted, meaning: it would have been better for them, for in what He gave them there is good, both immediate and deferred. ﴿And they said: "Allah is sufficient for us; Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. To Allah we turn in hope"﴾. That is, they said this statement when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave them what was theirs: Allah suffices us; He will give us of His bounty, and His Messenger will give us after this what we hope for and aspire to. ﴿To Allah we turn in hope﴾ that He will give us of His bounty what we hope for.

His saying: ﴿The alms are only for the poor﴾. When the hypocrites found fault with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning the division of the alms, Allah made clear to them their destination, to repel their slander and cut off their clamour. *Innama* (only) is one of the forms of restriction (*qasr*). The definite article in *al-sadaqat* is generic: the class of these alms is restricted to these categories mentioned and does not exceed them, but rather they belong to them and not to others.

The scholars differed as to whether it is obligatory to distribute the alms among these eight categories, or whether it is permissible to give them to some and not others according to what the imam or the owner of the alms sees fit. Al-Shafi'i and a group of scholars held the first view, while Malik and Abu Hanifa held the second, and this was also the view of Umar, Huzayfa, Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aliyya, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Maymun ibn Mihran.

Ibn Jarir said, and this is the view of the majority of scholars: The first group relied on the restriction in the verse and on the hadith of Ziyad ibn al-Harith al-Sada'i in Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and pledged allegiance to him. A man came and said: 'Give me from the charity.' He said to him: 'Allah has not been content with the judgment of a prophet or anyone else concerning the alms, until He Himself judged concerning them, and divided them into eight categories. If you are one of those categories, I will give you.'"

The others replied that the restriction in the verse is only to explain the manner of disbursement and the recipients, not to make it obligatory to cover all the categories. They also argued that in the chain of this hadith is ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad ibn Anʿum al-Ifriqi, who is weak.

What supports the view of the others is the saying of the Most High: ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:271]. The term *sadaqa* is applied to the obligatory as well as to the recommended.

It is also authentically reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "I have been commanded to take the charity from your wealthy and return it to your poor."

Malik claimed consensus for the other view. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: He means the consensus of the Companions, for he knows of no dissenter among them.

His saying: *lil-fuqara'* (for the poor): he mentioned them first because, according to the well-known view, they are more in need than the rest, due to the severity of their poverty and need.

The scholars differed concerning the distinction between the *faqir* (poor) and the *miskin* (needy) into several views. Yaqub ibn al-Sikkit, al-Qutaybi and Yunus ibn Habib said: the *faqir* is better off than the *miskin*. They said: the *faqir* is one who has some of what suffices him and sustains him, while the *miskin* has nothing. This was also the view of a group of jurists, among them Abu Hanifa.

Others said the opposite: they made the *miskin* better off than the *faqir*, and they argued from the saying of the Most High: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to needy men﴾ [al-Kahf 18:79]. He informed that they had a boat from the boats of the sea, which may equal a considerable amount of wealth. This is supported by the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeking refuge from poverty, together with his saying: "O Allah, let me live as a *miskin*, let me die as a *miskin*." This was the view of al-Asma'i and other lexicographers, and al-Tahawi reported it from the Kufans. It is one of the two views of al-Shafi'i and of most of his companions.

Others said: the *faqir* and the *miskin* are the same, with no difference between them. This is one of the two views of al-Shafi'i, and Ibn al-Qasim and the rest of Malik's companions held it, as did Abu Yusuf.

Others said: the *faqir* is the one in need who is restrained (in asking), and the *miskin* is the one who asks. This was stated by al-Azhari, preferred by Ibn Sha'ban, and is reported from Ibn Abbas.

Other views besides these have been stated, but multiplying them does not yield any beneficial result.

The most appropriate explanation of the nature of the *miskin* is what was established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The *miskin* is not this wanderer who goes around the people, and a morsel or two, or a date or two, turns him away." They said: "Then who is the *miskin*, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The one who does not find sufficient wealth to suffice him, and who is not noticed so that he may be given charity, and who does not ask people for anything."

His saying: ﴿And those employed to collect them﴾, that is, the agents and collectors whom the imam sends to collect the zakat; they are entitled to a share of it.

It has been disputed as to the amount they take from it. It is said: one-eighth, reported from Mujahid and al-Shafi'i.

It is said: according to the measure of their work in terms of wages, reported from Abu Hanifa and his companions.

It is said: they are given from the public treasury an amount equal to their wage, reported from Malik. But there is no basis for this, for Allah has informed that they have a share of the charity, so how can they be prevented from it and given from something else?

They differed as to whether the collector may be a Hashimite or not. Some prohibited it, and others permitted it, and they said: he is given from other than the charity.

His saying: ﴿And those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾. They are a people who existed in the early period of Islam. It has been said: they are the disbelievers whom the Prophet (ﷺ) would win over so that they might embrace Islam, and they did not enter Islam by force or the sword, but by gifts. It has been said: they are people who professed Islam outwardly but whose Islam was not sound, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would win them over with gifts. It has been said: they are those of the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam. It has been said: they are some of the great polytheists who had followers, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) gave in order to win their followers over to Islam.

The Prophet (ﷺ) gave a number of those who professed Islam outwardly, such as Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, al-Harith ibn Hisham, Suhayl ibn Amr and Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza. He gave each of them one hundred camels, to win them over with this, and he gave others less than these.

The scholars differed as to whether the share of "those whose hearts are to be reconciled" remains after Islam became dominant. Umar, al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi said: this category has been discontinued because of the might of Islam and its ascendancy. This is well known in the school of Malik and the people of opinion (Hanafis). Some Hanafis claimed that the Companions unanimously agreed on this.

A group of scholars said: their share remains, because the imam may sometimes need to win people over to Islam. Umar only discontinued them when he saw how the religion had been strengthened.

Yunus said: I asked al-Zuhri about them, and he said: I do not know of any abrogation (*naskh*, the cancelling of a ruling by a later one) of this. According to the first view, their share goes to the rest of the categories.

His saying: ﴿And for the captives﴾, that is, for the freeing of captives, by buying slaves and then freeing them.

This was reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, and Malik, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq and Abu Ubayd held this view.

Al-Hasan al-Basri, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri and Ibn Zayd said: they are the *mukatabun* (slaves who have contracted to buy their freedom), who are helped from the charity to pay the contract money. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, the people of opinion, and a narration from Malik. The better course is to apply what is in the verse to both views together, since the term "captives" applies both to buying a slave and freeing him, and to helping a *mukatab* with his contract money.

His saying: ﴿And the debtors﴾ are those who are overwhelmed by debts and have no means of repaying them. There is no disagreement about this, except that one who incurred debt through wastefulness is not given from it or from anything else, unless he repents.

The Prophet (ﷺ) helped from the charity one who had taken on a liability (*hamala*), and directed that he be helped from it.

His saying: ﴿And in the way of Allah﴾ are the fighters and those stationed on the frontiers (*al-murabitun*), who are given from the charity what they spend in their campaign and their garrison duty, even if they are wealthy. This is the view of most scholars.

Ibn Umar said: they are the pilgrims and those performing the 'umra. It is reported from Ahmad and Ishaq that they regarded the Hajj as being in the way of Allah.

Abu Hanifa and his two companions said: the fighter is not given (from the charity) unless he is poor and cut off from his means.

His saying: ﴿And the wayfarer﴾. This is the traveller. *Al-sabil* means the road, and the traveller is attributed to it because he constantly keeps to it. The intended meaning is one whose means have been cut off during his journey away from his homeland and place of residence. He is given from it even if he is wealthy in his own land, and even if he finds someone who would lend him money.

Malik said: if he finds someone who would lend him, he is not given.

His saying: ﴿An obligation from Allah﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun (*masdar*), because His saying "The alms are only for the poor" means: Allah has made the alms obligatory for them.

The meaning: that the restriction of the alms to these categories is a binding ruling which Allah has prescribed upon His servants, and He has forbidden them from exceeding it. And Allah is All-Knowing of the conditions of His servants and All-Wise in His actions. It has also been said that *fariḍatan* is in the accusative by an implied verb: that is, Allah prescribed that as an obligation.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: If you ask, why did He change from the preposition *li-* (for) to *fi-* (in) in the last four categories? I say: to signal that they are more firmly entitled to receive charity than those mentioned before. It has also been said that the reason for the change is that the first four categories are given the money so that they may dispose of it as they wish, whereas for the last four the money is not given to them, but is spent on the needs that justify their receiving a share of zakat. So it is said.

Al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was dividing a portion, the son of Dhu al-Khuwaysira al-Tamimi came and said: 'Be just, O Messenger of Allah!' He said: 'Woe to you! Who will be just if I am not just?' Umar ibn al-Khattab said: 'Permit me to strike off his neck.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Leave him, for he has companions, whose prayer one of you will consider insignificant compared to their prayer, and whose fasting you will consider insignificant compared to their fasting. They will pass through the religion as an arrow passes through its game...' [the hadith continues] until he said: 'And concerning them was revealed: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the alms﴾.'"

Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, commentary on Surah 9, verses 58–60 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you﴾ — he said: "yarzuʾuka" means he asks you (for gain).

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah, who said: "yaṭʿanu ʿalayka" means he slanders you.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) distributed the spoils of Hunayn, I heard a man say: 'Indeed, this is a distribution by which Allah was not sought.' So I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him. He said: 'May Allah have mercy on Musa; he was harmed with more than this and was patient.'" And there was revealed: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "This verse abrogated (naskh) every charity mentioned in the Qur'an, namely: ﴿Indeed, the charities are for the poor﴾ — the verse."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Hudhayfah regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, the charities are for the poor﴾ — the verse — he said: "If you wish, you may place it in one category of the eight categories which Allah named, or in two, or in three."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated something similar from Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Hasan, ʿAta', Ibrahim and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The poor (fuqara') are the poor among the Muslims, and the needy (masakin) are the wanderers."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Nahhas and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, who said: "The poor (faqir) is the one who has a disability (zamanah), and the needy (miskin) is the one in need who has no disability."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from ʿUmar regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, the charities are for the poor﴾, he said: "They are the disabled among the People of the Book."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿and those employed to collect them﴾, he said: "They are the collectors (al-sussa'), the officers of the charity."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿and those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾, he said: "They are a people who used to come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after they had embraced Islam, and he would give them a portion from the charities. When he gave them from the charity and they gained some good from it, they said: 'This is a good religion.' But if it was otherwise, they would find fault with it and abandon it."

al-Bukhari, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Saʿid, who said: "ʿAli ibn Abi Talib sent from Yemen to the Prophet (ﷺ) a small gold ore with its earth still in it, and he distributed it among four of those whose hearts are to be reconciled: al-Aqraʿ ibn Habis al-Handhali, ʿAlqamah ibn ʿUlathah al-ʿAmiri, ʿUyaynah ibn Badr al-Fazari, and Zayd al-Khayl al-Ta'i. Then the Quraysh and the Ansar said: 'He distributes among the chiefs of Najd and leaves us out?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I only do so to reconcile their hearts.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Zuhri that he was asked about those whose hearts are to be reconciled. He said: "Whoever embraces Islam from a Jew or a Christian." I said: "Even if he is wealthy?" He said: "Even if he is wealthy."

The same compilers narrated from Abu Jaʿfar, who said: "Today there are no whose hearts are to be reconciled."

The same compilers also narrated from al-Shaʿbi something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muqatil regarding His words: ﴿and for the captives (fi al-riqab)﴾, he said: "They are the mukatabun (slaves who have contracted to buy their freedom)."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Nakhaʿi something similar.

He also narrated from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: "The share of the captives is two halves: half for each mukatab from among those who claim Islam, and the other half is used to buy captives from among those who pray and fast, giving precedence to those who have embraced Islam, male or female, who free them for the sake of Allah."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he saw no harm in a man giving from his zakat for Hajj and freeing a slave from it (p-581).
