Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Uqayli in al-Du'afa' (The Weak Narrators), Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Khatib, in a narration of Malik from Ibn Umar, who said: "I saw Abdullah ibn Ubayy running ahead of the Prophet (ﷺ), with stones striking him, and he was saying: 'O Muhammad, we were only chatting and playing,' while the Prophet (ﷺ) was saying: ﴿Was it at Allah, His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾"

Far-fetched, far-fetched!' So Allah informed His Prophet (ﷺ) of that, and the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Hold these riders back for me.' He came to them and said: 'You said such-and-such.' They said: 'O Prophet of Allah, we were only chatting and playing.' So Allah revealed concerning them what you hear."

A similar report has been narrated through several chains from a group of the Companions.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿If We pardon a group﴾, that he said: "The group (ta'ifah) is a man or a small band."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 61–66 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "And among them are those who..." This is another category, concerning the disgraceful and abominable conduct of the hypocrites that Allah has related. They used to say to the Prophet (ﷺ), in a manner of disparagement and blame, "He is an ear" (*huwa udhun*).

Al-Jawhari said: "It is said *rajulun udhun* (a man who is an ear) when he listens to everyone's speech, and it applies to the singular and the plural alike." Their intent, may Allah humiliate them, was that when they harmed the Prophet and spread their tongues against him, and it reached him, they would apologise to him and he would accept it from them, because he hears everything that is said to him and believes it. The Arabs applied the term "ear" to one who hears what is said to him and believes it only as an exaggeration, for they named him after the organ that is the instrument of hearing, as though his whole being were a listening ear. A parallel is their calling a sentry *'ayn* (an eye). Their harming him consisted in their saying *huwa udhun*, because they attributed to him that he believes everything said to him and does not distinguish between the true and the false, deceived by his forbearance towards them and his pardoning of their offences, out of generosity, forbearance and overlooking.

Then Allah answered their saying, and said: ﴿Say: an ear of goodness for you﴾, with the genitive construction (*idafah*), according to the reading of the majority.

Al-Hasan recited it with tanwin (*udhunun*), and so did 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr from him. It is as though it were said: "Yes, he is an ear, but what a good ear he is, being an ear of goodness for you, and he is not an ear in any other respect," like their saying *rajulu sidqin* (a man of truthfulness), meaning excellence and righteousness.

The meaning is that he hears the good and does not hear the evil.

It was also recited as *udhnu* with the dhal pronounced with sukun and with damma. Then He explained his being an ear of goodness by His saying: ﴿He believes in Allah and believes the believers﴾, i.e., he affirms Allah and affirms the believers, because he knows of them the sincerity of their faith. The *lam* in *lil-mu'minin* is then for reinforcement (*lil-taqwiyah*), as the Kufans said, or it is connected to a suppressed verbal noun, as al-Mubarrad said.

Al-Jumhur recited *wa-rahmatun* with raf', as a conjunction to *udhunun*.

Hamzah recited it with jarr, as a conjunction to *khayrin*.

The meaning according to the first reading: he is an ear of goodness and he is a mercy for the believers. According to the second reading: he is an ear of goodness and an ear of mercy.

Al-Nahhas said: "This, according to the grammarians, is remote," meaning the reading with the genitive, "because the two nouns are separated by a wide gap, and this is unsightly in the case of the genitive."

The meaning is: the Prophet (ﷺ) is an ear of goodness to the hypocrites and a mercy to them, in that he did not expose their secrets nor disgrace them. It is as though He said: "He is an ear, as you said, but he is an ear of goodness for you, not an ear of evil." Thus He confirmed their saying about him, except that He explained it in a way that is praise of him and commendation of him, even though they intended by it blame and a deficiency in his perceptiveness. The meaning of ﴿for those of you who believe﴾ is: those who showed faith, even if they were not believers in truth. ﴿And those who harm the Messenger of Allah﴾ (ﷺ), by what preceded of their saying "he is an ear" and the like, of what truly constitutes harm to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾, i.e., severe in pain.

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited *wa-rahmatan lil-mu'minin* with the accusative, as the reason for a suppressed motivated element: i.e., "and a mercy, He grants you permission."

Then He mentioned that among the abominable conduct of the hypocrites is their rushing into false oaths, and so He said: ﴿They swear by Allah to you in order to please you﴾, and the address is to the believers.

That is because the hypocrites, in their private gatherings, used to revile the believers and the Prophet (ﷺ). When that reached the Messenger of Allah and the believers, the hypocrites would come and swear that they had not said what had been reported about them, intending by these false oaths to please the Messenger of Allah and those with him among the believers. So Allah censured that from them and said: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, i.e., the two of them have more right to that than pleasing the believers with false oaths, for if they feared Allah, believed in Him and abandoned hypocrisy, that would be better for them.

The singular pronoun in *yurdnuhu* (that they should please Him) is either for the glorification of the divine presence by singling Him out for mention, or because there is no difference between pleasing Allah and pleasing His Messenger, so that pleasing Allah is pleasing His Messenger; or the meaning is: Allah has more right that they should please Him, and His Messenger likewise, as Sibawayh said, and al-Nahhas preferred this; or because the pronoun is placed in the position of the demonstrative, for it is used to refer to one or to many; or the pronoun refers back to what was mentioned, and it applies to both of them.

Al-Farra' said: "The meaning is: and His Messenger has more right that they should please him, and *Allah* is an opening of speech, as you say *ma sha'a Allah wa-shi'ta* (what Allah wills and what you will)." This sentence, I mean ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The response to ﴿if they are believers﴾ is suppressed: i.e., if they are believers, then let them please Allah and His Messenger.

His saying: ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell﴾.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz recited *alam ta'lamu* with the second-person (*fawqiyyah*), while the rest recited it with the third-person (*tahtiyyah*).

*Al-muhaddadah* (opposition) is that one party comes to be on a boundary and the other on a boundary, like *al-mushaqqah* (hostility): one says *hadda fulanun fulanan*, i.e., he came to be on the other's boundary, his boundary. ﴿Then for him is the fire of Hell﴾.

Al-Jumhur recited *fa-anna* with the hamzah pronounced with fatha, as the predicate of a suppressed subject: i.e., "so it is due that for him is the fire of Hell."

Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the second *anna* is a substitute (*badal*) for the first. Al-Mubarrad claimed that this view is rejected, and that the correct position is what al-Jarmi said: the second is repeated for emphasis when the speech has become long.

Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "so the obligation of the fire is for him," but al-Mubarrad denied this and said: "This is an error, because *anna* with fatha and tashdid cannot begin a sentence, and its predicate is suppressed."

It was also recited with the hamzah pronounced with kasra.

Sibawayh said: "It is a good reading," and recited:

*"And indeed, when my mounts tire of their resting place, I am, of my portion of the matter, the one who breaks away."*

The accusative of *khalidan* is a circumstantial clause. The demonstrative in His saying *dhalika* refers to the punishment mentioned, and it is the subject, its predicate being ﴿the great disgrace﴾, i.e., the disgrace that reaches the furthest extent, beyond which no other reaches, and it is humiliation and abasement.

His saying: ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down concerning them﴾. It was said: it is a statement and not a command.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "let them beware" (*li-yahdhar*).

So the meaning according to the first view is that the hypocrites used to fear the descent of the Qur'an concerning them, and according to the second, it is a command to them to beware of that. ﴿That a surah be sent down concerning them﴾ is in the accusative position, i.e., "lest a surah be sent down," and it is permissible according to Sibawayh's view that it be in the genitive position by the presumption of *min* with its governance; and it is permissible that it be in the accusative as a double object.

Sibawayh permitted *hadhartu Zaydan* (I was wary of Zayd), and recited:

*"Wary of matters that do not harm him, and secure from what does not save him from the decrees."*

Al-Mubarrad prohibited the accusative construction as an object.

The meaning of ﴿concerning them﴾ is: concerning the believers in the matter of the hypocrites, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the believers; but it is preferable that the pronoun refer to the hypocrites, i.e., concerning them, the surah informs them ﴿of what is in their hearts﴾, i.e., of what they conceal, let alone what they show. Although they know what is in their hearts, the purpose of the surah's informing them is to make them aware that the believers have come to know what is in their hearts. Then Allah commanded His Messenger to answer them, and so He said: ﴿Say: mock, indeed Allah will bring out what you fear﴾. This is a command of threat: i.e., go ahead and mock, for Allah will bring out what you fear of its appearance, until the believers become aware of it, whether by the sending down of a surah, or by informing His Messenger of that, or the like.

His saying: ﴿And if you asked them, they would surely say: we were only conversing and playing﴾. I.e., if you asked them about what they said of disparagement of the religion and defamation of the believers, after that reaches you and Allah informs you of it, they would surely say: "We were only conversing and playing, and we were not in any matter concerning you or the believers."

Then Allah commanded him to answer on their behalf, and so He said: ﴿Say: was it Allah and His signs and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. He affirmed that this had occurred from them and did not heed their denial, because they were lying in their denial. Rather, He treated them as those who acknowledge that it occurred from them, in that He made the one mocked the object, and the *ba'* is for the negation particle, for that happens only after the mockery has occurred and been established.

Then He said: ﴿Do not make excuses﴾, a prohibition to them against occupying themselves with false excuses, for these are not accepted from them.

Al-Wahidi has transmitted from the leading scholars of the language that the meaning of *i'tidhar* (making an excuse) is the erasing and cutting off of the trace of a sin, from their saying *i'tadhara al-manzil* when it became effaced, and *i'tadharat al-miyah* when the waters ceased to flow. ﴿You have disbelieved﴾, i.e., you have displayed disbelief by what has occurred from you of the mockery mentioned. ﴿After your faith﴾, i.e., after your display of faith, while you conceal disbelief. ﴿If We pardon a group among you﴾, and they are those who sincerely held faith, abandoned hypocrisy, and repented from it. Al-Zajjaj said: "The *ta'ifah* (group) in the language is the company." Ibn al-Anbari said: "The term of plurality is applied to the singular among the Arabs." ﴿We will punish another group﴾ because ﴿they were criminals﴾, persisting in hypocrisy and not repenting from it. It was recited *nu'adhdhib* with the *nun*, and with the *ta'* (second letter on top) on the passive construction, and with the *ya'* on the active construction, its subject being Allah, glorified is He.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Nabtal ibn al-Harith used to come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and sit with him and listen to him, then he would convey his speech to the hypocrites. He is the one who said to them: 'Muhammad is only an ear; whoever speaks to him, he believes him.' So Allah revealed concerning him: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, he is an ear﴾, the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: "A group of hypocrites gathered, among them Khilas ibn Suwayd ibn Samit, Mukhshi ibn Himyar and Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, and they wanted to slander the Prophet (ﷺ). Some of them forbade others and said: 'We fear that it will reach Muhammad and he will attack you.' Some of them said: 'Muhammad is only an ear; we will swear to him and he will believe us.' So the verse was revealed: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾, the verse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿he is an ear﴾, that it means he hears from everyone. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿An ear of goodness for you; he believes in Allah and believes the believers﴾, meaning: he affirms Allah and affirms the believers.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn 'Asakir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Umayr ibn Sa'd, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning me: ﴿and they say, he is an ear﴾. That was because 'Umayr ibn Sa'd used to listen to the conversations of the people of Madinah, then come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and whisper them to him, until they were harmed by 'Umayr ibn Sa'd and disliked sitting with him, and said: ﴿He is an ear﴾. So this was revealed concerning him."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that a man among the hypocrites said: 'By Allah, these are our best and our nobles, and if what Muhammad says is true, they are worse than donkeys.' A man among the Muslims heard this and said: 'By Allah, what Muhammad says is true, and you are worse than a donkey.' The man carried the report to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him. So he sent for the man and summoned him, and said: 'What led you to say what you said?' The man began to swear by Allah, cursing himself, that he had not said that. The Muslim man kept saying: 'O Allah, confirm the truthful and expose the liar.' So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿They swear by Allah to you in order to please you﴾, the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi something similar, and named the Muslim man 'Amir ibn Qays from the Ansar.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Dahhak, concerning ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger﴾, that it means: whoever is hostile to Allah and His Messenger.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 61–66 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿The hypocrites fear﴾ (to the end of the verse), that he said: "They speak words among themselves, then they say: ﴿Perhaps Allah will not expose us﴾ concerning this."

Abu Nu'aym narrated in al-Hilyah (Hilyat al-Awliya') from Shurayh ibn Ubayd that "a man said to Abu al-Darda': 'O assembly of reciters (qurra'), what is wrong with you? You are more cowardly and more stingy than us when you are asked, and greater gulpers of food when you eat.' Abu al-Darda' turned away from him and did not answer him with anything. He informed Umar ibn al-Khattab of this, so Umar set off to the man who had said that, seized him by his garment, choked him, and led him to the Prophet (ﷺ). The man said: 'We were only chatting and playing.' Then Allah revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say: 'We were only chatting and playing.'﴾"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: "A man said in a gathering one day during the expedition of Tabuk: 'We have never seen the like of these reciters of ours: they have the greatest appetites, the most lying tongues, and are the most cowardly at the time of encounter.' A man in the gathering said: 'You lie, but you are a hypocrite; I will inform the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Qur'an was revealed." Abdullah said: "I saw him clinging to the girth-strap of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) camel, with stones striking his feet, and he was saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, we were only chatting and playing,' while the Prophet (ﷺ) was saying: ﴿Was it at Allah, His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾"

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Uqayli in al-Du'afa' (The Weak Narrators), Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Khatib, in a narration of Malik from Ibn Umar, who said: "I saw Abdullah ibn Ubayy running ahead of the Prophet (ﷺ), with stones striking him, and he was saying: 'O Muhammad, we were only chatting and playing,' while the Prophet (ﷺ) was saying: ﴿Was it at Allah, His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾"

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, regarding the verse, that he said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on his expedition to Tabuk, there were people among the hypocrites before him who said: 'Does this man hope that the palaces and fortresses of Syria will be opened to him? Far-fetched, far-fetched!' So Allah informed His Prophet (ﷺ) of that, and the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Hold these riders back for me.' He came to them and said: 'You said such-and-such.' They said: 'O Prophet of Allah, we were only chatting and playing.' So Allah revealed concerning them what you hear."

A similar report has been narrated through several chains from a group of the Companions.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿If We pardon a group﴾, that he said: "The group (ta'ifah) is a man or a small band."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 61–66 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "And among them are those who..." This is another category, concerning the disgraceful and abominable conduct of the hypocrites that Allah has related. They used to say to the Prophet (ﷺ), in a manner of disparagement and blame, "He is an ear" (*huwa udhun*).

Al-Jawhari said: "It is said *rajulun udhun* (a man who is an ear) when he listens to everyone's speech, and it applies to the singular and the plural alike." Their intent, may Allah humiliate them, was that when they harmed the Prophet and spread their tongues against him, and it reached him, they would apologise to him and he would accept it from them, because he hears everything that is said to him and believes it. The Arabs applied the term "ear" to one who hears what is said to him and believes it only as an exaggeration, for they named him after the organ that is the instrument of hearing, as though his whole being were a listening ear. A parallel is their calling a sentry *'ayn* (an eye). Their harming him consisted in their saying *huwa udhun*, because they attributed to him that he believes everything said to him and does not distinguish between the true and the false, deceived by his forbearance towards them and his pardoning of their offences, out of generosity, forbearance and overlooking.

Then Allah answered their saying, and said: ﴿Say: an ear of goodness for you﴾, with the genitive construction (*idafah*), according to the reading of the majority.

The meaning according to the first reading: he is an ear of goodness and he is a mercy for the believers. According to the second reading: he is an ear of goodness and an ear of mercy.

Thus He confirmed their saying about him, except that He explained it in a way that is praise of him and commendation of him, even though they intended by it blame and a deficiency in his perceptiveness. Then He mentioned that among the abominable conduct of the hypocrites is their rushing into false oaths, and so He said: ﴿They swear by Allah to you in order to please you﴾, and the address is to the believers.

That is because the hypocrites, in their private gatherings, used to revile the believers and the Prophet (ﷺ). When that reached the Messenger of Allah and the believers, the hypocrites would come and swear that they had not said what had been reported about them, intending by these false oaths to please the Messenger of Allah and those with him among the believers. So Allah censured that from them and said: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, i.e., the two of them have more right to that than pleasing the believers with false oaths, for if they feared Allah, believed in Him and abandoned hypocrisy, that would be better for them.

The singular pronoun in *yurdnuhu* (that they should please Him) is either for the glorification of the divine presence by singling Him out for mention, or because there is no difference between pleasing Allah and pleasing His Messenger, so that pleasing Allah is pleasing His Messenger; or the meaning is: Allah has more right that they should please Him, and His Messenger likewise, as Sibawayh said, and al-Nahhas preferred this; or because the pronoun is placed in the position of the demonstrative, for it is used to refer to one or to many; or the pronoun refers back to what was mentioned, and it applies to both of them.

Al-Farra' said: "The meaning is: and His Messenger has more right that they should please him, and *Allah* is an opening of speech, as you say *ma sha'a Allah wa-shi'ta* (what Allah wills and what you will)." This sentence, I mean ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The response to ﴿if they are believers﴾ is suppressed: i.e., if they are believers, then let them please Allah and His Messenger.

His saying: ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell﴾.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz recited *alam ta'lamu* with the second-person (*fawqiyyah*), while the rest recited it with the third-person (*tahtiyyah*).

*Al-muhaddadah* (opposition) is that one party comes to be on a boundary and the other on a boundary, like *al-mushaqqah* (hostility): one says *hadda fulanun fulanan*, i.e., he came to be on the other's boundary, his boundary. ﴿Then for him is the fire of Hell﴾.

Al-Jumhur recited *fa-anna* with the hamzah pronounced with fatha, as the predicate of a suppressed subject: i.e., "so it is due that for him is the fire of Hell."

Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the second *anna* is a substitute (*badal*) for the first. Al-Mubarrad claimed that this view is rejected, and that the correct position is what al-Jarmi said: the second is repeated for emphasis when the speech has become long.

Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "so the obligation of the fire is for him," but al-Mubarrad denied this and said: "This is an error, because *anna* with fatha and tashdid cannot begin a sentence, and its predicate is suppressed."

It was also recited with the hamzah pronounced with kasra.

Sibawayh said: "It is a good reading," and recited:

*"And indeed, when my mounts tire of their resting place, I am, of my portion of the matter, the one who breaks away."*

The demonstrative in His saying *dhalika* refers to the punishment mentioned, and it is the subject, its predicate being ﴿the great disgrace﴾, i.e., the disgrace that reaches the furthest extent, beyond which no other reaches, and it is humiliation and abasement.

His saying: ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down concerning them﴾. It was said: it is a statement and not a command.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "let them beware" (*li-yahdhar*).

So the meaning according to the first view is that the hypocrites used to fear the descent of the Qur'an concerning them, and according to the second, it is a command to them to beware of that. ﴿That a surah be sent down concerning them﴾ is in the accusative position, i.e., "lest a surah be sent down," and it is permissible according to Sibawayh's view that it be in the genitive position by the presumption of *min* with its governance; and it is permissible that it be in the accusative as a double object.

Sibawayh permitted *hadhartu Zaydan* (I was wary of Zayd), and recited:

*"Wary of matters that do not harm him, and secure from what does not save him from the decrees."*

Al-Mubarrad prohibited the accusative construction as an object.

The meaning of ﴿concerning them﴾ is: concerning the believers in the matter of the hypocrites, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the believers; but it is preferable that the pronoun refer to the hypocrites, i.e., concerning them, the surah informs them ﴿of what is in their hearts﴾, i.e., of what they conceal, let alone what they show. Although they know what is in their hearts, the purpose of the surah's informing them is to make them aware that the believers have come to know what is in their hearts. Then Allah commanded His Messenger to answer them, and so He said: ﴿Say: mock, indeed Allah will bring out what you fear﴾. This is a command of threat: i.e., go ahead and mock, for Allah will bring out what you fear of its appearance, until the believers become aware of it, whether by the sending down of a surah, or by informing His Messenger of that, or the like.

His saying: ﴿And if you asked them, they would surely say: we were only conversing and playing﴾. I.e., if you asked them about what they said of disparagement of the religion and defamation of the believers, after that reaches you and Allah informs you of it, they would surely say: "We were only conversing and playing, and we were not in any matter concerning you or the believers."

Then Allah commanded him to answer on their behalf, and so He said: ﴿Say: was it Allah and His signs and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. He affirmed that this had occurred from them and did not heed their denial, because they were lying in their denial. Then He said: ﴿Do not make excuses﴾, a prohibition to them against occupying themselves with false excuses, for these are not accepted from them.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The *ta'ifah* (group) in the language is the company." Ibn al-Anbari said: "The term of plurality is applied to the singular among the Arabs." ﴿We will punish another group﴾ because ﴿they were criminals﴾, persisting in hypocrisy and not repenting from it. It was recited *nu'adhdhib* with the *nun*, and with the *ta'* (second letter on top) on the passive construction, and with the *ya'* on the active construction, its subject being Allah, glorified is He.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Nabtal ibn al-Harith used to come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and sit with him and listen to him, then he would convey his speech to the hypocrites. He is the one who said to them: 'Muhammad is only an ear; whoever speaks to him, he believes him.' So Allah revealed concerning him: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, he is an ear﴾, the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: "A group of hypocrites gathered, among them Khilas ibn Suwayd ibn Samit, Mukhshi ibn Himyar and Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, and they wanted to slander the Prophet (ﷺ). Some of them forbade others and said: 'We fear that it will reach Muhammad and he will attack you.' Some of them said: 'Muhammad is only an ear; we will swear to him and he will believe us.' So the verse was revealed: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾, the verse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿he is an ear﴾, that it means he hears from everyone. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿An ear of goodness for you; he believes in Allah and believes the believers﴾, meaning: he affirms Allah and affirms the believers.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn 'Asakir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Umayr ibn Sa'd, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning me: ﴿and they say, he is an ear﴾. That was because 'Umayr ibn Sa'd used to listen to the conversations of the people of Madinah, then come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and whisper them to him, until they were harmed by 'Umayr ibn Sa'd and disliked sitting with him, and said: ﴿He is an ear﴾. So this was revealed concerning him."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that a man among the hypocrites said: 'By Allah, these are our best and our nobles, and if what Muhammad says is true, they are worse than donkeys.' A man among the Muslims heard this and said: 'By Allah, what Muhammad says is true, and you are worse than a donkey.' The man carried the report to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him. So he sent for the man and summoned him, and said: 'What led you to say what you said?' The man began to swear by Allah, cursing himself, that he had not said that. The Muslim man kept saying: 'O Allah, confirm the truthful and expose the liar.' So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿They swear by Allah to you in order to please you﴾, the verse."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi something similar, and named the Muslim man 'Amir ibn Qays from the Ansar.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Dahhak, concerning ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger﴾, that it means: whoever is hostile to Allah and His Messenger.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 61–66 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿The hypocrites fear﴾ (to the end of the verse), that he said: "They speak words among themselves, then they say: ﴿Perhaps Allah will not expose us﴾ concerning this."

Abu Nu'aym narrated in al-Hilyah (Hilyat al-Awliya') from Shurayh ibn Ubayd that "a man said to Abu al-Darda': 'O assembly of reciters (qurra'), what is wrong with you? You are more cowardly and more stingy than us when you are asked, and greater gulpers of food when you eat.' Abu al-Darda' turned away from him and did not answer him with anything. He informed Umar ibn al-Khattab of this, so Umar set off to the man who had said that, seized him by his garment, choked him, and led him to the Prophet (ﷺ). The man said: 'We were only chatting and playing.' Then Allah revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say: 'We were only chatting and playing.'﴾"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: "A man said in a gathering one day during the expedition of Tabuk: 'We have never seen the like of these reciters of ours: they have the greatest appetites, the most lying tongues, and are the most cowardly at the time of encounter.' A man in the gathering said: 'You lie, but you are a hypocrite; I will inform the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Qur'an was revealed." Abdullah said: "I saw him clinging to the girth-strap of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) camel, with stones striking his feet, and he was saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, we were only chatting and playing,' while the Prophet (ﷺ) was saying: ﴿Was it at Allah, His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾"

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Uqayli in al-Du'afa' (The Weak Narrators), Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Khatib, in a narration of Malik from Ibn Umar, who said: "I saw Abdullah ibn Ubayy running ahead of the Prophet (ﷺ), with stones striking him, and he was saying: 'O Muhammad, we were only chatting and playing,' while the Prophet (ﷺ) was saying: ﴿Was it at Allah, His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾"

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, regarding the verse, that he said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on his expedition to Tabuk, there were people among the hypocrites before him who said: 'Does this man hope that the palaces and fortresses of Syria will be opened to him? Far-fetched, far-fetched!' So Allah informed His Prophet (ﷺ) of that, and the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Hold these riders back for me.' He came to them and said: 'You said such-and-such.' They said: 'O Prophet of Allah, we were only chatting and playing.' So Allah revealed concerning them what you hear."

A similar report has been narrated through several chains from a group of the Companions.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿If We pardon a group﴾, that he said: "The group (ta'ifah) is a man or a small band."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 9, verses 67–70**

His saying: ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾. Here he mentions the whole state of the hypocrites: that their males are like their females in this, and that they are extreme in hypocrisy and in distance from faith. There is an indication in this of the negation of their being among the believers, and a rejection of their saying: ﴿And they swear by God that they are surely of you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56]. Then he explained this general statement by clarifying the opposition of their state to the state of the believers, so he said: ﴿They enjoin what is reprehensible﴾, which is everything ugly, by reason or by the Law, ﴿and forbid what is right﴾, which is everything good, by reason or by the Law.

Al-Zajjaj said: This is connected to his saying: ﴿And they swear by God that they are surely of you, and they are not of you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56], meaning they are not among the believers. ﴿But they are of one another﴾, meaning they resemble one another in enjoining what is reprehensible and forbidding what is right. ﴿And they withhold their hands﴾, meaning they are stingy regarding what ought to be spent from wealth in charity, in kindness to relatives, and in jihad. So "withholding" (al-qabd) is a metonymy (kinayah) for stinginess, just as "extending" (al-bast) is a metonymy for generosity.

"Forgetting" (al-nisyan) means abandoning. That is, they abandoned what He commanded them, so He abandoned them from His mercy and grace. The literal sense of forgetting cannot properly be attributed to God, Glorified is He, and it is used here only by way of mushakalah (a rhetorical device of attributing the response to a similar act), which is well known in the science of eloquence (ʿilm al-bayan). Then He judged them to be ﴿fāsiqūn﴾ (transgressors), that is, those who have departed from obedience to God into His disobedience. This construction indicates that they are the complete transgressors.

Then He explained the outcome of the state of the people of hypocrisy and disbelief: it is the Fire of Hell. The phrase ﴿khālidīna fīhā﴾ (abiding therein) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) anticipated (muqaddarah), meaning they will be those who are destined to abide. In this verse there is evidence that the verb "promised" (waʿada) is used for evil as it is used for good. ﴿It is sufficient for them﴾, meaning it is their adequate recompense; they do not need anything beyond its punishment. Yet God has cursed them, meaning He expelled them and removed them far from His mercy. ﴿And for them is a lasting punishment﴾, meaning another kind of punishment, constant, which does not cease from them.

His saying: ﴿As those before you﴾. He likened the state of the hypocrites to the disbelievers who were before them, shifting from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khiṭāb). The kaf (as) here is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: you are like those before you. Or it is in the accusative position, meaning: you have done the like of the deeds of those before you among the nations.

Al-Zajjaj said: The estimate is: God promised the disbelievers the Fire of Hell as a promise, just as He promised those before you. It was also said: the meaning is: you have done like the deeds of those before you in abandoning enjoining what is right and forbidding what is reprehensible, so the modified noun (al-muḍāf) was omitted.

Then he described the state of those disbelievers who were before them, and explained the aspect of their comparison with them and the likening of their state to theirs: they were more intense than these hypocrites and the disbelievers contemporary with the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿in strength and in more wealth and children, and they enjoyed﴾, meaning they took their enjoyment, ﴿their share﴾, meaning their portion which God had decreed for them of the pleasures of this world. ﴿So you have enjoyed﴾, meaning you [have enjoyed] ﴿your share﴾ [p. 584], meaning your portion which God has decreed for you, ﴿as those before you enjoyed their share﴾, meaning you benefited from it as they benefited from it. The purpose of this comparison is to censure these hypocrites and disbelievers because of their resemblance to those before them among the disbelievers in enjoying what God had provided them.

It has been asked: what is the benefit of mentioning enjoyment of one's share regarding the earlier people once, then regarding the hypocrites a second time, then repeating it regarding the earlier people a third time? It is answered: God censured the earlier people for enjoying what they were given of the worldly portions and for being deprived of the bliss of the Hereafter because of their absorption in those portions. When He established this, He then returned to liken the state of the hypocrites to their state, and this is an utmost hyperbole.

His saying: ﴿And you engaged in discourse as those engaged﴾. It is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: like the group who engaged, or like the engagement in which they engaged. It was also said: its origin is "alladhīn" (those), and the nūn was omitted. The better view is that "alladhī" (who/which) is a relative pronoun like "man" and "mā," used for the singular and the plural. It is said: "I waded (khuḍtu) the water, I wade through it, khawḍan and khiyāḍan," and the place is "makhāḍah," which is what people cross on foot and on mounts; its plural is "makhāḍ" and "makhāwid." It is also said: from this, "the people engaged (khāḍa) in the speech," and "they engaged in it together (takhāwaḍū fīhi)," meaning they discussed it together. The meaning is: you engaged in the affairs of this world and in frivolous play. It was also said: in the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), with denial, meaning you entered into that.

By his saying "those" (ulāʾika) he refers to those characterized by these attributes among those compared and those compared to. ﴿Their deeds have become void﴾, meaning they have been nullified. By "deeds" is meant what they did that had the form of obedience, not these deeds mentioned here, for these are among the acts of disobedience. The meaning of "in this world and in the Hereafter" is that they are void in every respect. As for their voiding in this world, it is because what they expected to result from their deeds in it does not come to them; rather, what they hoped for of wealth becomes poverty, of honour becomes humiliation, and of strength becomes weakness. As for the Hereafter, it is because they will go to the punishment of the Fire and will not benefit from anything of the deeds they performed that they thought were obedience and drawing near (to God). ﴿And those are the losers﴾, meaning those firmly established in loss, the complete ones in it, in this world and in the Hereafter.

﴿Has there not come to them﴾, meaning to the hypocrites, ﴿the news of those before them﴾, meaning their report which has significance, which is what they did and what was done to them. Since he had compared their state with theirs in what preceded, in general terms about those compared to, he mentioned here six groups whose reports the Arabs had heard, because their lands, which is the Levant (al-Shām), are near the lands of the Arabs. So the interrogative is for affirmation. The first of them is the people of Noah, who were destroyed by drowning. The second is the people of ʿĀd, who were destroyed by the barren wind (al-rīḥ al-ʿaqīm). The third is the people of Thamud, who were seized by the Cry (al-ṣayḥah). The fourth is the people of Abraham, upon whom God sent gnats (al-baʿūḍ). The fifth are the companions of Madyan, who are the people of Shuʿayb, and the quake (al-rajfah) seized them. The sixth are the inhabitants of the overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikāt), which are the towns of the people of Lot, whom God destroyed by what He rained upon them of stones. They were called "al-Mu'tafikāt" because they were overturned with their people until their highest part became their lowest; and al-ʾitifāk is overturning.

﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, meaning the messengers of these six groups. It was also said: the messengers of the inhabitants of the overturned cities, because their messenger was Lot, and he was sent to every town among their towns with a messenger. The "fa" (so) in ﴿So God would not have wronged them﴾ is for coordination with an omitted premise indicated by the context, meaning: so they denied them, and God destroyed them, and He did not wrong them thereby, for He had sent His messengers to them, and they warned them and cautioned them. ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ through their disbelief in God and their not submitting to His prophets. This construction indicates that their wronging of themselves was continuous.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿They enjoin what is reprehensible﴾, that he said: it is denial, and he said: it is the most reprehensible of reprehensible things. ﴿And they forbid what is right﴾: the testimony that there is no god but God and the affirmation of what God has sent down, and this is the greatest of what is right.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And they withhold their hands﴾, that he said: they do not extend them with expenditure in a due right.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿They forgot God, so He forgot them﴾, that he said: they abandoned God, so He abandoned them from His honour and reward.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿As those before you﴾, that he said: the conduct of the disbelievers is like the conduct of the disbelievers.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: How much the night resembles the previous night! ﴿As those before you, who were stronger than you in strength﴾, up to His saying: ﴿And you engaged in discourse as those engaged﴾. "These are the Children of Israel; we have resembled them. By Him in whose hand is my soul, we will surely follow them, so that even if a man entered a lizard's hole, you would enter it."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, regarding His saying: ﴿With their share﴾, that he said: with their religion.

They also narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "al-khalāq" is the religion.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: ﴿So they enjoyed their share﴾, that he said: with their portion in this world.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And you engaged in discourse as those engaged﴾, that he said: you played as they played.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And the overturned cities﴾, that he said: the people of Lot, whose land was overturned with them, so its highest part was made its lowest.

Then he explained this general statement by clarifying the opposition of their state to the state of the believers, so he said: ﴿They enjoin what is reprehensible﴾, which is everything ugly, by reason or by the Law, ﴿and forbid what is right﴾, which is everything good, by reason or by the Law.

Al-Zajjaj said: This is connected to his saying: ﴿And they swear by God that they are surely of you, and they are not of you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56], meaning they are not among the believers. ﴿But they are of one another﴾, meaning they resemble one another in enjoining what is reprehensible and forbidding what is right. ﴿And they withhold their hands﴾, meaning they are stingy regarding what ought to be spent from wealth in charity, in kindness to relatives, and in jihad. So "withholding" (al-qabd) is a metonymy (kinayah) for stinginess, just as "extending" (al-bast) is a metonymy for generosity.

"Forgetting" (al-nisyan) means abandoning. That is, they abandoned what He commanded them, so He abandoned them from His mercy and grace. The literal sense of forgetting cannot properly be attributed to God, Glorified is He, and it is used here only by way of mushakalah (a rhetorical device of attributing the response to a similar act), which is well known in the science of eloquence (ʿilm al-bayan). Then He judged them to be ﴿fāsiqūn﴾ (transgressors), that is, those who have departed from obedience to God into His disobedience. This construction indicates that they are the complete transgressors.

Then He explained the outcome of the state of the people of hypocrisy and disbelief: it is the Fire of Hell. The phrase ﴿khālidīna fīhā﴾ (abiding therein) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) anticipated (muqaddarah), meaning they will be those who are destined to abide. In this verse there is evidence that the verb "promised" (waʿada) is used for evil as it is used for good. ﴿It is sufficient for them﴾, meaning it is their adequate recompense; they do not need anything beyond its punishment. Yet God has cursed them, meaning He expelled them and removed them far from His mercy. ﴿And for them is a lasting punishment﴾, meaning another kind of punishment, constant, which does not cease from them.

His saying: ﴿As those before you﴾. He likened the state of the hypocrites to the disbelievers who were before them, shifting from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khiṭāb). The kaf (as) here is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: you are like those before you. Or it is in the accusative position, meaning: you have done the like of the deeds of those before you among the nations.

Al-Zajjaj said: The estimate is: God promised the disbelievers the Fire of Hell as a promise, just as He promised those before you. It was also said: the meaning is: you have done like the deeds of those before you in abandoning enjoining what is right and forbidding what is reprehensible, so the modified noun (al-muḍāf) was omitted.

Then he described the state of those disbelievers who were before them, and explained the aspect of their comparison with them and the likening of their state to theirs: they were more intense than these hypocrites and the disbelievers contemporary with the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿in strength and in more wealth and children, and they enjoyed﴾, meaning they took their enjoyment, ﴿their share﴾, meaning their portion which God had decreed for them of the pleasures of this world. ﴿So you have enjoyed﴾, meaning you [have enjoyed] ﴿your share﴾ [p. 584], meaning your portion which God has decreed for you, ﴿as those before you enjoyed their share﴾, meaning you benefited from it as they benefited from it. The purpose of this comparison is to censure these hypocrites and disbelievers because of their resemblance to those before them among the disbelievers in enjoying what God had provided them.

It has been asked: what is the benefit of mentioning enjoyment of one's share regarding the earlier people once, then regarding the hypocrites a second time, then repeating it regarding the earlier people a third time? It is answered: God censured the earlier people for enjoying what they were given of the worldly portions and for being deprived of the bliss of the Hereafter because of their absorption in those portions. When He established this, He then returned to liken the state of the hypocrites to their state, and this is an utmost hyperbole.

His saying: ﴿And you engaged in discourse as those engaged﴾. It is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: like the group who engaged, or like the engagement in which they engaged. It was also said: its origin is "alladhīn" (those), and the nūn was omitted. The better view is that "alladhī" (who/which) is a relative pronoun like "man" and "mā," used for the singular and the plural. It is said: "I waded (khuḍtu) the water, I wade through it, khawḍan and khiyāḍan," and the place is "makhāḍah," which is what people cross on foot and on mounts; its plural is "makhāḍ" and "makhāwid." It is also said: from this, "the people engaged (khāḍa) in the speech," and "they engaged in it together (takhāwaḍū fīhi)," meaning they discussed it together. The meaning is: you engaged in the affairs of this world and in frivolous play. It was also said: in the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), with denial, meaning you entered into that.

By his saying "those" (ulāʾika) he refers to those characterized by these attributes among those compared and those compared to. ﴿Their deeds have become void﴾, meaning they have been nullified. By "deeds" is meant what they did that had the form of obedience, not these deeds mentioned here, for these are among the acts of disobedience. The meaning of "in this world and in the Hereafter" is that they are void in every respect. As for their voiding in this world, it is because what they expected to result from their deeds in it does not come to them; rather, what they hoped for of wealth becomes poverty, of honour becomes humiliation, and of strength becomes weakness. As for the Hereafter, it is because they will go to the punishment of the Fire and will not benefit from anything of the deeds they performed that they thought were obedience and drawing near (to God). ﴿And those are the losers﴾, meaning those firmly established in loss, the complete ones in it, in this world and in the Hereafter.

﴿Has there not come to them﴾, meaning to the hypocrites, ﴿the news of those before them﴾, meaning their report which has significance, which is what they did and what was done to them. Since he had compared their state with theirs in what preceded, in general terms about those compared to, he mentioned here six groups whose reports the Arabs had heard, because their lands, which is the Levant (al-Shām), are near the lands of the Arabs. So the interrogative is for affirmation. The first of them is the people of Noah, who were destroyed by drowning. The second is the people of ʿĀd, who were destroyed by the barren wind (al-rīḥ al-ʿaqīm). The third is the people of Thamud, who were seized by the Cry (al-ṣayḥah). The fourth is the people of Abraham, upon whom God sent gnats (al-baʿūḍ). The fifth are the companions of Madyan, who are the people of Shuʿayb, and the quake (al-rajfah) seized them. The sixth are the inhabitants of the overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikāt), which are the towns of the people of Lot, whom God destroyed by what He rained upon them of stones. They were called "al-Mu'tafikāt" because they were overturned with their people until their highest part became their lowest; and al-ʾitifāk is overturning.

﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, meaning the messengers of these six groups. It was also said: the messengers of the inhabitants of the overturned cities, because their messenger was Lot, and he was sent to every town among their towns with a messenger. The "fa" (so) in ﴿So God would not have wronged them﴾ is for coordination with an omitted premise indicated by the context, meaning: so they denied them, and God destroyed them, and He did not wrong them thereby, for He had sent His messengers to them, and they warned them and cautioned them. ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ through their disbelief in God and their not submitting to His prophets. This construction indicates that their wronging of themselves was continuous.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿They enjoin what is reprehensible﴾, that he said: it is denial, and he said: it is the most reprehensible of reprehensible things. ﴿And they forbid what is right﴾: the testimony that there is no god but God and the affirmation of what God has sent down, and this is the greatest of what is right.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And they withhold their hands﴾, that he said: they do not extend them with expenditure in a due right.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿They forgot God, so He forgot them﴾, that he said: they abandoned God, so He abandoned them from His honour and reward.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿As those before you﴾, that he said: the conduct of the disbelievers is like the conduct of the disbelievers.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: How much the night resembles the previous night! ﴿As those before you, who were stronger than you in strength﴾, up to His saying: ﴿And you engaged in discourse as those engaged﴾. "These are the Children of Israel; we have resembled them. By Him in whose hand is my soul, we will surely follow them, so that even if a man entered a lizard's hole, you would enter it."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, regarding His saying: ﴿With their share﴾, that he said: with their religion.

They also narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "al-khalāq" is the religion.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: ﴿So they enjoyed their share﴾, that he said: with their portion in this world.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And you engaged in discourse as those engaged﴾, that he said: you played as they played.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And the overturned cities﴾, that he said: the people of Lot, whose land was overturned with them, so its highest part was made its lowest.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 9, verses 71–72:

His saying: ﴿The believers, men and women, are protectors of one another﴾. That is, their hearts are united in mutual affection, love and compassion, because of what the matter of religion has gathered them together upon and the faith in Allah that has joined them. Then He described their praiseworthy attributes, just as He described the attributes of those before them among the hypocrites, so He said: ﴿They enjoin what is right﴾. That is, what is known to be right in the Sharia and not disapproved, and among that is the affirmation of the Oneness of Allah, glorified is He, and abandoning the worship of anything other than Him. ﴿And forbid what is wrong﴾. That is, what is disapproved of in the religion and not known as right. He singled out the establishment of the prayer (iqamat al-salat) and the giving of zakat (iyta' al-zakat) from among the acts of worship for mention, because they are the two great pillars in what concerns the bodies (p-585) and the wealth, and the meaning of this has already been discussed. ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾, by doing what He commanded them to do or abandoning what He forbade them from. The reference of "those" (ulā'ika) is to the believing men and women who possess these attributes. The "sin" (al-sin) in ﴿Allah will surely have mercy on them﴾ is for emphasis in fulfilling the promise. ﴿Indeed Allah is Mighty﴾, not overcome, ﴿Wise﴾ in His sayings and His deeds.

Then He mentioned, in summary, the details of what falls under mercy with regard to mercy in the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. The explicit mention (of the believers) in place of a pronoun is for the sake of greater emphasis. The meaning of the rivers flowing beneath the gardens is that they flow beneath their trees and their mansions, and its verification has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. ﴿And pleasant dwellings﴾, that is, residences in which they dwell, made of pearls and rubies. And "gardens of Eden" (jannat 'adn): it is said "'adana bil-makan" when one settles in a place, and from it comes "ma'din" (mine/source). It is said: it is the highest part of Paradise; it is said: its middle; and it is said: palaces of gold which none enter except a prophet, a truthful one (siddiq), or a martyr.

He described Paradise with several attributes. The first: the rivers flowing beneath it. The second: that they abide therein forever. The third: the goodness of its dwellings. The fourth: that it is the abode of 'Adn, that is, a lasting residence that is never cut off; this is according to the linguistic meaning of 'adn. It is also said that it is a proper name. The indefiniteness in ﴿and approval﴾ (ridwan) is for belittling: that is, and an approval that is insignificant compared with ﴿the approval of Allah, which is greater﴾ than all of that which Allah has given them. In it is evidence that none of the blessings, however great and magnificent, is comparable to the approval of Allah, glorified is He, and that even the least of His approval is not equaled by any of the bodily pleasures, even if they reach the utmost limit beyond which there is no further limit. O Allah, be pleased with us with an approval that is not tainted by displeasure and is not clouded by distress, O You in whose hand is all good, the small and the great. The reference of "that" (dhalika) in His saying is to what was mentioned before of what Allah has promised the believing men and women: ﴿that is the great triumph﴾, above every triumph that people consider a triumph.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying ﴿They enjoin what is right﴾: he said: they call to faith in Allah and His Messenger, and to spending in the way of Allah, and to whatever is obedience to Allah. ﴿And forbid what is wrong﴾, from polytheism and disbelief. He said: enjoining right and forbidding wrong is one of the obligations of Allah which He prescribed upon the believers.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿The believers, men and women, are protectors of one another﴾: he said: their brotherhood is in Allah; they love one another for the majesty of Allah and for loyalty to Allah. And there has been established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), concerning enjoining right and forbidding wrong, of the hadiths what is well known.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "I asked 'Imran ibn Husayn and Abu Hurayrah about the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and pleasant dwellings in gardens of Eden﴾. They both said: 'You have come to the one who knows (al-Khabir) and fallen upon him.' We asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'It is a palace of pearl in Paradise. In that palace are seventy houses of red ruby; in each house are seventy chambers of green emerald; in each chamber are seventy couches; upon each couch are seventy beds of every color; upon each bed is a maiden of the wide-eyed houris (al-hur al-'in); in each chamber are seventy tables; upon each table are seventy kinds of every food; in each chamber are seventy male and female servants. The believer is given strength each morning sufficient for all of that.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿gardens of Eden﴾: he said: "ma'din" of the man, which is where he is.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, and said: their "ma'din" therein, forever.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿and approval from Allah is greater﴾: he meant: when they are informed that Allah is pleased with them, that is greater in their estimation than the gifts and the Tasnim.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah will say to the people of Paradise: 'O people of Paradise!' and they will say: 'Labbayka Rabbana wa Sa'dayka, and the good is in Your hands.' He will say: 'Are you pleased?' They will say: 'Our Lord, and why would we not be pleased, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?' He will say: 'Shall I not give you something better than that?' They will say: 'O our Lord, and what is better than that?' He will say: 'I will cause My approval to descend upon you, so I will never be displeased with you after it, ever.'"

Then He mentioned, in summary, the details of what falls under mercy with regard to mercy in the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. The explicit mention (of the believers) in place of a pronoun is for the sake of greater emphasis. The meaning of the rivers flowing beneath the gardens is that they flow beneath their trees and their mansions, and its verification has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. ﴿And pleasant dwellings﴾, that is, residences in which they dwell, made of pearls and rubies. And "gardens of Eden" (jannat 'adn): it is said "'adana bil-makan" when one settles in a place, and from it comes "ma'din" (mine/source). It is said: it is the highest part of Paradise; it is said: its middle; and it is said: palaces of gold which none enter except a prophet, a truthful one (siddiq), or a martyr.

He described Paradise with several attributes. The first: the rivers flowing beneath it. The second: that they abide therein forever. The third: the goodness of its dwellings. The fourth: that it is the abode of 'Adn, that is, a lasting residence that is never cut off; this is according to the linguistic meaning of 'adn. It is also said that it is a proper name. The indefiniteness in ﴿and approval﴾ (ridwan) is for belittling: that is, and an approval that is insignificant compared with ﴿the approval of Allah, which is greater﴾ than all of that which Allah has given them. In it is evidence that none of the blessings, however great and magnificent, is comparable to the approval of Allah, glorified is He, and that even the least of His approval is not equaled by any of the bodily pleasures, even if they reach the utmost limit beyond which there is no further limit. O Allah, be pleased with us with an approval that is not tainted by displeasure and is not clouded by distress, O You in whose hand is all good, the small and the great. The reference of "that" (dhalika) in His saying is to what was mentioned before of what Allah has promised the believing men and women: ﴿that is the great triumph﴾, above every triumph that people consider a triumph.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying ﴿They enjoin what is right﴾: he said: they call to faith in Allah and His Messenger, and to spending in the way of Allah, and to whatever is obedience to Allah. ﴿And forbid what is wrong﴾, from polytheism and disbelief. He said: enjoining right and forbidding wrong is one of the obligations of Allah which He prescribed upon the believers.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿The believers, men and women, are protectors of one another﴾: he said: their brotherhood is in Allah; they love one another for the majesty of Allah and for loyalty to Allah. And there has been established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), concerning enjoining right and forbidding wrong, of the hadiths what is well known.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "I asked 'Imran ibn Husayn and Abu Hurayrah about the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and pleasant dwellings in gardens of Eden﴾. They both said: 'You have come to the one who knows (al-Khabir) and fallen upon him.' We asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'It is a palace of pearl in Paradise. In that palace are seventy houses of red ruby; in each house are seventy chambers of green emerald; in each chamber are seventy couches; upon each couch are seventy beds of every color; upon each bed is a maiden of the wide-eyed houris (al-hur al-'in); in each chamber are seventy tables; upon each table are seventy kinds of every food; in each chamber are seventy male and female servants. The believer is given strength each morning sufficient for all of that.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿gardens of Eden﴾: he said: "ma'din" of the man, which is where he is.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, and said: their "ma'din" therein, forever.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿and approval from Allah is greater﴾: he meant: when they are informed that Allah is pleased with them, that is greater in their estimation than the gifts and the Tasnim.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah will say to the people of Paradise: 'O people of Paradise!' and they will say: 'Labbayka Rabbana wa Sa'dayka, and the good is in Your hands.' He will say: 'Are you pleased?' They will say: 'Our Lord, and why would we not be pleased, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?' He will say: 'Shall I not give you something better than that?' They will say: 'O our Lord, and what is better than that?' He will say: 'I will cause My approval to descend upon you, so I will never be displeased with you after it, ever.'"

The command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to wage this jihad is a command to his community after him. Fighting the disbelievers (kuffar) means battling them until they embrace Islam, and striving against the hypocrites (munafiqun) means establishing the proof against them until they abandon hypocrisy and believe in Allah.

Al-Hasan said: the jihad against the hypocrites is by enforcing the prescribed punishments (hudud) upon them. Qatada chose this view.

It has been said in explaining this: the hypocrites were the most frequent committers of acts that entail the hudud.

Ibn al-Arabi said: this is a claim without proof. The sinner is not a hypocrite. Hypocrisy (nifaq) is what is in the heart permanently, not what the limbs manifest outwardly. The reports about those who received the hudud show by their context that they were not hypocrites.

His words: ﴿And be harsh with them﴾. Ghilaz (harshness) is the opposite of ra'fa (tenderness), and it is hardness of heart and roughness of manner. It has been said: this verse abrogated (naskh) everything of pardon, reconciliation and forgiveness.

Then he mentioned among the traits of the hypocrites that they swear false oaths, so he said: ﴿They swear by Allah that they said nothing﴾.

The imams of tafsir differed regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse. It was said: it was revealed concerning al-Jullas ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit and Wadi'a ibn Thabit. This was when the Qur'an had frequently descended during the expedition of Tabuk concerning the hypocrites and their condemnation. They said: "If Muhammad is truthful about our brothers, who are our masters and our best, then we are worse than donkeys." Amir ibn Qays said to him: "Yes, by Allah, Muhammad is truthful and believed, and you are worse than the donkey." Amir informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of this. Al-Jullas came and swore by Allah that Amir was lying, and Amir swore that he had indeed said it, and he said: "O Allah, send down upon Your Prophet something." Then it was revealed.

It was also said: the one who heard it was Asim ibn Adi. It was said: Huthayfa. It was said: rather, the stepson of his wife, that is, the wife of al-Jullas, whose name was Umayr ibn Sa'd. Al-Jullas then intended to kill him so that he would not report his statement.

It was said: this verse was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Ubayy (p-586), the head of the hypocrites, when he said: "Our likeness and the likeness of Muhammad is only as the saying of the speaker: 'Fatten your dog and it will devour you.'" And: ﴿If we return to Madina, the mightier will surely expel the weaker from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. The Prophet (ﷺ) was informed of this, so Abd Allah ibn Ubayy came and swore that he had not said it.

It was said: it was the saying of all the hypocrites, and the verse was revealed about them all. Even assuming the speaker was one or two, attributing the saying to all of them is on the basis that those who did not say it and did not swear agreed with those who had said it and sworn.

Then Allah responded to the hypocrites, refuted them, and made clear that they had sworn falsely. He said: ﴿They have certainly uttered the word of disbelief﴾, which is what has been explained earlier according to the differing earlier opinions, ﴿and they disbelieved after their Islam﴾, that is, they disbelieved by this word after displaying Islam, even though they were disbelievers inwardly.

The meaning is: they did what necessitates their disbelief, on the assumption that their Islam was sound.

His words: ﴿and they planned what they could not attain﴾. It was said: this is their plan to kill the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of al-Aqaba during the expedition of Tabuk. It was said: they planned to place a crown on the head of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy. It was said: it is the plan of al-Jullas to kill whoever heard him saying that statement, so he informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

His words: ﴿And they did not resent except that Allah and His Messenger enriched them from His bounty﴾. That is: they found fault with and denied only what is truly deserving of praise and commendation, namely Allah's enriching them from His bounty. The exception here is a restrictive exception (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of generals, and it is of the type of the saying of al-Nabigha:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched by the clashing of the battalions."

And of the type of the poet's saying:

"They resented nothing of the Banu Umayya except that ***they are forbearing when they become angry."

So this is the emphasis of praise through what resembles blame.

These hypocrites had been in straitened living, but when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madina, their livelihood widened and their wealth increased.

His words: ﴿So if they repent, it will be better for them﴾, that is: if repentance and return to the truth come from them, that which they did of repentance will be better for them in religion and in the world.

Al-Jullas ibn Suwayd repented and his Islam became good. In this is evidence for the acceptance of repentance from the hypocrite and the disbeliever.

The scholars differed regarding accepting repentance from the zindiq (heretic who conceals disbelief). Malik and his followers prevented accepting it, because the soundness of his repentance cannot be known, since at every moment he displays repentance and Islam. ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is: they turn away from repentance and faith, ﴿Allah will punish them with a painful punishment in this world﴾ by killing, captivity and the plunder of their wealth, ﴿and in the Hereafter with the punishment of the Fire﴾. ﴿And they will have no protector on earth﴾ who would be an ally to them, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who would support them.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ka'b ibn Malik, who said: "When the Qur'an was revealed mentioning the hypocrites, al-Jullas said: 'By Allah, if this man is truthful, we are worse than the donkeys.' Umayr ibn Sa'd heard it and said: 'By Allah, O Jullas, you are the most beloved of people to me and the best of them in my estimation, and the most precious to me that anything displeasing should reach him. You have said a statement which, if I mention it, will expose you, and if I remain silent about it, it will destroy me, and one of the two is more grievous to me than the other.' So he went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned to him what al-Jullas had said. Al-Jullas swore by Allah that he had not said it, and that Umayr had lied about him. So Allah revealed: ﴿They swear by Allah that they said nothing﴾," the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Anas ibn Malik who said: "Zayd ibn Arqam heard a man of the hypocrites saying while the Prophet (ﷺ) was delivering a sermon: 'If this man is truthful, we are worse than the donkeys.' Zayd said: 'He, by Allah, is truthful, and you are worse than the donkey.' This was reported to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the speaker denied it. So Allah revealed: ﴿They swear by Allah that they said nothing﴾," the verse.

Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting in the shade of a tree and said: 'There will come to you a man who looks at you with the eyes of a devil. When he comes, do not speak to him.' Not long after, a man with blue eyes appeared, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called him and said: 'Why do you and your companions revile me?' The man left and brought his companions, and they swore by Allah that they had not said it, until he overlooked them. And Allah revealed: ﴿They swear by Allah that they said nothing﴾," the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada who said: "It was mentioned to us that two men fought, one of them from Juhayna and the other from Ghifar. Juhayna were allies of the Ansar. The Ghifari prevailed over the Juhani. Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said to the Aws: 'Help your brother! By Allah, our likeness and the likeness of Muhammad is only as the saying of the speaker: "Fatten your dog and it will devour you." By Allah, ﴿If we return to Madina, the mightier will surely expel the weaker from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8].' A man among the Muslims reported this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who sent for him and asked him. He began to swear by Allah that he had not said it. So Allah revealed: ﴿They swear by Allah﴾," the verse. Regarding this occasion there are various reports, and what we have mentioned suffices.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi, concerning His words: ﴿and they planned what they could not attain﴾, that he said: they intended to crown Abd Allah ibn Ubayy with a crown.

The first lam, in ﴿لَئِنْ آتانا مِن فَضْلِهِ﴾ ("If He gives us of His bounty"), is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam). The second lam, in "لَنَصَّدَّقَنَّ" ("we will surely give charity"), is the lam of the response to both the oath and the condition (lam al-jawab li-l-qasam wa-l-shart). [p. 587]

The meaning of "لَنَصَّدَّقَنَّ" is "we will surely bring forth charity," and charity is more general than the obligatory (zakat) and other than it. ﴿وَلَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ﴾ ("and we will surely be among the righteous") means: among the body of the people of righteousness, from the believers who fulfil the obligations of the religion and abstain from its prohibitions.

﴿فَلَمَّا آتَاهُم مِّن فَضْلِهِ بَخِلُوا بِهِ وَتَوَلَّوْا وَهُم مُّعْرِضُونَ﴾ ("But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away while they were averse") means: when He gave them what they had asked for of provision, they were stingy with it, that is, with what He had given them of His bounty, so they gave nothing of it in charity, as they had sworn. "وَتَوَلَّوْا" ("and turned away") means they turned away from obedience to God and from bringing forth charity from what God had given them of His bounty. And the state "وَهُم مُّعْرِضُونَ" ("while they were averse") means they were averse at all times, both before God gave them the provision and after.

On His saying, ﴿فَأَعْقَبَهُمْ نِفَاقًا فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ يَلْقَوْنَهُ﴾ ("so He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him"): the agent is God, glorified is He. That is, God caused hypocrisy to follow them, as a consequence of the stinginess and aversion that had occurred from them, a hypocrisy existing in their hearts, firmly established in them, persisting in them until the day they meet God, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to stinginess: that is, stinginess caused them to follow with hypocrisy in their hearts, until the day they meet their stinginess, that is, the recompense for their stinginess.

The meaning of ﴿فَأَعْقَبَهُمْ﴾ ("He caused it to follow them") is that God, glorified is He, made the hypocrisy firmly rooted in their hearts, up to that limit, the consequence of what had occurred from them of stinginess. The "ب" (ba') in ﴿بِمَا أَخْلَفُوا اللَّهَ مَا وَعَدُوهُ﴾ ("because they broke their promise to God in what they had promised Him") indicates causation: that is, because of their breaking what they had promised of giving charity and righteousness. Likewise the "ب" in ﴿وَبِمَا كَانُوا يَكْذِبُونَ﴾ ("and because they used to lie") means: and because of their denial of what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought.

Then He rebuked them, saying: ﴿أَلَمْ يَعْلَمُوا﴾ ("Did they not know?"), meaning the hypocrites. It is also read with the second person (ta'), addressing the believers. ﴿أَنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ سِرَّهُمْ وَنَجْوَاهُم﴾ ("that God knows their secret and their private counsel") means all that they conceal of hypocrisy and all that they confide to one another in private, of defamation of the Prophet (ﷺ), of his companions, and of the religion of Islam. ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَّامُ الْغُيُوبِ﴾ ("and that God is the Knower of the unseen") means nothing is hidden from Him of the hidden things, whatever they may be, and among that is what proceeds from the hypocrites.

On His saying, ﴿الَّذِينَ يَلْمِزُونَ الْمُطَّوِّعِينَ﴾ ("those who criticise those who give voluntarily"): the relative clause (al-mawsul) is in the accusative position, or in the nominative by way of censure (al-dhamm), or in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "سِرَّهُمْ وَنَجْوَاهُم" ("their secret and their private counsel"). The meaning of "يَلْمِزُونَ" is "they find fault with," and its explanation has already been given. "الْمُطَّوِّعِينَ" means "those who volunteer" (al-mutatawwi'in), and "tatawwu'" means voluntary giving.

The meaning is: the hypocrites used to find fault with the Muslims when they volunteered something of their wealth and brought it out for charity. They would say: "God has no need of this!" and they would say: "They only did this for show (riya')," and it was not purely for God. And "فِي الصَّدَقَاتِ" ("concerning the charities") is connected to "يَلْمِزُونَ": that is, they find fault with them regarding it.

On His saying, ﴿وَالَّذِينَ لَا يَجِدُونَ إِلَّا جُهْدَهُمْ﴾ ("and those who find nothing but their effort"): it is conjoined to "الْمُطَّوِّعِينَ": that is, they find fault with the volunteers and with those who find nothing but their effort. It has also been said that it is conjoined to "الْمُؤْمِنِينَ" ("the believers"): that is, they find fault with the volunteers from among the believers, and with those who find nothing but their effort.
