Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Ibn Jarir, al-Baghawi in his Mu'jam, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifah transmitted from Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Salam, from his father, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to the mosque that was founded upon piety, the Mosque of Quba', he said: 'God has praised you well concerning purification. Will you not tell me?' meaning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves, and God loves those who purify themselves﴾. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we find it written upon us in the Torah: cleansing with water, and we do it today.'"

The chain of Ahmad in this hadith is thus: Yahya ibn Adam narrated to us, Malik, meaning Ibn Mighwal, narrated to me, I heard Sayyar Abu al-Hakim, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Salam.

It has been related from a group of the Successors (tabi'un) something like this concerning the mention of the occasion of revelation of the verse.

It is not hidden from you that some of these hadiths do not contain the identification of the Mosque of Quba' and its people; some are weak; and some have no explicit statement that the mosque founded upon piety is the Mosque of Quba'. In any case, those hadiths that explicitly state that the mosque founded upon piety is the Mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ) are not outweighed by these, in their authenticity and clarity.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿So it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell﴾, that he said: "Meaning its foundations in the fire of Hell."

Musaddad in his Musnad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: "I saw the smoke coming out of the Mosque of Harm at the place where it collapsed, in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts﴾, that he said: "Meaning doubt." ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾, meaning death.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Habib ibn Abi Thabit concerning His saying: ﴿a source of doubt in their hearts﴾, that he said: "Rage in their hearts." ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾, he said: "Until they die."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sufyan concerning His saying: ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾, that he said: "Unless they repent."

[p. 601]

When he had explained the disgraceful conduct and vices of the hypocrites regarding their failure to join the expedition to Tabuk, and had mentioned their categories and drawn out the appropriate ruling for each, he returned to explaining the virtue of jihad and encouraging it. The mention of "purchase" (shira') is a figure of speech, as in His words: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ (2:16). Glorified is He, He likened His rewarding the fighters with Paradise for their giving up their souls and their wealth in the way of Allah to a purchase. The basic meaning of purchase (shira') among people is the transfer of an item out of ownership in exchange for something else of equal value, or of lesser or greater value. So these fighters sold their souls to Allah in exchange for the Paradise He has prepared for the believers, that is, on condition that they be among its people and dwellers. They have thus given their souls, and these are the most precious of possessions, and giving them is the utmost of generosity:

*He gives his soul when the coward withholds his;*
*and giving the soul is the furthest reach of generosity.*

Allah has bestowed upon them Paradise, which is the greatest thing that servants seek and approach through their deeds. By "souls" here is meant the souls of the fighters, and by "wealth" what they spend in jihad.

His words ﴿They fight in the way of Allah﴾ explain the sale implied by the purchase mentioned, as if it were said: How do they sell their souls and wealth for Paradise? It was said: They fight in the way of Allah. Then He explained this fighting in the way of Allah by His words ﴿so they kill and are killed﴾. The meaning is that they advance to kill the disbelievers in war and offer their souls in doing so. If they do this, they have earned Paradise, even if they are not killed after having distinguished themselves in jihad and exposed themselves to death by advancing against the disbelievers.

Al-A'mash, al-Nakha'i, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read the passive verb (*yuqtalun*, "are killed") placed before the active (*yaqtulun*, "they kill"). The rest read the active verb placed before the passive.

His words ﴿a promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an﴾ are an announcement from Allah, glorified is He, that the obligation of jihad and the entitlement to Paradise through it has been established as a promise from Allah in the Torah and the Gospel, just as it occurs in the Qur'an. The words *wa'dan* (a promise) and *haqqan* (binding) are in the accusative either as verbal nouns of the verb (*masdar*, adverbial accusative), or the second is an adjective (*na't*, qualifier) of the first. The phrase *fi al-Tawrah* (in the Torah) is related to an omitted element, meaning: a promise established in them.

His words ﴿And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah?﴾ contain, in this context, an emphasis on encouraging the fighters in jihad and urging them to give their souls and wealth, which is clear. For He first informed them that He had bought from them their souls and wealth in exchange for their having Paradise, and He used this majestic expression, namely that Paradise has become their property. Then He informed them a second time that He had promised this in His revealed books. Then He informed them that after this true promise the promised thing must come to pass, for no one is more faithful to his covenant than Allah, glorified is He, who is true in His promise and does not break His appointment. Then He increased them in joy and delight, saying: ﴿So rejoice in your bargain which you have made﴾. That is, show your happiness over this. Good tidings (bishara) is the display of happiness, and its manifestation appears in the skin of the face; that is why it is said *asarir al-wajh* (the creases of the face), meaning the places where happiness appears.

This has already been explained. The *fa'* (so) indicates that the rejoicing follows from what precedes it.

The meaning is: show happiness over this bargain which you have made with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for you have profited from it a profit that no one among people has gained except one who does the same as you have done. The reference of *dhalika* (that) is either to Paradise, or to the very bargain in which they profited Paradise. Describing the triumph, which is attaining what is sought, as great indicates that it is a triumph with no equal.

His words ﴿the repentant﴾ are the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are the repentant, that is, the believers. *Al-ta'ib* (the repentant) means the one who returns, that is, they are those who return to obedience to Allah from a state contrary to obedience.

Al-Zajjaj said: In my view, His words ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ are in the nominative as a subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is implied, meaning: the repentant and those after them up to the end of the verse have Paradise too, even if they did not fight. He said: This is better, for if these were attributes of the believers mentioned in His words ﴿He has bought from the believers﴾, the promise would be specific to fighters.

A group of commentators held the view of al-Zajjaj, that this statement is separate from what precedes it. Others held that these attributes refer back to the believers in the first verse, and that they are in the form of a condition, meaning: none is entitled to Paradise by that bargain except one who is among the believers possessing these attributes.

In the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, the reading is: "the repentant, the worshippers" to the end of the verse.

On this there are two views. One: they are attributes of the believers. Two: the accusative is in the sense of praise.

It has been said that these attributes are in the nominative as substitutions (*badal*) for the pronoun in *yuqatilun* (they fight). The author of al-Kashshaf permitted that *al-ta'ibun* be the subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is *al-'abiduna* (the worshippers), and what follows are predicates in the same manner, meaning: the repentant from disbelief in truth, combining these qualities. There is much remoteness in this, as is clear. *Al-'abidun* (the worshippers) are those who perform what they were commanded of worshipping Allah with sincerity. *Al-hamidun* (the praisers) are those who praise Allah, glorified is He, in ease and in hardship. *Al-sa'ihun* (the travellers/fasters): it has been said they are those who fast, and this is the view of the majority of commentators, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿worshipping, traveling women﴾ (66:5). It is said that the fasting person is a *sa'ih* (traveller) because he abstains from pleasures just as the traveller in the land abstains from them. From this is the saying of Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib:

*And by the travellers, who do not taste the breaking of the fast*
*for their Lord, and by those who ride the laboring camels.*

Another said:

*You see him praying his night and his day,*
*ever abundant in the remembrance of Allah, a traveller.*

Al-Zajjaj said: The view of al-Hasan is that the *sa'ihun* here are those who fast the obligatory fast. It was also said they are those who persist in fasting.

Ata' said: The *sa'ihun* are the fighters.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: The *sa'ihun* are the emigrants.

Ikrimah said: They are those who travel in search of hadith and knowledge.

It was said: They are those who roam in their thoughts over the oneness of their Lord, His dominion, and the lessons in what He has created.

The linguistic basis of *al-siyahah* (travelling) is going over the surface of the earth as water flows. It is among the things that help the servant in obedience, because he is cut off from creation and gains reflection by contemplating the creatures of Allah, glorified is He. ﴿Those who bow and prostrate﴾ means those who pray. ﴿Those who enjoin good﴾ are those who take charge of people in what is recognized as good in the law [p. 602] ﴿and forbid evil﴾ are those who stand against whoever does an evil, that is, something the law forbids. ﴿And those who guard the limits of Allah﴾ are those who keep the laws He sent down in His books and through His messengers. He placed the conjunction *wa* (and) before the last two attributes, namely ﴿and those who forbid evil and those who guard﴾, etc., because enjoining good and forbidding evil are like one characteristic, and then He joined *al-hafizun* (the guardians) to it with *wa* because of its closeness. It was said that conjunction among attributes comes with *wa* and without it, as in His saying: ﴿Forgiver of sin, Acceptor of repentance, severe in punishment﴾ (40:3). It was said that the *wa* is superfluous. It was said it is the well-known "*wa* of the eight" among grammarians, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿thayyibat wa abkaran (matrons and virgins)﴾ (66:5), and His saying: ﴿and its gates were opened﴾ (39:73), and His saying: ﴿seven, and the eighth is their dog﴾ (18:22). Abu Ali al-Farisi denied the "*wa* of the eight," and Ibn Khalawayh debated him on this. ﴿And give good news to the believers﴾, those described by the qualities mentioned before.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and others, who said: Abdullah ibn Rawahah said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Stipulate for your Lord and for yourself whatever you wish." He said: "I stipulate for my Lord that you worship Him and associate nothing with Him, and I stipulate for myself that you protect me from what you protect yourselves and your wealth from." They said: "If we do that, what will we have?" He said: "Paradise." They said: "The bargain has profited; we will neither cancel it nor ask to cancel it." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah has bought from the believers their souls﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "This verse was revealed upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in the mosque: ﴿Indeed, Allah has bought from the believers their souls﴾. So the people shouted *takbir* in the mosque. A man of the Ansar came forward, holding the two ends of his cloak over his shoulder, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, has this verse been revealed?' He said: 'Yes.' The Ansari said: 'A profitable bargain; we will neither cancel it nor ask to cancel it.'"

Ibn Sa'd narrated from Ubadah ibn al-Samit that the Prophet (ﷺ) stipulated at the Pledge of al-Aqabah with those among the Ansar who pledged to him: that they bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that he is the Messenger of Allah, that they establish prayer, give zakat, hear and obey, not dispute the command with its people, and protect him from what they protect themselves and their families from. They said: "Yes." A speaker among the Ansar said: "Yes, this is for you, O Messenger of Allah. What will we have?" He said: "Paradise."

Ibn Sa'd also narrated it through another channel, but there is nothing in the story of al-Aqabah indicating that it was the occasion of the revelation of the verse.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Whoever dies upon these nine is in the way of Allah: ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The martyr is one who possesses the nine qualities mentioned in this verse.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him: The worshippers are those who establish prayer.

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from him also, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first to be called to Paradise are the praisers, those who praise Allah in ease and in hardship."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ubayd ibn Umayr, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the *sa'ihun*, and he said: They are the fasters."

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated through the channel of Ubayd ibn Umayr, from Abu Hurayrah, similarly as a raised report (marfu').

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn al-Najjar narrated through the channel of Abu Salih from Abu Hurayrah, similarly as a raised report.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, similarly as a raised report.

It has also been related from Abu Hurayrah as a statement of his own (mawquf), and that is more authentic than the raised version through his channel. The hadith of Ubayd ibn Umayr is mursal (its chain omits a companion), though he traced it back through Abu Hurayrah in the second narration.

Similar statements have been related from a group of Companions: among them Aishah according to Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir; among them Ibn Abbas according to Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh; and among them Ibn Mas'ud according to those mentioned before. Similar things have also been related from a group of the Successors.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Umamah that "a man asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to travel (*siyahah*), and he said: 'The travelling of my community is jihad in the way of Allah.'" Abd al-Haqq authenticated it.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Rabi' concerning this verse, who said: "These are deeds about which the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: Allah decreed for Himself in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an for this community that whoever of them is killed while doing these deeds is a martyr with Allah, and whoever dies upon them, his reward is due from Allah."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The martyr is one who, if he died upon his bed, would enter Paradise."

He said: Ibn 'Abbas said, "Whoever dies with nine (of these qualities) in him is a martyr," and he recited this verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾, that it means "with Paradise." Then He said ﴿those who repent, who worship, who praise...﴾ up to His saying ﴿and those who observe the limits set by Allah﴾. He means: those who are steadfast in obedience to Allah. This is a condition that Allah stipulated for the people of jihad (struggle in the way of Allah). When they fulfil to Allah His condition, He fulfils to them their condition.

[p. 601]

The author of al-Kashshaf permitted that *al-ta'ibun* be the subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is *al-'abiduna* (the worshippers), and what follows are predicates in the same manner, meaning: the repentant from disbelief in truth, combining these qualities. There is much remoteness in this, as is clear. *Al-'abidun* (the worshippers) are those who perform what they were commanded of worshipping Allah with sincerity. *Al-hamidun* (the praisers) are those who praise Allah, glorified is He, in ease and in hardship. *Al-sa'ihun* (the travellers/fasters): it has been said they are those who fast, and this is the view of the majority of commentators, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿worshipping, traveling women﴾ (66:5). It is said that the fasting person is a *sa'ih* (traveller) because he abstains from pleasures just as the traveller in the land abstains from them. From this is the saying of Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib:

*And by the travellers, who do not taste the breaking of the fast*
*for their Lord, and by those who ride the laboring camels.*

Another said:

*You see him praying his night and his day,*
*ever abundant in the remembrance of Allah, a traveller.*

Al-Zajjaj said: The view of al-Hasan is that the *sa'ihun* here are those who fast the obligatory fast. It was also said they are those who persist in fasting.

Ata' said: The *sa'ihun* are the fighters.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: The *sa'ihun* are the emigrants.

Ikrimah said: They are those who travel in search of hadith and knowledge.

It was said: They are those who roam in their thoughts over the oneness of their Lord, His dominion, and the lessons in what He has created.

The linguistic basis of *al-siyahah* (travelling) is going over the surface of the earth as water flows. It is among the things that help the servant in obedience, because he is cut off from creation and gains reflection by contemplating the creatures of Allah, glorified is He. ﴿Those who bow and prostrate﴾ means those who pray. ﴿Those who enjoin good﴾ are those who take charge of people in what is recognized as good in the law [p. 602] ﴿and forbid evil﴾ are those who stand against whoever does an evil, that is, something the law forbids. ﴿And those who guard the limits of Allah﴾ are those who keep the laws He sent down in His books and through His messengers. He placed the conjunction *wa* (and) before the last two attributes, namely ﴿and those who forbid evil and those who guard﴾, etc., because enjoining good and forbidding evil are like one characteristic, and then He joined *al-hafizun* (the guardians) to it with *wa* because of its closeness. It was said that conjunction among attributes comes with *wa* and without it, as in His saying: ﴿Forgiver of sin, Acceptor of repentance, severe in punishment﴾ (40:3). It was said that the *wa* is superfluous. It was said it is the well-known "*wa* of the eight" among grammarians, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿thayyibat wa abkaran (matrons and virgins)﴾ (66:5), and His saying: ﴿and its gates were opened﴾ (39:73), and His saying: ﴿seven, and the eighth is their dog﴾ (18:22). Abu Ali al-Farisi denied the "*wa* of the eight," and Ibn Khalawayh debated him on this. ﴿And give good news to the believers﴾, those described by the qualities mentioned before.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and others, who said: Abdullah ibn Rawahah said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Stipulate for your Lord and for yourself whatever you wish." He said: "I stipulate for my Lord that you worship Him and associate nothing with Him, and I stipulate for myself that you protect me from what you protect yourselves and your wealth from." They said: "If we do that, what will we have?" He said: "Paradise." They said: "The bargain has profited; we will neither cancel it nor ask to cancel it." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah has bought from the believers their souls﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "This verse was revealed upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in the mosque: ﴿Indeed, Allah has bought from the believers their souls﴾. So the people shouted *takbir* in the mosque. A man of the Ansar came forward, holding the two ends of his cloak over his shoulder, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, has this verse been revealed?' He said: 'Yes.' The Ansari said: 'A profitable bargain; we will neither cancel it nor ask to cancel it.'"

Ibn Sa'd narrated from Ubadah ibn al-Samit that the Prophet (ﷺ) stipulated at the Pledge of al-Aqabah with those among the Ansar who pledged to him: that they bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that he is the Messenger of Allah, that they establish prayer, give zakat, hear and obey, not dispute the command with its people, and protect him from what they protect themselves and their families from. They said: "Yes." A speaker among the Ansar said: "Yes, this is for you, O Messenger of Allah. What will we have?" He said: "Paradise."

Ibn Sa'd also narrated it through another channel, but there is nothing in the story of al-Aqabah indicating that it was the occasion of the revelation of the verse.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Whoever dies upon these nine is in the way of Allah: ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The martyr is one who possesses the nine qualities mentioned in this verse.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him: The worshippers are those who establish prayer.

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from him also, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first to be called to Paradise are the praisers, those who praise Allah in ease and in hardship."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ubayd ibn Umayr, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the *sa'ihun*, and he said: They are the fasters."

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated through the channel of Ubayd ibn Umayr, from Abu Hurayrah, similarly as a raised report (marfu').

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn al-Najjar narrated through the channel of Abu Salih from Abu Hurayrah, similarly as a raised report.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, similarly as a raised report.

It has also been related from Abu Hurayrah as a statement of his own (mawquf), and that is more authentic than the raised version through his channel. The hadith of Ubayd ibn Umayr is mursal (its chain omits a companion), though he traced it back through Abu Hurayrah in the second narration.

Similar statements have been related from a group of Companions: among them Aishah according to Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir; among them Ibn Abbas according to Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh; and among them Ibn Mas'ud according to those mentioned before. Similar things have also been related from a group of the Successors.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Umamah that "a man asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to travel (*siyahah*), and he said: 'The travelling of my community is jihad in the way of Allah.'" Abd al-Haqq authenticated it.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Rabi' concerning this verse, who said: "These are deeds about which the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: Allah decreed for Himself in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an for this community that whoever of them is killed while doing these deeds is a martyr with Allah, and whoever dies upon them, his reward is due from Allah."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The martyr is one who, if he died upon his bed, would enter Paradise."

He said: Ibn 'Abbas said, "Whoever dies with nine (of these qualities) in him is a martyr," and he recited this verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾, that it means "with Paradise." Then He said ﴿those who repent, who worship, who praise...﴾ up to His saying ﴿and those who observe the limits set by Allah﴾. He means: those who are steadfast in obedience to Allah. This is a condition that Allah stipulated for the people of jihad (struggle in the way of Allah). When they fulfil to Allah His condition, He fulfils to them their condition.

When Allah, glorified is He, made clear at the beginning of the surah and what follows it that disavowal (al-bara'ah) from the polytheists (mushrikun) and the hypocrites (munafiqun) is obligatory, He here clarified what further confirms this, and stated explicitly that it is binding, even if they were of close kinship (ulu qurba), and that kinship has no effect in a ruling of this kind.

The people of tafsir (exegesis) have mentioned that *ma kana* (لَمْ يَكُنْ, "it was not" / "it is not for") in the Qur'an comes in two ways. The first is as negation, like ﴿It is not for any soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 145].

The second is in the sense of prohibition, like ﴿It is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53], and ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists﴾. This verse includes the severing of allegiance (muwalah) to the disbelievers, the prohibition of seeking forgiveness for them, and supplicating for them with what is not permissible for one who is a disbeliever.

This is not contradicted by what is established from him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, in the Sahih (authentic collection) that he said on the day of Uhud, when the polytheists broke his front tooth and wounded his face: "O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know." This is because it is possible that this was before the prohibition of seeking forgiveness for the polytheists had reached him. And even if it had reached him, as the occasion of revelation suggests, it was a long time before the day of Uhud, and it will come. Therefore, his utterance of this supplication for his people was only by way of narrating about the prophets before him, as in Sahih Muslim, from 'Abd Allah, who said: "It is as if I am looking at the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, relating about a prophet among the prophets whose people struck him, while he was wiping the blood from his face and saying: 'My Lord, forgive my people, for they do not know.'"

In al-Bukhari: "The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, mentioned a prophet before him whose people had wounded him, and the Prophet began to report about him that he said: 'O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know.'"

His words, ﴿after it has become clear to them that they are the companions of the Hellfire﴾: this clause contains the reason for the prohibition of seeking forgiveness.

The meaning: this clarity necessitates severing allegiance to whoever is like this, and not giving weight to kinship, because they died in polytheism.

Allah, glorified is He, has said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [an-Nisa': 116]. So seeking forgiveness for them is in the category of opposing the promise and threat of Allah.

His words, ﴿And the istighfar (seeking forgiveness) of Ibrahim for his father was not except because of a promise he had made to him﴾, up to the end of the verse: Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the cause of Ibrahim's seeking forgiveness for his father: it was because of a promise that Ibrahim had made to his father to seek forgiveness for him. But he abandoned that and disowned him when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah and was not deserving of forgiveness. This indicates that he had only promised him before it became clear to him that he was among the people of the Fire and among the enemies of Allah. So there is no need for the question that many exegetes raise, namely how this was hidden from Ibrahim. For the prohibition of seeking forgiveness for one who persists in disbelief and dies upon it was not hidden from him, and he only knew it by Allah's informing him that he was an enemy of Allah, for the establishment of this enmity indicates disbelief. Likewise, our Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, did not know of the prohibition of that except after Allah informed him with this verse. And this is a ruling that is established only by revelation (sam') and not by reason ('aql).

It has been said: the intended meaning of Ibrahim's seeking forgiveness for his father is his calling him to Islam, but this is very weak.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "istighfar" in this verse is the prohibition of praying over the funerals of disbelievers, so it is like His saying: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died ever﴾ [at-Tawbah: 84]. There is no need to interpret istighfar as salat (prayer), and there is no compulsion to do so. Then Allah, glorified is He, concluded this verse with a great praise of Ibrahim, saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was awwah (plaintive/tender-hearted)﴾, and he is one who frequently utters "awwah," as the intensive form indicates.

The people of knowledge have differed about the meaning of *awwah*. Ibn Mas'ud and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: it is one who frequently supplicates.

al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it is one who is merciful to the servants of Allah.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that it means the believer, in the language of Abyssinia (al-Habashah).

al-Kalbi said: it is one who mentions Allah in a barren land.

The same is related from Ibn al-Musayyab. It has been said: it is one who frequently remembers Allah without restriction, related from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir.

It has been said: it is one who frequently recites, related from Ibn 'Abbas.

It has been said: it is the jurist (faqih), said by Mujahid and al-Nakha'i.

It has been said: it is the humble one, submissive, related from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Hadd.

It has been said: it is one who, when he mentions his sins, seeks forgiveness for them, related from Abu Ayyub.

It has been said: it is the compassionate one, said by 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya.

And he said: it is the one who teaches good.

It has been said: it is the one who turns back from everything that Allah dislikes, said by 'Ata'.

What corresponds to the meaning of *awwah* linguistically is that it is said to be one who frequently utters "ah" (ta'awwuh) over his sins, so he says, for example: "Ah, because of my sins! Ah, because of what I am punished for on account of them," and similar. This was said by al-Farra', and it is related from Abu Dharr. The meaning of *ta'awwuh* is that a sound is heard from the chest from the exhalation of a sigh (su'ada').

In al-Sihah (the lexicon) it says: the man has "awwa" (tā'wīh) and "ta'awwa" (ta'awwuh) when he says "awh," and the noun from it is "ah'ah" with a long vowel. He said:

*When I rise to saddle her in the night, she sighs the sigh of a sorrowful man.*

And *halim* (ﺣَﻠِﻴﻢ, forbearing) is one who has much forbearance, as the intensive form indicates. He is one who pardons sins and bears patiently with harm. It has been said: he is one who never punishes anyone except for the sake of Allah.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others have related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from his father, who said: "When death approached Abu Talib, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, entered while Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah were with him. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, so I may plead for you with it before Allah.' Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah said: 'O Abu Talib, will you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?' The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, kept presenting it to him, while Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah kept opposing him with that statement. Abu Talib said, as the last thing he said to them: 'He is upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib,' and he refused to say: 'There is no god but Allah.' The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'I will surely seek forgiveness for you as long as I am not prohibited from you.' So the verse was revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet…﴾, up to the end of the verse, and Allah revealed about Abu Talib: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from 'Ali, who said: "I heard a man seeking forgiveness for his parents while they were polytheists. I said: 'You seek forgiveness for your parents while they are polytheists?' He said: 'Did not Ibrahim seek forgiveness for his father?' I mentioned that to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and so the verse was revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet…﴾, up to the end of the verse."

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn 'Asakir related from 'Ali, who said: "I informed the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, of the death of Abu Talib, and he wept, and said: 'Go and wash him, shroud him, and bury him. May Allah forgive him and have mercy upon him.' I did so. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, kept seeking forgiveness for him for days, and he did not leave his house until there was revealed to him: ﴿It is not for the Prophet…﴾, up to the end of the verse."

It has been related that the cause of the revelation of the verse was the Prophet's, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, seeking forgiveness for Abu Talib, from many chains: among them from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, in Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh, and it is *mursal* (a narration in which the Companion is omitted). Among them from 'Amr ibn Dinar, in Ibn Jarir, and it is also *mursal*. Among them from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, in Ibn Jarir, and it is also *mursal*. Among them from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, in Ibn Sa'd, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn 'Asakir. Among them from al-Hasan al-Basri in Ibn 'Asakir, and it is *mursal*.

It has also been related that it was revealed because of the Prophet's, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, visiting the grave of his mother and seeking forgiveness for her, through the route of Ibn 'Abbas in al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh, and through the route of Ibn Mas'ud in Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and from Buraydah in Ibn Mardawayh. What is in the two Sahihs takes precedence over what is not in them, on the assumption that it is authentic, so how much more so when most of it is weak.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ up to His saying: ﴿as they raised me when I was small﴾ [al-Isra': 23–24], that he said: "Then He made an exception, saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet…﴾, up to His saying: ﴿except for a promise he had made to him﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿And when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah﴾, that he said: "It became clear to him when he died, and he knew that repentance had been cut off from him."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Abu Bakr al-Shafi'i in his Fawa'id, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Ibrahim kept seeking forgiveness for his father until he died. When he died, it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, so he disowned him."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir that "a man used to raise his voice in remembrance (dhikr), and a man said: 'If only this one would lower his voice!' The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'Leave him, for he is an awwah.'"

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir that "the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to a man called Dhu al-Nijadayn: 'He is an awwah,'" and that was because he used to frequently remember Allah by means of the Qur'an and supplication.

Ahmad also related it, saying: "Musa ibn Lahi'ah narrated to us, from al-Harith ibn Yazid, from 'Ali ibn Rabah, from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir," and he mentioned it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Hadd, who said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the awwah?' He said: 'The humble one, the submissive one, the one who supplicates much.'"

If this is established, it must be adhered to and given precedence over what the lexicographers have said about the meaning of *awwah*. Its chain in Ibn Jarir is as follows: "al-Muthanna narrated to me, al-Hajjaj ibn Minhal narrated to me, 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Bahram narrated to us, Shahr ibn Hawshab narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad," and he mentioned it.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was awwah, forbearing﴾, that he said: "It was of his forbearance that when a man of his people harmed him, he would say to him: 'May Allah guide you.'"

And *halim* (ﺣَﻠِﻴﻢ, forbearing) is one who has much forbearance, as the intensive form indicates. He is one who pardons sins and bears patiently with harm. It has been said: he is one who never punishes anyone except for the sake of Allah.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others have related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from his father, who said: "When death approached Abu Talib, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, entered while Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah were with him. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, so I may plead for you with it before Allah.' Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah said: 'O Abu Talib, will you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?' The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, kept presenting it to him, while Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah kept opposing him with that statement. Abu Talib said, as the last thing he said to them: 'He is upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib,' and he refused to say: 'There is no god but Allah.' The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'I will surely seek forgiveness for you as long as I am not prohibited from you.' So the verse was revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet…﴾, up to the end of the verse, and Allah revealed about Abu Talib: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from 'Ali, who said: "I heard a man seeking forgiveness for his parents while they were polytheists. I said: 'You seek forgiveness for your parents while they are polytheists?' He said: 'Did not Ibrahim seek forgiveness for his father?' I mentioned that to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and so the verse was revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet…﴾, up to the end of the verse."

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn 'Asakir related from 'Ali, who said: "I informed the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, of the death of Abu Talib, and he wept, and said: 'Go and wash him, shroud him, and bury him. May Allah forgive him and have mercy upon him.' I did so. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, kept seeking forgiveness for him for days, and he did not leave his house until there was revealed to him: ﴿It is not for the Prophet…﴾, up to the end of the verse."

It has been related that the cause of the revelation of the verse was the Prophet's, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, seeking forgiveness for Abu Talib, from many chains: among them from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, in Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh, and it is *mursal* (a narration in which the Companion is omitted). Among them from 'Amr ibn Dinar, in Ibn Jarir, and it is also *mursal*. Among them from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, in Ibn Jarir, and it is also *mursal*. Among them from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, in Ibn Sa'd, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn 'Asakir. Among them from al-Hasan al-Basri in Ibn 'Asakir, and it is *mursal*.

It has also been related that it was revealed because of the Prophet's, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, visiting the grave of his mother and seeking forgiveness for her, through the route of Ibn 'Abbas in al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh, and through the route of Ibn Mas'ud in Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and from Buraydah in Ibn Mardawayh. What is in the two Sahihs takes precedence over what is not in them, on the assumption that it is authentic, so how much more so when most of it is weak.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ up to His saying: ﴿as they raised me when I was small﴾ [al-Isra': 23–24], that he said: "Then He made an exception, saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet…﴾, up to His saying: ﴿except for a promise he had made to him﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿And when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah﴾, that he said: "It became clear to him when he died, and he knew that repentance had been cut off from him."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Abu Bakr al-Shafi'i in his Fawa'id, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Ibrahim kept seeking forgiveness for his father until he died. When he died, it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, so he disowned him."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir that "a man used to raise his voice in remembrance (dhikr), and a man said: 'If only this one would lower his voice!' The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'Leave him, for he is an awwah.'"

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir that "the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to a man called Dhu al-Nijadayn: 'He is an awwah,'" and that was because he used to frequently remember Allah by means of the Qur'an and supplication.

Ahmad also related it, saying: "Musa ibn Lahi'ah narrated to us, from al-Harith ibn Yazid, from 'Ali ibn Rabah, from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir," and he mentioned it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Hadd, who said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the awwah?' He said: 'The humble one, the submissive one, the one who supplicates much.'"

If this is established, it must be adhered to and given precedence over what the lexicographers have said about the meaning of *awwah*. Its chain in Ibn Jarir is as follows: "al-Muthanna narrated to me, al-Hajjaj ibn Minhal narrated to me, 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Bahram narrated to us, Shahr ibn Hawshab narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad," and he mentioned it.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was awwah, forbearing﴾, that he said: "It was of his forbearance that when a man of his people harmed him, he would say to him: 'May Allah guide you.'"

When the preceding verse was revealed, forbidding seeking forgiveness for the polytheists, a group of those who had been seeking forgiveness for them feared punishment from God because of that seeking of forgiveness. So God, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿And God would not send astray a people after He has guided them﴾, and so on. That is: God, glorified is He, does not bring misguidance upon a people, nor does He call them misguided after He has guided them to Islam and to the observance of its laws, so long as they do not commit any of the prohibited acts after it has become clear to them that it is prohibited. Before it has become clear to them, there is no sin upon them and they are not held accountable for it. The meaning of ﴿until He makes clear to them what they should avoid﴾ is: until it becomes clear to them what they are obligated to avoid of the prohibitions of the Law. ﴿Indeed, God is All-Knowing of everything﴾: of what is lawful and unlawful for His servants, and of all the other things He has created.

﴿Indeed, to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. And you have, besides God, no protector or helper.﴾ Then He made clear to them that dominion over the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, glorified is He, and no partner shares in it with Him, and no disputer contends with Him. He disposes of His dominion as He wills, among those dispositions being that He gives life to whom His will decrees life, and causes death to whom His will decrees death. And for His servants, besides Him, there is no protector who befriends them, nor a helper who supports them. So they should not seek forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were of near kin, for kinship does not benefit at all nor have any effect; rather, the disposal of all things belongs to God alone.

His saying: ﴿Certainly God has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾ refers to what he (ﷺ) had done of granting permission to remain behind, or to what he had done of seeking forgiveness for the polytheists. It is not a necessary condition of repentance that a sin should precede it from the one who repents or on whose behalf it is made, because all the servants are in need of repentance and seeking forgiveness. The repentance of God toward the Prophet may be of the category that he left what was preferable and more fitting, as in His saying: ﴿God pardon you; why did you grant them permission?﴾. It is also possible that the mention of the Prophet (ﷺ) is for the sake of instructing sinners, so that they avoid sins and repent of what they have become involved in. Likewise, God, glorified is He, turned in forgiveness to the Emigrants and the Helpers regarding the sins they had committed.

Of this kind is what is authentically reported from him (ﷺ), that he said: "God looked upon the people of Badr and said: 'Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you.'" Then God, glorified is He, described the Emigrants and the Helpers as those ﴿who followed the Prophet﴾, so they did not remain behind from him. The ﴿hour of hardship﴾ is the expedition of Tabuk, for they were in severe hardship. So what is meant by "the hour" is all the times of that campaign, and not one specific hour. ﴿Hardship﴾ means difficulty of the matter.

His saying: ﴿After the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved﴾. In kāda there is a dummy pronoun (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and "qulūb" (hearts) is in the nominative, being the subject of "tazīgh" (swerve), according to Sibawayh. It is also said that it is in the nominative by "kāda", and the sense would be: "after the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved."

Al-A'mash, Hamzah and Hafs read "yazīgh" with the yā' (third person masculine form).

Abu Hatim said: Whoever reads with the yā' cannot take "al-qulūb" as the subject of kāda.

Al-Nahhas said: What he (Abu Hatim) disallowed is permitted according to others, on the basis of the masculine form for a plural. The meaning of "tazīgh" is that they would be destroyed through exertion, hardship and severity. It is also said that its meaning is: they would incline away from the truth and abandon support and resistance. It is also said that its meaning is: they were resolved to remain behind from the campaign because of the great severity they were in.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, it is "min ba'di mā zāghat" (after they had swerved). According to this reading, those are the ones who remained behind. The repetition of the repentance toward them in His saying: ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness that they might repent﴾ is a clear emphasis and attention to its matter. This holds if the pronoun refers to those whose repentance was mentioned earlier. If the pronoun refers to the group, then there is no repetition.

His saying: ﴿And [He turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind﴾: that is, He turned in forgiveness to the three who were left behind, meaning deferred, and their repentance was not accepted immediately as the repentance of those remaining behind mentioned earlier had been accepted.

Ibn Jarir said: The meaning of "khullifū" is "left," as one says: "I left so-and-so," meaning I separated from him.

ʿIkrimah ibn Khalid read "khulifū" with the short vowel, meaning: they remained after the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers had set out for the campaign.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad read "khālafū" (they opposed). These three were Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn al-Rabi' or Ibn Rabi'ah al-'Amiri, and Hilal ibn Umayyah al-Waqifi, all of them from the Helpers. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not accept their repentance until the Qur'an was revealed that God had turned in forgiveness to them. It is also said that the meaning of "khullifū" is: they became corrupt, derived from "khulūf al-fam" (bad breath of the mouth).

His saying: ﴿Until, when the earth became constricted for them despite its vastness﴾: its meaning is that they were deferred from acceptance of repentance until this limit, which is the time when the earth became constricted for them despite its vastness. "Mā" here is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah): that is, "with its vastness." This was because people turned away from them and did not speak with them, from everyone, for the Prophet (ﷺ) had forbidden people from speaking with them. "Al-rahb" means wide, as one says: "manzil rahb" and "raḥīb" and "rihāb" (a spacious dwelling).

In this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of shunning people of sins as a discipline for them, so that they may desist from sins.

The meaning of "the constriction of their souls upon them" is that their hearts became constricted by the loneliness that befell them and the estrangement that resulted for them. In His saying: ﴿And they knew that there is no refuge from God except in Him﴾, the word "ẓann" (thought/assumption) is used to mean knowledge: that is, they knew that there was no refuge at all to which they could flee except God, glorified is He, through repentance and seeking forgiveness.

His saying: ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness that they might repent﴾: that is, He returned to them with acceptance and mercy, and sent down in the Qur'an the repentance upon them, so that they might be upright, or He enabled them to repent for whatever in the future time they might commit of error, so that they would repent of it, return to God regarding it, and feel remorse for what had occurred from them. ﴿Indeed, God is the Accepting of repentance﴾, that is, the Greatly Accepting of the repentance of those who repent, ﴿the Merciful﴾, that is, the Greatly Merciful to whoever of His servants seeks it.

His saying: ﴿And be with the truthful﴾. This command to be with the truthful, after the story of the three, contains an indication that these three attained through truthfulness what they attained of God's repentance. The apparent meaning of the verse is a command to the servants in general.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And God would not send astray a people after He has guided them﴾, that he said: It was revealed when they took ransom from the polytheists on the day of the captives.

He said: It was not permitted for you to take it until you were given permission. But God would not punish a people for a sin they had committed ﴿until He makes clear to them what they should avoid﴾. He said: until He forbids them before that.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding the verse that he said: It is God's clarification to the believers concerning seeking forgiveness for the polytheists specifically, and in His clarification of His obedience and disobedience generally, whether they did or abstained.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, al-Bayhaqi and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab: "Tell us about the matter of the hour of hardship." He said: "We set out with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to Tabuk in intense heat. We stopped at a station, and we were struck there by thirst until we thought our necks would be cut off. So much so that a man would slaughter his camel, squeeze its dung and drink it, and put what remained on his liver. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said: 'O Messenger of God, indeed God has accustomed you to good in supplication, so supplicate for us.' He raised his hands and did not lower them until the sky spoke, then it poured heavily and then it flowed. They filled what they had with them, then we went to look and we did not find that it had passed beyond the army."

It is agreed among the narrators that the hour of hardship is the expedition of Tabuk.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mandah, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah regarding His saying: ﴿And [He turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind﴾ that he said: They were Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayyah and Murarah ibn al-Rabi', and all of them were from the Helpers.

Ibn Mandah and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported "from Ka'b ibn Malik who said: I never remained behind from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in any campaign he undertook, except the campaign of Tabuk. Except that I had remained behind in the campaign of Badr, and he did not reproach anyone who remained behind from it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out seeking the caravan of Quraysh, until God brought them together with their enemy without prior appointment. And I witnessed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) the night of ʿAqabah, when we agreed together upon Islam, and I would not love to have it in exchange for the battle of Badr, though Badr is more remembered among people and more famous." Then he mentioned the long story well known in the books of hadith and biography, which is known to the people of knowledge, so we will not lengthen by mentioning it.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying: ﴿And [He turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind﴾, that he said: It means they were left behind from repentance; it was not accepted from them when God accepted the repentance of Abu Lubabah and his companions.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from ʿIkrimah something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Nafi' regarding His saying: ﴿And be with the truthful﴾ that he said: It was revealed concerning the three who were left behind. It was said to them: "Be with Muhammad and his companions."

Ibn Jarir reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿And be with the truthful﴾ that he said: "With Abu Bakr and ʿUmar."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from al-Dahhak regarding the verse that he said: "With Abu Bakr and ʿUmar and their companions."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "With ʿAli ibn Abi Talib."

Ibn ʿAsakir reported from Abu Ja'far who said: "With the three who were left behind."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported "from Ka'b ibn Malik who said: I never remained behind from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in any campaign he undertook, except the campaign of Tabuk. Except that I had remained behind in the campaign of Badr, and he did not reproach anyone who remained behind from it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out seeking the caravan of Quraysh, until God brought them together with their enemy without prior appointment. And I witnessed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) the night of ʿAqabah, when we agreed together upon Islam, and I would not love to have it in exchange for the battle of Badr, though Badr is more remembered among people and more famous." Then he mentioned the long story well known in the books of hadith and biography, which is known to the people of knowledge, so we will not lengthen by mentioning it.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying: ﴿And [He turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind﴾, that he said: It means they were left behind from repentance; it was not accepted from them when God accepted the repentance of Abu Lubabah and his companions.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from ʿIkrimah something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Nafi' regarding His saying: ﴿And be with the truthful﴾ that he said: It was revealed concerning the three who were left behind. It was said to them: "Be with Muhammad and his companions."

Ibn Jarir reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿And be with the truthful﴾ that he said: "With Abu Bakr and ʿUmar."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from al-Dahhak regarding the verse that he said: "With Abu Bakr and ʿUmar and their companions."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "With ʿAli ibn Abi Talib."

Ibn ʿAsakir reported from Abu Ja'far who said: "With the three who were left behind."

When the preceding verse was revealed, forbidding seeking forgiveness for the polytheists, a group of those who had been seeking forgiveness for them feared punishment from God because of that seeking of forgiveness. So God, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿And God would not send astray a people after He has guided them﴾, and so on. That is: God, glorified is He, does not bring misguidance upon a people, nor does He call them misguided after He has guided them to Islam and to the observance of its laws, so long as they do not commit any of the prohibited acts after it has become clear to them that it is prohibited. Before it has become clear to them, there is no sin upon them and they are not held accountable for it. The meaning of ﴿until He makes clear to them what they should avoid﴾ is: until it becomes clear to them what they are obligated to avoid of the prohibitions of the Law. ﴿Indeed, God is All-Knowing of everything﴾: of what is lawful and unlawful for His servants, and of all the other things He has created.

﴿Indeed, to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. And you have, besides God, no protector or helper.﴾ Then He made clear to them that dominion over the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, glorified is He, and no partner shares in it with Him, and no disputer contends with Him. He disposes of His dominion as He wills, among those dispositions being that He gives life to whom His will decrees life, and causes death to whom His will decrees death. And for His servants, besides Him, there is no protector who befriends them, nor a helper who supports them. So they should not seek forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were of near kin, for kinship does not benefit at all nor have any effect; rather, the disposal of all things belongs to God alone.

His saying: ﴿Certainly God has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾ refers to what he (ﷺ) had done of granting permission to remain behind, or to what he had done of seeking forgiveness for the polytheists. It is not a necessary condition of repentance that a sin should precede it from the one who repents or on whose behalf it is made, because all the servants are in need of repentance and seeking forgiveness. The repentance of God toward the Prophet may be of the category that he left what was preferable and more fitting, as in His saying: ﴿God pardon you; why did you grant them permission?﴾. It is also possible that the mention of the Prophet (ﷺ) is for the sake of instructing sinners, so that they avoid sins and repent of what they have become involved in. Likewise, God, glorified is He, turned in forgiveness to the Emigrants and the Helpers regarding the sins they had committed.

Of this kind is what is authentically reported from him (ﷺ), that he said: "God looked upon the people of Badr and said: 'Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you.'" Then God, glorified is He, described the Emigrants and the Helpers as those ﴿who followed the Prophet﴾, so they did not remain behind from him. The ﴿hour of hardship﴾ is the expedition of Tabuk, for they were in severe hardship. So what is meant by "the hour" is all the times of that campaign, and not one specific hour. ﴿Hardship﴾ means difficulty of the matter.

His saying: ﴿After the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved﴾. In kāda there is a dummy pronoun (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and "qulūb" (hearts) is in the nominative, being the subject of "tazīgh" (swerve), according to Sibawayh. It is also said that it is in the nominative by "kāda", and the sense would be: "after the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved."

Al-A'mash, Hamzah and Hafs read "yazīgh" with the yā' (third person masculine form).

Abu Hatim said: Whoever reads with the yā' cannot take "al-qulūb" as the subject of kāda.

Al-Nahhas said: What he (Abu Hatim) disallowed is permitted according to others, on the basis of the masculine form for a plural. The meaning of "tazīgh" is that they would be destroyed through exertion, hardship and severity. It is also said that its meaning is: they would incline away from the truth and abandon support and resistance. It is also said that its meaning is: they were resolved to remain behind from the campaign because of the great severity they were in.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, it is "min ba'di mā zāghat" (after they had swerved). According to this reading, those are the ones who remained behind. The repetition of the repentance toward them in His saying: ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness that they might repent﴾ is a clear emphasis and attention to its matter. This holds if the pronoun refers to those whose repentance was mentioned earlier. If the pronoun refers to the group, then there is no repetition.

His saying: ﴿And [He turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind﴾: that is, He turned in forgiveness to the three who were left behind, meaning deferred, and their repentance was not accepted immediately as the repentance of those remaining behind mentioned earlier had been accepted.

Ibn Jarir said: The meaning of "khullifū" is "left," as one says: "I left so-and-so," meaning I separated from him.

ʿIkrimah ibn Khalid read "khulifū" with the short vowel, meaning: they remained after the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers had set out for the campaign.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad read "khālafū" (they opposed). These three were Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn al-Rabi' or Ibn Rabi'ah al-'Amiri, and Hilal ibn Umayyah al-Waqifi, all of them from the Helpers. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not accept their repentance until the Qur'an was revealed that God had turned in forgiveness to them. It is also said that the meaning of "khullifū" is: they became corrupt, derived from "khulūf al-fam" (bad breath of the mouth).

His saying: ﴿Until, when the earth became constricted for them despite its vastness﴾: its meaning is that they were deferred from acceptance of repentance until this limit, which is the time when the earth became constricted for them despite its vastness. "Mā" here is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah): that is, "with its vastness." This was because people turned away from them and did not speak with them, from everyone, for the Prophet (ﷺ) had forbidden people from speaking with them. "Al-rahb" means wide, as one says: "manzil rahb" and "raḥīb" and "rihāb" (a spacious dwelling).

In this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of shunning people of sins as a discipline for them, so that they may desist from sins.

The meaning of "the constriction of their souls upon them" is that their hearts became constricted by the loneliness that befell them and the estrangement that resulted for them. In His saying: ﴿And they knew that there is no refuge from God except in Him﴾, the word "ẓann" (thought/assumption) is used to mean knowledge: that is, they knew that there was no refuge at all to which they could flee except God, glorified is He, through repentance and seeking forgiveness.

His saying: ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness that they might repent﴾: that is, He returned to them with acceptance and mercy, and sent down in the Qur'an the repentance upon them, so that they might be upright, or He enabled them to repent for whatever in the future time they might commit of error, so that they would repent of it, return to God regarding it, and feel remorse for what had occurred from them. ﴿Indeed, God is the Accepting of repentance﴾, that is, the Greatly Accepting of the repentance of those who repent, ﴿the Merciful﴾, that is, the Greatly Merciful to whoever of His servants seeks it.

His saying: ﴿And be with the truthful﴾. This command to be with the truthful, after the story of the three, contains an indication that these three attained through truthfulness what they attained of God's repentance. The apparent meaning of the verse is a command to the servants in general.

He said: It was not permitted for you to take it until you were given permission. But God would not punish a people for a sin they had committed ﴿until He makes clear to them what they should avoid﴾. He said: until He forbids them before that.

They filled what they had with them, then we went to look and we did not find that it had passed beyond the army."
